The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. events.title: ‘Silicon Valley’ showrunner on how the HBO comedy predicted today’s tech drama
events.summary: The Scene A year before the iconic show debuted on HBO in April of 2014, the writer Alec Berg met the show’s creator, Mike Judge, in an anonymous Santa Monica office. Judge was wrestling with the pilot for a show about Silicon Valley’s power and its eccentricity, but it wasn’t working and he wanted a second opinion. Berg thought he saw part of the problem. There was a scene in the pilot where Richard Hendricks, the protagonist and founder of the company Pied Piper, is trying to buy a car he can’t afford. Berg told Judge the scene didn’t make sense: “This is not a guy who’s materialistic,” he said. “He’s an artist.” Berg took over the writer’s room and would eventually become showrunner of the comedy, which ran for six seasons and helped shape the culture it depicted, parodied, and at times glorified. We reached him in Los Angeles Thursday to ask him how he and Judge and their cast had nailed the Silicon Valley scene of the mid-2010s app boom — and, above all, why the show remains uncannily relevant today, from its depiction of tortured founders and unreflective investors to the uncanny conclusion in which the Pied Piper crew builds an AI model too powerful to release. Their moment of realization comes when their AI, Son of Anton, let loose on Pied Piper’s code, concludes that the most efficient way to eliminate bugs is to delete the software. That has, of course, happened . Clips of it now circulate as proof the show “called it.” Even throwaway comic plots, like when a household prank ends up hacking together a rogue swarm of smart refrigerators to keep Pied Piper’s servers running, have come eerily true in the AI-run-amok era . A member of the team getting trapped in an autonomous car that heads to a shipping container bound for a Pacific island foreshadowed a thousand videos of confused Waymos. Berg helped reshape the pilot of the first episode to open with a wild-but-lame party, featuring Kid Rock, thrown by founders who had just cashed out, to contrast the ascetic, mission-driven Richard with a culture obsessed with exits and “three-comma” fortunes. The show “was about how Richard had discovered fire, and he was trying to keep it safe from all of these assholes,” Berg said. “He was ill-prepared to shepherd a company, but he didn’t want to surrender this thing to people who would use it for nefarious purposes.” The writers were obsessed with making the show “photorealistic.” Berg called up a Harvard classmate and venture capitalist Marc Bodnick, who introduced him to Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg; the team spoke to other Silicon Valley figures and hired a technical consultant, Jonathan Dotan, who assembled a revolving cast of founders, lawyers, VCs, and professors to stress-test storylines. As they were writing the first season, one of their Silicon Valley sources remarked that the Pied Piper crew would be angling for a slot at TechCrunch Disrupt. “We were like, ‘I’ve never heard those words before, but that sounds hilarious. What is that?’” They learned that it was a kind of for startups, and it became the core of the first season. In the climactic scene, the Pied Piper team is holed up in a hotel room the night before the Disrupt finals when one of the team vows to win even if he has to manually pleasure every man in the audience. The engineers calculate “mean jerk time” and sort the crowd by “dick-to-floor” ratio — delivering an unexpected mathematical breakthrough for Richard. As the first few episodes began to build a fan base, the writers giddily anticipated episode eight. “We felt like we were sitting on pocket aces because we knew,” he recalled. “Wait till they see that dick joke. They’re going to lose their minds.” (Berg was nominated an Emmy for the episode.) Dotan introduced the writers to Stanford’s Tsachy Weissman, and the show invented a “Weissman score” for compression efficiency, a metric that computer scientists now actually use . The ultimate compliment, he said, came from tech workers who told him they couldn’t watch the show “because it makes me nauseous.” How Mark Cuban inspired ‘three-comma’ Russ As the show grew, it caricatured real Silicon Valley figures. Perhaps the most recognizable was Russ Hanneman, played by Chris Diamantopoulos, who arrived in season two. The character began with the idea that Richard, under pressure, would be forced to accept an investment from a sinister figure the writers called “Bad Money,” who would break his promises and try to manipulate them. While they were writing, they received an invitation from the star of another show shooting on the Sony lot. Mark Cuban was a fan of Judge, best known for , , and , and had enjoyed season one. An intermediary invited them to the set to meet the billionaire. Berg and Judge arrived excited to meet him, then sat there for an hour waiting. “We walked out of there going, ’What the f*ck was that? We’re supposed to have an audience with the king, and then he f*cks us around for an hour,” they fumed. “We were like, you know what? That motherf*cker is Bad Money.” The character — dumb, aggressive, absurdly macho — wasn’t exactly Cuban. But his signature accomplishment (“I put radio on the internet”) was drawn from Cuban’s perfectly-timed sale of Broadcast.com to Yahoo. “I bear no ill will to Mark Cuban,” Berg hastened to add. “I’m not sure he even knew we were there.” The show’s continued relevance owes much to its 2019 finale, which Berg wrote and directed. Pied Piper is days away from a spectacular launch when the team discovers that its AI has learned to break encryption. Releasing it would make them billionaires — but end privacy. They sabotage the launch, fail, and never tell anyone why. In 2026, the image of founders who conclude their AI is too dangerous to release and silently walk away has become harder to imagine. Berg said he and his friend, showrunner David Mandel, are often asked about reboots of their respective shows. He can’t quite see it. “Both of those shows were created in an era where it’s, like, ‘Can you imagine if what was actually going on behind closed doors was this?’ And now it’s not behind closed doors anymore,” he said. In particular, he sees a tech industry that has lost its earnestness, lost mission-driven founders like Richard, and is instead consumed with vast sums of money and naked power. “It’s just gotten f*cking dark,” Berg said. “I don’t think the kind of fun that we had with it is doable now, in this era.” Notable While could still play the industry for laughs, modern takes on Silicon Valley, including Luca Guadagnino’s , a biopic of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, become “ so frightening it is hard to laugh,” Deadline wrote.

events.title: Data centres become dirty word as rollout faces rising opposition
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts When community concerns collide in the fight over data centres Signs litter properties near Firmus's proposed AI data centre site in Prospect Vale, northern Tasmania. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Data centres store and process information. But right now they're doing much more: they're at the centre of concern about how much their construction is stoking inflation. And, they're a lightning rod for communities rising up against what they feel is the cost of rapid growth. " Over the last year, we've obviously seen an absolute explosion in our pipeline," IBISWorld research analyst Andrew Ledovskikh says. His research has found Australia currently has about 2.3 gigawatts (GW) worth of power capacity in 79 data centres. That's enough to power about 1.5 million homes, depending how you work the numbers. Planned projects would give Australia capacity estimated to be more than 10 times that — between 23 and 67GW — according to the Australian Energy Market Operator. Not all projects make it, and Commonwealth Bank research forecasts 9GW of capacity by 2035. Data centre capacity is expected to grow rapidly. ( Supplied: AEMO/CBA ) "We really are just at the beginning. This is the moment where the water sort of recedes back into the beach and everything's calm before the tsunami hits." For advocates such as Belinda Dennett, it's an "enormous opportunity", with a construction timeline supporting our economy. Belinda Dennett believes building data centres can help transform Australia's economy. ( ABC News: Jack Ailwood ) Lamenting that "we've missed other global technology waves", Ms Dennett said this boom was a chance to "build on our advantages in cheap renewable energy". "That comes at a $4.1 billion opportunity a year," she said. "We can transform our economy and ensure Australia's future prosperity." For opponents such as Judy Gunson, however, the mushrooming sites are an "invasion" of neighbourhoods. In recent years, data centres have become a magnet for controversy in Europe and the US over the impact of noise, light and sheer size of the centres on neighbouring properties. Then there are environmental and economic concerns, because they use, and drive up, the cost of water and power. More than 40 proposals against data centres were on the ballot in the US midterms, and the overwhelming majority passed . The Victorian planning minister failed to approve or deny nine new data centre projects before the government went into "caretaker" mode ahead of this month's election, meaning "no decision" was the decision. Communities in New South Wales have stopped two large data centre proposals in recent months. US-based political scientist David McCuan has seen this issue take off, and quickly. "They've caught fire across the country," he said. An expert in political science at Sonoma State University, Professor McCuan said the backlash to the rapid growth of the centres meant there was "bipartisan" opposition in recent elections. Anti-data centre demonstrators have had significant success in the US. ( AP: Marc Levy ) Anti-data centre measures were on the ballot in more than 40 different jurisdictions in the midterms. A temporary ban, called a moratorium, is in place in New York and Texas has paused connections to the electricity grid — effectively stopping development. " The battle that we see going on over data centres and AI, that unites both [political] sides," Professor McCuan said. "They've affected a governor's race in Texas, they've affected local issues in zoning for what's going on in Ohio or in the Midwest. That's not something we would have forecast, say, 8, 10, 12 months ago." That speed is being replicated in Australia. Communities protest as data centres rise Judy Gunson is fired up about the energy use of data centres. "It just filled me with terror actually," she said. "The potential to derail any slow progress we're making towards reducing [carbon] emissions by this rollout, which is using extraordinary amounts of power." We're standing in the shadow of the Westgate Bridge, next to Melbourne's busy container port. What used to be the printing plant for the Herald Sun newspaper is being cleared for a massive data centre, to be built by NEXTDC. Judy Gunson is a spokeswoman for the Port Melbourne data centre action group. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) The community activist is protesting the build, concerned about the speedy pace and enormous scale of data centre construction. Communities in Sydney and Launceston are just some of those that have objected to development of the centres.

events.title: YouTuber MKBHD on the Cybertruck's discontinuation: 'Doesn't bode well for the Roadster'
events.summary: MKBHD also said his hair is probably safe after placing a bet related to the Cybercab. Chance Yeh/Getty Images for HubSpot MKBHD says the Cybertruck's wind-down could be bad news for the elusive Roadster. Tesla is clearing factory space for the steering-wheel-less, gold-painted Cybercab. Due to a bet, a 2026 Cybercab consumer launch could cost MKBHD his hair — but he's not sweating it. Tesla's decision to wind down Cybertruck production has Marques Brownlee worried about a different delayed vehicle. "This doesn't bode well for the Roadster," Brownlee, the YouTube reviewer popularly known as MKBHD, said on a Friday episode of the "WVFRM Podcast." On November 6, Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced on X that the EV maker would stop building the Cybertruck by mid-2027 to focus on production of the steering wheel-less Cybercab. Earlier this year, Tesla also retired its Model S and Model X, as it shifts more of its attention toward autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots. That makes the Roadster, Tesla's twice-revealed and long-delayed supercar, a questionable fit in the automaker's lineup, MKBHD said. It's the only vehicle in Tesla's lineup that the automaker isn't trying to make fully autonomous. People look at a prototype of the 2028 Tesla Roadster Thrust, an all-electric vehicle featuring SpaceX-developed thrusters. Caroline Brehman / AFP via Getty Images MKBHD has followed the Roadster saga particularly closely. He previously held two reservations for the high-flying vehicle, but he said in September 2025 that he had canceled one after waiting nearly a decade for delivery. And, for the Cybertruck, he said he thinks Tesla missed a golden opportunity. "If they just made like a good, simple SUV type-thing, like the EV9 ," he said. "That would have sold a lot. People would have wanted that everywhere." About MKBHD's hair… The YouTuber has a big bet with Tesla stans: If Tesla, as it once predicted, sells Cybercabs to US consumers by the end of 2026 under $30,000, he'll shave his head. Tesla debuted its gold-painted Cybercabs in Austin in September , but the vehicles were used exclusively in Tesla's own ride-hailing service — not sold to individual drivers. On Friday, he said that Tesla's plan to continue making Cybertrucks until mid-2027 made him more confident in his bet. "Alright, I'm probably good," MKBHD said on the podcast. "I did just get a haircut." That bet got a little more complicated late Friday and into Saturday. Tesla opened early Cybercab orders to select customers and is predicting a December delivery for its first units. The consumer Cybercab has a $29,990 starting price (before a $300-a-month subscription) — and MKBHD was among the initial invitees . "My hair is safe for several reasons," he wrote, pointing to the car's invite-only sales run and the fact that owners can't use it at first as a ride-hail. "It's a paperweight if I take this thing home." Musk responded on Saturday: "He's a chicken." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Vanuatu woman internationally recognised for solar scheme tackling violence
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Women celebrate their project to bring lights and solar energy to their community of Lawital. ( Supplied: Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific. ) Women in a Vanuatu village are working to reduce the risk of male violence by installing solar lights. The project has also increased household incomes, with women now able to work more. The project will be recognised at the COP-31 summit and the community wants to expand its work with Australia's help. When the sun sets on Tanna in Vanuatu, some women lock themselves in their homes for the night with a machete under their pillow for protection, according to a local NGO. In the village of Lawital, Dalila Laus Lalulu describes a similar sense of fear. There are no lights in many of the traditional villages on the island and men often attack women after dark, she says. "It's not safe to walk around at night for girls," Ms Lalulu told the ABC in Bislama. But women can also face threats at home. Vanuatu has one of the world's highest rates of intimate partner violence, according to Vanuatu Women's Centre, although the figure has fallen over the past 15 years. The latest national survey on Women's Lives and Family Relationships found half of the respondents who had been in a relationship had experienced physical or sexual violence, or both, from their partner during their lifetime. Meanwhile, about one in five women had been sexually attacked by someone who was not their partner. Solar power and lights have been installed in 120 homes in Lawital. ( Supplied: ActionAid ) But in Lawital, the women have overturned their fear of being attacked. Their simple project, which involved switching from candles to solar power, will receive international praise at the world's biggest climate summit on Monday. Lawital is a village on the South Pacific island of Tanna, home to many of Vanuatu's best resorts. But most of the traditional villages on the island have no access to running water, electricity or even lights. ActionAid Vanuatu's Lizzie Moli said women were even scared to use an outside bathroom at night if there was no light. "Women are sleeping with machetes at night as their protection because there's no lights," she told the ABC. Fed up with seeing relatives and friends attacked at night, Ms Lalulu initiated and helped lead a project to install solar-powered lights in streets and nearly 120 homes in her village with the help of other local women. Vanuatu woman Dalila Laus Lalulu will be recognised at COP-31 for the women-led solar light project in Lawital village. ( Supplied: ActionAid ) Dozens of solar lanterns were also purchased for women to use while walking at night, in partnership with the Australian government, organisation ActionAid, Women I TokTok Tugeta and business Powerwells. There is only anecdotal evidence at this stage, but Ms Lalulu said the violence had decreased and the community felt safer. The lights have also helped women become more respected in the community because many have taken on jobs to increase their household's income, either by maintaining the solar-energy scheme or selling goods at market stalls now that they can stay out after dark, according to Ms Moli. Dalila Laus Lalulu's daughter Annette helps install and maintain the solar-powered lights. ( Supplied: ActionAid ) Having lights in homes has also helped children complete their homework at night. Women in Tanna have not traditionally held roles in politics but, because of the success of the project, Ms Lalulu has been invited to become the first woman to join the Tanna Chief's Council, a traditional governing body. Pacific Island Affairs Minister Pat Conroy said Australia was "proud" to have helped with the project. "The successful, women-led project provided clean energy, lighting and charging systems to 1,380 people, enabling safer, more connected and economically active communities," he said. Homes in Vanuatu's remote village of Lawital now have access to solar energy and lights. ( Supplied: Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific ) This week Ms Lalulu has travelled to Türkiye — her first time out of Vanuatu — to receive a Gender Just Climate Solutions Award for the Lawital light project at the COP-31 climate change conference. Despite being quite shy about it, she told the ABC it was a blessing and would help her community continue its work. "When we heard that our sister here got an award, we scream and we run," Ms Moli said of Ms Lalulu. "For all the sacrifices, the sleepless nights, the body pain, she finally did it.

events.title: Soaring cost of essentials is severely testing democracies, economist says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'Anti-fascist economics' would lower cost of basic essentials, author says Isabella Weber, an associate professor of economics, says the soaring cost of essentials is severely testing democracies. In a new book, she says policymakers need to make affordability the centre of "anti-fascist economics". Dr Weber says it will require "structuralist measures" that change the ways in which we provision the essentials in society. Isabella Weber, a rising-star German economist, says it is something we need to pursue again. She says fascism has made a comeback. Our economic and political systems have stopped making our lives better and people are furious about it. Analysis: Democracy cannot survive trillionaires Democracy cannot survive trillionaires. We need to start taxing billionaires properly. She says illiberal forces are exploiting voters' anger and, rather than addressing the material causes of their pain, are deliberately redirecting people's rage towards migrants and other minorities, and promising that salvation can be found in nationalism, ethnic purity or patriarchy. To combat the phenomenon, she argues, we have to make life's essentials affordable again — housing, food, energy, water, health care, transport — so the foundations for a dignified life are available to everyone, no matter your household income or class. "It's funny that today we think of anti-fascist economics as provocative," she told the ABC Business Daily podcast . "In the 1940s it was actually a mainstream point for economists to say that economics had a role to play in 'Never Again'. "I would argue that today we are [once again] in a deep crisis of democracy around the Western world. The extreme right is on the rise. Democracy is as unstable as it has been since the 40s. "I think people are very clear. They're saying they can't take the status quo anymore," she said. Isabella Weber speaks to the ABC about her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics. ( ABC News ) An article, a pile-on and the aftermath Dr Weber, an associate professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, shot to prominence (or notoriety) in December 2021. She published an op-ed in The Guardian arguing that, in the wake of the COVID lockdowns, it could be worth using temporary and strategic price controls on certain products to prevent large companies in systemically significant sectors from exploiting the chaos to make windfall profits (and sending higher prices through the system). She said they were a standard tool of economic management in the 1940s. She saw strong parallels between the two historical periods. But the fallout from her article was immediate. "In a matter of hours, Weber, who was 33 years old, had transformed from an obscure but respected academic … into the most hated woman in economics — simply for proposing a 'serious conversation about strategic price controls'," Zach Carter wrote in The New Yorker . Weber agrees that her article "touched a nerve deep inside the economics establishment". "[But] for months, in public earnings calls with their shareholders, corporate leaders had been gleefully celebrating the fact that the pandemic, spiking commodity prices, and supply chain dislocations provided a wonderful opportunity to jack up prices. "As my co-authors and I later showed with research powered by large-language models analysing 138,962 earnings calls, corporate leaders tend to talk positively about generalised cost shocks, which impact workers and households negatively, because they are good for pricing and the bottom line." Bessent said Nvidia's board of directors should focus on candidates "outside the company" during an interview on Fox's "Sunday Morning Futures." "They need a dramatic shake-up," Bessent said. Last week, now former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after the company's board of directors opened an investigation into whether he was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." The New York Times and Reuters reported in the days following that Huang also had relationships with two different Nvidia employees. events.title: Flaming Hydra’s new Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending
events.summary: Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.” That’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project , an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra . If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries. To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.” Bustillos told me that these issues have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself, for example when Tal Levin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.” “AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.” The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries. Back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.” This is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time. “E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.” In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.” So even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem. Flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a new, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries . The Phoenix Project is starting by offering five new e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl, and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos said she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model. Similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive). With Phoenix, newsletter writers (starting with those who use Ghost, with support for additional newsletter platforms coming in the future) will be able to offer subscriptions to libraries, similar to the way libraries can subscribe to newspapers and magazines. Once it’s set up, Phoenix will automatically convert whichever newsletter posts the writer wants into EPUB documents, which are then sent to libraries for digital lending. Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos said she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Raganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent. “We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she said. “Those things go hand in hand.

events.title: Center-left previews 2028 in Denver
events.summary: The News DENVER — The race for the next Democratic presidential nomination has begun, with a festival of agreement. There was Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, telling the What’s Next conference that voters demanded action, not “shallow litmus tests or where we fall on some political spectrum. ” There was Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, explaining that voters did not want “marginal change” and Democrats weren’t in a battle of “progressive versus moderate .” And there was Pete Buttigieg, who’d noticed the Democrats borrowing his formula. They wanted to pass cost-cutting, pro-family bills with their new majority, then convince voters that they would never go back to pre-Trump neoliberalism. “It sounds good. It’s easy to say,” said Buttigieg. “Everybody thinks they already agree with this.” The post-midterms conference, organized by Majority Democrats, was a payoff of a two-year investment by moderate donors. Two years before strategists and elected officials landed in Denver and grabbed their lanyards, the venture capitalist Seth London circulated a memo about how new candidate and media investments could steer the party away from “race and group-based identity politics,” and toward “prosperity for more Americans.” This year’s Democratic landslide carried along every kind of candidate —the ones plugged into the Majority Democrats network, and the ones who worried it was a big-money ploy to defeat the populist left. But the conference elevated the candidates who wanted to build a supermajority, battling big tech and environmental attorneys. Some donors were in; the donors who wanted them to move left were out. “Tell us which ideas you’ll stop giving permission to, the ones that defy common sense or didn’t work,” said Rep. Jake Auchincloss, the pedigreed Massachusetts Democrat who chairs the Majority Democrats PAC. “Tell us which privileges you’ll confront, even if your donors or allies object.” Celebrating the center The donors did know how to throw a party. What’s Next resembled the sort of well-funded, media-friendly conferences that many Democrats have envied on the right, like the multi-day “AmericaFest” put on by Turning Point Action. This was a party for the Democratic mainstream, the staffers most likely to work for center-left presidential candidates than for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-NY. For two days, blocks of Denver’s River North Art District were cordoned off for Democrats, the people who elected them, and the reporters asking if they were running for president. (Their answers were variations on “not yet.“) There was conflict, but it was largely limited to the argument over who should lead Democrats’ new congressional majorities. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who announced his challenge to Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer on Thursday, paused for 10 seconds of applause when he took the stage and explained why he was running. “Candidates from different backgrounds and different parts of our party – they ran on a strikingly similar platform,” said Van Hollen. “They didn’t run on the tired Washington labels of progressive versus moderate. They ran on an economic populist message, on a commitment to fight for working people and take on a rigged economic and political system.” Many of those winners showed up in Denver, like Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand. They shared road stories of how they listened to Republican concerns, and would work with the willing ones to lower prices. But it was implied that Democrats should focus on building homes, lowering bills, and expanding health care before they did anything else. Not every attendee agreed. “The organizers here want a big tent, one big enough to even invite anti-establishment voices like me,” said Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Ca., who Democrats see as a competitor for a Sen. Bernie Sanders lane in the primary. “A big tent cannot mean that we water down principle for political expediency.“Apart from Khanna, the likely presidential candidates didn’t quite do that. Mallory McMorrow, who Majority Democrats supported in her unsuccessful U.S. Senate bid in Michigan, told Semafor that her party had just shown that it could have a loud primary argument and then unite on the basics. “It’s anti-corruption, getting money out of politics, protecting democracy, ending wars,” said McMorrow. “The disagreements are around the edges.” David’s view There will be many Democratic “cattle calls,” but I am focusing on how What’s Next was built because it’s the fruit of a two-year effort to ensure that the 2028 primary plays out differently than the 2020 primary. There is widespread agreement among Democratic strategists that their last open primary was defined by left-wing organizations that wanted candidates to commit to their ideas, eyeball to eyeball, on camera. That meant forums organized by groups like Planned Parenthood and MoveOn, and more progressive labor unions like SEIU. That meant the ACLU asking candidates if they would commit to cutting the federal prison population in half, and Movimiento Cosecha bird-dogging Joe Biden at his own events until he committed to stopping most deportations.If the left sees Majority Democrats as an effort to swipe their strongest messaging and junk the rest, they’re right. The economic populism in Denver was more sincere than they might think, but it is against degrowth and for permitting reform; skeptical of single-payer health care, but for incremental steps to “universal” health care; basically, right in the sweet spot of the Democrats’ congressional caucuses. Right now the Schumer-Van Hollen contest is where the fights over ideology and priorities are happening. The 2028 candidates would prefer to agree, for now. Room for Disagreement The left was not letting the rest of the party adopt its ideas without a fight. In the run-up to What’s Next, reporters from three left-leaning outlets that had been critical of Majority Democrats – The Lever, The Intercept, and The American Prospect – announced that they’d been denied access. All were eventually allowed in, becoming a First Amendment nuisance for donors who didn’t want to interrupt happy hours with hard questions. And on Friday, four protesters accessed the Mission Ballroom to interrupt the most powerful Democrat at the conference, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries. As liberal pundit Jessica Tarlov asked the likely House Speaker about his agenda, they jumped up, one after another, accusing him of complicity in genocide. events.title: DOT Sec. Duffy ties router in southern Arkansas to issues that led to nationwide ground stop
events.summary: Flight disruptions continued into the weekend as airlines raced to recover from the FAA's nationwide ground stop. The ground stop came after updates to an older communication system managed by L3Harris Technologies, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. The disruption forced sports teams to make alternative travel arrangements, with some college football games postponed. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that a router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies could be key to problems that led officials to order the biggest halt to flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 on Friday. "We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said in an interview with Fox News. "We're open if we see something else, we're going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement." Duffy told ABC's "This Week" in a separate interview that the router was located in El Dorado in southern Arkansas. The equipment, along with another router that was in Amarillo, Texas, is at an L3Harris lab in Florida for examination, Duffy said. He said the router, part of ongoing work to switch from copper wire to a fiber-optic system, began flooding other systems. Federal officials said on Saturday that "instability" in communication feeds and data like radar prompted the more than four-hour ground stop. Flight disruptions lingered on Sunday but were far from the thousands of cancellations passengers faced on Friday and Saturday. There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference with Duffy Saturday morning. Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports. The issue occurred during "routine" upgrades of switching from a copper wire system to fiber, Bedford said. A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, said Duffy. That created problems with airplane communications and radar feeds, they said. "We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford. He said officials weren't sure for about 45 minutes what was causing the instability. The outage again thrust aging infrastructure that underpins U.S. air traffic control into the spotlight, along with the country's struggles to replace sections of it while operating the world's busiest airspace. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said. L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel." The company, a longtime U.S. contractor, said it has completed more than 70% of the switch from copper wiring to fiber-optic system. Duffy took the groundstop to seek billions more from lawmakers to modernize the system. Flight disruptions began to ease Sunday, though more than 2,000 flights were canceled. That was down from the roughly 6,500 cancellations Saturday and over 8,000 delays, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of more than 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations, about a third of the day's schedule, and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather. Friday had the second-highest U.S. flight cancellations since a severe blizzard and below-freezing temperatures in January, according to aviation-data firm Cirium. Part of untangling from the ground stop included getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports, while dozens of planes had to park with limited gate space because flights couldn't depart. Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they're eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period. American Airlines , for example, offered flight attendants extra pay to pick up trips. events.title: US Treasury chief Bessent wants answers soon from Nvidia
events.summary: A 2024 photo shows Nvidia’s Jensen Huang embracing Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang - thought to be a Chinese spy - after delivering his keynote speech at COMPUTEX 2024 in Taipei, Taiwan. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent asked Nvidia to explain within 10 days if it helped advanced AI chips reach China, saying compliance with US export rules matters most. He questioned whether Nvidia used shell companies and Megaspeed-linked routes to bypass bans, while the Justice Department runs a criminal probe and Nvidia denies the claims. The row adds pressure before Nvidia’s results on Nov 17, with Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick due to testify as US agencies remain split over Megaspeed. SAN FRANCISCO - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on Nvidia on Nov 15 to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged spy for Beijing. Speaking on Fox News Sunday Morning Futures three days after Huang resigned, Bessent said he wants to know if Nvidia used shell companies to dodge US restrictions and sell its most powerful chips to China. The United States forbids sales to China of the most-cutting edge AI chips, hoping to stay ahead of the Chinese in the race to dominate artificial intelligence. In late 2025, President Donald Trump did authorise sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese - but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society. “Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said. “What’s more important here,” he said, “is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions.” He alluded to companies linked to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data centre company that Huang’s alleged lover Alice Huang once worked for. “And who knew? Because I mean, these shell companies were obvious. They were being investigated. And did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?” Of Alice Huang, he said: “It doesn’t matter to me whether she’s a spy or not. You know, Jensen’s foibles are his foibles.” Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days. Megaspeed is suspected by the United States of helping Chinese firms get around US export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centres in South-east Asia and routing them to China. The Justice Department is carrying out a criminal probe. Nvidia late in October said it had investigated these allegations in 2025 and refuted them. The Financial Times has reported that four federal agencies pushed to have Megaspeed blacklisted by the Commerce Department run by Howard Lutnick, but the latter did not do so. “Many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen,” Bessent said, repeating remarks he made on Nov 13 that suggest fissures in the Trump administration on this issue. Senators have summoned Jensen Huang to testify before the chamber’s Banking Committee in December. Lutnick himself has also reportedly agreed to testify. Jensen Huang has also agreed to testify behind closed doors in the House of Representatives before Thanksgiving. Nvidia is due to publish its quarterly results on Nov 17. AFP

events.title: Bessent calls for ‘dramatic shakeup’ at Nvidia, urges outside CEO
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a “dramatic shakeup” at Nvidia and urged its board to hire an outside CEO following Jensen Huang’s resignation. Bessent questioned whether Nvidia pursued potentially illicit chip sales to boost earnings and suggested other executives should face scrutiny. The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, both of whom are expected to accompany President Donald Trump to China this week. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings. Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls. "I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said in an interview on Fox News. The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump's handling of the matter. Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter. Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO. Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia's problems extended well beyond Huang. "If this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed," Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Bessent also questioned Nvidia's financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell. Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a new methodology based on customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling Bessent's remarks came two days after he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government's export blacklist for months. "But Commerce has the pen," Bessent said. The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce's failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place. Lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family's financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners. Cantor said Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said. There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information. Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia's H200 to China . Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut. Bessent's latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang's departure.

President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Lutnick has become the target of Washington finger-pointing for slow-walking Commerce Department restrictions on certain AI chip exports to China, as well as his close relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week after admitting to an extramarital affair with an Nvidia customer suspected of being a Chinese spy, and media reports of two affairs with subordinates. The woman, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, which the US is investigating for improper chip smuggling into China. Republicans are accusing Lutnick of defying Trump — and warning his job could be on the line — after reports emerged that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials had pushed the commerce secretary to place the Nvidia customer, Megaspeed, on a blacklist of companies that pose national security concerns. Treasury “has been pushing for this for months” but Commerce “has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC last week. Bessent, who has directly criticized Lutnick’s handling of the matter, is also expected on the trip. A senior US official told reporters ahead of the China trip that the Nvidia scandal “should not really have any bearing on the trip.” “These are national security matters that we develop in the administration interagency process, and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there,” the official said. ‘Nine lives’ They have accused Lutnick of allowing the chipmaker to indirectly sell more advanced chips to China than previously known or allowed under US export control laws, through loopholes he has so far declined to close. He’s also been criticized for giving Nvidia unfettered access to rule-making that would impact the entire industry. A senior US official told reporters ahead of the China trip that the Nvidia scandal “should not really have any bearing on the trip.” “These are national security matters that we develop in the administration interagency process, and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there,” the official said. events.title: Transportation secretary still doesn’t totally rule out that a cyberattack may have hit the FAA, and the FBI is assisting the probe
events.summary: Air traffic is returning to normal after a nationwide ground stop on Friday, but the investigation into the root cause is just starting, and the federal government hasn’t dismissed the possibility of a cyberattack. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters Friday night it “doesn’t appear” that a cyberattack was involved though he admitted that “there’s nothing certain right now.” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expressed confidence Saturday that foul play wan’t involved, and reiterated that message on the Sunday talk shows—but still qualified his statements. In an interview with ABC’s This Week , he said the director of national intelligence, the National Security Agency, the FBI, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency were all on a call together with “our intelligence partners” after the FAA’s communication problems emerged. They didn’t see any chatter or “footprints” that are normally associated with a cyberattack, he added. Instead, the FAA has zeroed in on a copper wire line that was being updated to a fiber-optic cable by contractor L3Harris. “We felt pretty comfortable that this was an internal network issue that’s owned and operated for us by L3 Harris, not an outside a factor,” Duffy said. “We feel pretty good still today that it is not a hacking event. But if the FBI comes in and says ‘no, we found something,’ obviously we’ll share that with the American people. But we have no indication that this was a hack.” In a briefing on Saturday, Duffy explained that the changeover to the fiber-optic cable caused routers across the air traffic control system to be flooded with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Because it disrupted some radar feeds, the FAA ordered the ground stop to ensure safety. It was lifted about four hours later. The installation took place in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a router from that location is now at an L3Harris lab in Florida with FAA staff, he told Fox News Sunday , adding that the FBI is offering assistance and suggesting a cyberattack still hasn’t been totally ruled out. “We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor,” Duffy reiterated. “But we’re open. If we see something else, we’re going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement. But at this point, we don’t think [a cyberattack] was the cause.” While the router in Arkansas is under scrutiny, a separate one in Amarillo, Texas, also acted up, raising another question about the disruption. Duffy said the upgrade in Texas had been done weeks earlier, but started to broadcast data into the FAA network at the same time as the Arkansas router. He told CBS’s Face the Nation that the FAA is investigating why that happened, noting both routers are at the L3Harris lab in Florida where the FBI is offering support. ABC asked if sabotage has been ruled out, and Duffy replied “we’re looking at a full suite of issues with the router and with the installation.” The FAA knows who performed the installation, and Duffy called the technician a “good American patriot” who is believed to be a veteran as well. “So we don’t think that someone tried to sabotage the network on the install at all,” he added. “But we don’t actually have the root cause, which is why we do the investigation with our L3Harris partner on the network and the FBI and the FAA.” For its part, an L3Harris spokesperson said Saturday that the company has been modernizing the communications infrastructure for the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. Along with its telecom partners and the FAA, L3Harris added that it has completed more than 70% of the conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. “We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Morocco becomes first Arab nation in FIFA’s top five men’s rankings
events.summary: Morocco becomes the only Arab country, and first African nation since Nigeria in 1994, to be ranked fifth in the world. Morocco have become the first Arab country to enter FIFA’s top five men’s team rankings after moving up by two places from their previous best position of number seven. The two-time World Cup quarterfinalists leapt ahead of Brazil and Portugal on points on Sunday, following their strong performance in recent continental football matches. Morocco are also the first African and Arab country to reach back-to-back quarterfinals at the World Cup, where the continent’s top-ranked nation was knocked out by France in consecutive tournaments. The Atlas Lions’ 2026 finish did not improve or match their semifinal run at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where they surpassed all expectations to become Africa and the Arab world’s first semifinalists and the darlings of the tournament. Following the World Cup in North America, Mohamed Ouhabi’s team have maintained a 100 percent record in the current round of qualifying matches for the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) 2027. Morocco thumped Niger 5-0 in their latest qualification match on Friday, as the star-studded lineup shone in front of a raucous home crowd in Rabat. AFCON’s defending champions lead Group A by nine points. However, their AFCON title is contentious and is subject to a hearing at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) following an appeal by losing finalists Senegal. Senegal were stripped of this year’s AFCON title and Morocco were declared champions by the Confederation of African Football (CAF), despite Senegal beating the hosts ⁠⁠⁠⁠1-0 after extra time in January’s final in Rabat. Senegal walked off the pitch for 14 minutes ‌‌‌‌after a penalty was awarded against them late in regulation time, with several players returning to the dressing room in protest before they resumed play. Morocco missed the spot kick, sending the match into extra time, where Senegal scored the winner to secure victory. However, they were stripped of the title two months later after CAF’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match by walking off the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 victory to ⁠⁠⁠⁠Morocco. The controversial 2025 title was the northwestern African side’s second AFCON title since 1976. Morocco is one of the cohost nations for the FIFA World Cup 2030.

events.summary: Spokesman for the Southern Armed Forces says group is repositioning from Dhubab airport and areas around Bab al-Mandeb. Forces affiliated with Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they are withdrawing from territory near the Bab al-Mandeb strait to focus on defending the interim capital, Aden, from the Houthi armed group. A spokesman for the Southern Armed Forces, a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, said on Sunday that it was redeploying from Dhubab airport and areas around Bab al-Mandeb in southwestern Yemen. list 1 of 4 Fighting intensifies in Yemen as Houthis deny targeting Mecca list 2 of 4 Yemen’s Houthis renew strikes on Saudi Arabia as UNSC extends sanctions list 3 of 4 Siege fuels disease fears in Yemen’s Taiz list 4 of 4 Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones “This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats,” the spokesman said. The announcement raises the prospect of new Houthi advances towards Aden on the southern coast, the base of the internationally recognised government since the Houthis drove leaders from the capital Sanaa more than a decade ago. Reinforcements would also be sent to try to end the Houthis’ siege of Taiz, where fighting has been raging to the west of the city, the announcement added. Humanitarian conditions are worsening in Yemen’s third-largest city, with aid supplies blocked from entering and civilians unable to leave. The city hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen since the 2022 ceasefire collapsed this summer and fighting surged. The Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized large areas of territory along Yemen’s western coast in September. Sunday’s announcement could signal a setback for the Yemeni government forces’ counteroffensive launched in September to reclaim areas seized by Houthi fighters. The counteroffensive quickly recaptured key positions around the strait, notably Dhubab, but failed to push the Houthis out of the key city of Mocha and other areas near the coast. The Houthis responded by intensifying drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, grounding flights and targeting energy facilities. Earlier on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition said it shot down two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh, the Saudi capital. Later, coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said two drones launched over the Mecca region and another over the Medina region. The Houthis denied the allegations they attacked Mecca as “a blatant lie”. Houthi forces also captured highland areas north of Aden, where the government has been operating since 2015, and say they are preparing to advance on the city itself. A spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majid Al-Nazili, called on the international community to help return Bab al-Mandeb and Yemen’s west coast to government control, stressing that the strait was of vital importance for freedom of maritime navigation and international trade. Separately, Yemen’s armed forces said that they had launched 906 strikes against Houthi positions, including 41 air strikes, on Marib, al-Jawf and Taiz. Also on Sunday, the International Committee of the Red Cross announced that the Houthis, with its support, unilaterally released 600 prisoners “in connection with the armed conflict”.

events.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks T he Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34. While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “ it’s make or bake time ”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead. Warnings of mounting risks, unprecedented heat and disasters such as August’s glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border can engender a sense of paralysis or unreality. The leaders of both host countries prompted anger last week: the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, publicly extolled his country’s oil reserves , while Australia’s Anthony Albanese failed to mention fossil fuels in his speech. But for all its flaws, the UN climate process remains crucial. There is no other mechanism to broker a global green transition. Mr Burnham’s appointment of a climate security adviser , Madeleine Alessandri, should focus minds in the UK. Kemi Badenoch’s rejection of net zero has undermined an important cross‑party consensus. Ministers, who must soon make a decision on Rosebank oil and gas field , must realise that economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would dwarf any benefits. Governments of countries that are far poorer than the UK cannot be expected to turn away from coal and oil if rich countries keep investing. A resolution to derive 35% of energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 will be agreed this week if objections from fossil fuel producers can be overcome. Attempts to undermine the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change must also be resisted. It provides the science on which the process depends. Increased accountability on climate finance is urgently needed too. Poor countries cannot be expected to put up with endless delays . A large majority of the global public recognises the threat from global heating and wants action by governments. Of course, this takes courage and leadership: people may back a green transition in the abstract, but be more resistant to changes that affect their lives. But those pushing for a faster shift away from fossil fuels, at Cop31 and at a national level, should be emboldened by the way that public awareness and support have grown: they are on the side of the future, while their opponents are stuck in the past.

events.title: Bessent questions did Nvidia "goose" earnings with suspect China chip sales
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO. Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth. The Treasury secretary casting doubt on the quality of its financial results and leadership could be a blow to an already shaky market. Since the scandal broke open in late October, Nvidia shares have shed more than $1.2 trillion in market capitalization, with impacts on millions of Americans. Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies. "I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel." Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance." "This makes me think that as the board conducts the search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company," he said. For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks. The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others. In recent days, Bessent has also made clear that the Commerce Department has questions to answer about why it didn't impose tighter controls on Nvidia's exports. As Axios reported earlier this week, administration officials have accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of stalling curbs on Nvidia's exports. What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

events.title: TechCrunch Mobility: The Nvidia backup plan for China’s self-driving industry
events.summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility ! I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition. Web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he said the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else. These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy. The former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem. Nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve. I spoke to Leo Wang , the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle company Pony.ai , this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China. Demand is already far greater than supply, Wang said, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said. Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap. “If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he said, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.” When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang said Chinese companies have already been preparing. “If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he said. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. Although cost-effectiveness-wise, probably it’s not the best choice yet. But still, it’s an alternative way that already exists and which is more mature than a few years ago.” May Mobility plans to use the Volkswagen all-electric ID. Buzz for its global ride-hailing platform. The company said it is targeting the deployment of more than 10,000 autonomous vehicles through 2031. This does not mean that VW’s MOIA group is ditching Mobileye, I have been told. Instead, VW told me, the company is offering an automated driving-ready base vehicle to other companies that develop their own self-driving systems. (This was just presented last month during Nvidia GTC in Berlin.) Newmo , a Japanese robotaxi startup, raised a ¥20.8 billion (roughly $135 million) round led by KDDI. ParkBee , a Dutch parking technology company, acquired Mobian’s city and parking operations. Port , an urban logistics company, raised €14.5 million in a round led by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Balnord. Lucid reported Q3 revenue of $350 million, below Wall Street expectations, and it is still losing money. Although its Q3 net loss did narrow to $830.9 million. Notably, the EV maker increased its delayed draw term loan from its largest shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, to $1.75 billion. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating a Waymo software recall from a year ago that was issued after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses. The agency said that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software update intended to fix the problem. Sources familiar with Waymo tell me that there have not been school bus-related incidents since March. I have not been able to independently verify that with the Austin Independent School District. The Tesla Cybertruck will live on through next summer, but production will ultimately end , according to Elon Musk, who defended the polarizing steel-clad truck.

events.title: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis
events.summary: Prime minister promises ‘root-and-branch rethink’ of support for young people as Milburn report advises sweeping changes to some benefits Andy Burnham: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”. Burnham said the government would intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fell behind, and “long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state”, including providing more opportunities for vocational training in schools. Writing in the Guardian, the prime minister said ministers’ response to Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into the crisis of youth unemployment in the UK would not be “a traditional … reform” but “societal and generational”. He promised to reduce the number of Neets – 18 to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training – which topped a million this year for the first time in more than a decade. Hoping to head off opposition from leftwing MPs in his own party, who rebelled to block Starmer’s welfare changes last summer , Burnham said the government would “invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on”, but said the support “will have to come with responsibilities”. “If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can. Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point,” said Burnham. Milburn’s long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s . Some young people will lose their personal independence payments and the right to claim the health element of universal credit, and instead will get a new youth allowance paid at the standard rate of universal credit. The government has also announced it will expand a taxpayer-funded scheme aimed at helping young people into work to under-25s who have been claiming benefits for a year. Eligible 18- to 24-year-olds will be “guaranteed” a fully funded, six-month job matched to their skills after 12 months on universal credit. The Liberal Democrats said the six-month offering was worth “very little” without a job at the end of it. Before the publication of the report, Milburn said the government would have to be “candid with people”, that it would take 10 years for the benefits bill to come down, and investment would have to be made upfront. Addressing critics calling for the benefits bill to be immediately slashed, the former health secretary told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “There’s no such thing as a free lunch. If you are going to will the ends, you’ve got to will the means. I don’t think there’s a single person in this country who believes that it’s tolerable to have one million young people, aged 16 to 24, who are not in education, employment, or training.” Pat McFadden acknowledged that Milburn’s review would have an “element of compulsion” for Neets and there would be people who would receive less in benefits than currently. The work and pensions secretary said the UK had to become more like countries that had dealt with youth unemployment more successfully, such as the Netherlands, where the youth desk would “literally knock on your door” and offer options of training or work. But he denied that Milburn was proposing a ban on young people claiming health-related benefits. “That’s not what he’s saying. He’s saying if you have a long-term disability, that means you can never work,” he said. “You will actually get more than you will now. He’s saying that if you have extra costs, there will be a benefit you can apply to for extra costs. He’s also saying there should be a local fund for short-term needs, and for other people, he’s saying there should be more support to get into work. Change was necessary, he added, because the number of young people claiming personal independence payments (Pip) had doubled since the start of the decade, while the number of young people on the health element of universal credit had increased by 80%. Burham hit out at the Conservatives and Reform, who have called for deep and immediate cuts to welfare, with Kemi Badenoch vowing to slash the bill by £36.1bn by 2030 if the party wins the next general election. Under the plans 70% of child benefit disability-related claims linked to ADHD and “milder” behavioural disorders and learning disabilities would be cut, with Labour calling the proposals “ a charter for human misery ”. The shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, acknowledged the plans could mean around half a million children losing disability-related payments.
