events.title: Is Nvidia cooked without Jensen Huang?
events.summary: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . A post-Huang era We're about to learn just how much one person truly matters to the AI economy. Jensen Huang was larger than life at Nvidia. He was the AI boom's most recognizable evangelist, the chip maker's chief visionary and dealmaker, and the force behind Nvidia's ascent to the most valuable company on the planet. As Zak Jason writes, the cult of the tech founder has very much become America's religion . And Huang was "its most convincing saint." A week ago, Huang admitted to an affair and apologized to his family. Nvidia disclosed it was investigating whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. And then The New York Times reported a second affair, this one with an Nvidia executive who was one of Huang's direct reports. He resigned on Thursday. Huang's abrupt downfall is a stress test of founder worship. The market put a price on it: Nvidia's market cap tumbled $573 billion last week, more than all but 18 companies in the entire S&P 500. "It's like the Bulls without Jordan," author Stephen Witt, who wrote a biography on Huang, said on CNBC. "I don't know how they are going to replace this guy." That is the essence of key-man risk , as my colleagues Sarah E. Needleman and Tim Paradis reported. When one leader is so closely identified with the strategy, the products, and the culture, their departure can create a vacuum that no org chart (let alone one with 60 direct reports to the CEO) can immediately fill. Much of Silicon Valley came to Huang's defense in recent days. Sarah Guo, a venture capitalist, called him "one of the most extraordinary entrepreneurs of all time." Sequoia's Shaun Maguire said Huang's "contributions to American innovation and AI leadership cannot be overstated." A petition to reinstate Huang as Nvidia CEO circulated over the weekend, collecting more than 100,000 signatures, including those of Elon Musk and other prominent figures. Our own Alistair Barr also points to new reports that are casting doubt on the intelligence behind Jensen Huang's downfall. For sure, there are several examples of seemingly irreplaceable CEOs — Steve Jobs at Apple and Travis Kalanick at Uber — whose companies still thrived under new leadership. And even some of Huang's biggest proponents aren't standing by him. "No one was a bigger defender of Jensen than I was but there are rules about sex with subordinates," CNBC's Jim Cramer said on X . "Just because someone is brilliant doesn't mean he can do what he wants." The question is whether Nvidia, which lacked a defined succession plan, can prove to be more durable than its founder's legend . If it can't? Dick Costolo, the former Twitter CEO, floated an idea . "Prediction: 3-4 years from now, [Nvidia] will miss a quarter or two, and they will bring Jensen back to run the company," he said. "Like fame, everybody is outraged for 15 minutes, and there is nothing Americans love more than the comeback story." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Gen Z shatters America's political orthodoxies
events.summary: Young Americans are challenging beliefs their parents and grandparents once considered sacred — from socialism and Israel to Christianity . Why it matters: Neither party can count on old political loyalties to win over a generation increasingly willing to break with the past. Socialism: 35 years after the Soviet Union collapsed, some 57% of Americans ages 18–34 view socialism positively, compared with 43% for capitalism, according to a September 2026 Gallup poll . Among Americans 55 and older, 65% view capitalism positively, compared with 34% for socialism. Israel: Decades after Israel fought wars against neighboring Arab states, some 53% of Americans ages 18–34 sympathize more with Palestinians, compared with 23% who sympathize more with Israelis, according to Gallup's February 2026 survey . Christianity: After centuries as the overwhelming religious identity of Americans, only 54% of Americans ages 18–29 now identify as Christian, compared with 76% of those 65 and older, according to nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute's 2025 Census of American Religion , released in April 2026. Between the lines : The return of forces that voters haven't felt in generations can scramble their priorities all over again. After decades of relatively low inflation, prices surged during the COVID era, with annual inflation hitting 9.1% in June 2022 — its highest rate since 1981. In 2024, young voters who ranked the economy and jobs as their top issue favored Trump by 24 points , according to CIRCLE's analysis of AP VoteCast. Two years later, 78% of financially struggling young students backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 16% for Republicans, according to a November 5 CIRCLE analysis . State of play: Young voters showed both parties how quickly their support can shift between elections in last week's midterms. Some 66% of voters ages 18–29 backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 31% for Republicans, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE , citing preliminary NORC data. That 35-point Democratic advantage compares with a 14-point margin in the 2024 House election, according to separate Edison Research exit polling. Trump's 2024 gains among young voters , especially men, now look less like a lasting GOP realignment and more like a warning about how quickly younger Americans can change course. Zoom in: Socialism's fading stigma reached the ballot box in America's two largest cities. Democratic socialists now stand poised to lead New York and Los Angeles after Nithya Raman defeated Karen Bass in Tuesday's mayoral election, joining New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both built campaigns around affordable housing and inequality, tapping into younger Americans' financial frustrations. The bottom line: Young Americans aren't necessarily embracing socialism because they've rejected their grandparents' Cold War beliefs, PRRI CEO Melissa Deckman told Axios. They're questioning capitalism because their own economic experiences have left them disillusioned. "What they're seeing isn't working, and the American dream is increasingly out of reach for them," said Deckman, author of " The Politics of Gen Z ."

events.title: Nvidia's next CEO will inherit more than Jensen Huang's job
events.summary: Huang's exit leaves his successor with the task of rebuilding the trust of Nvidia's tens of thousands of employees amid intense public scrutiny. Getty Images Huang's exit leaves Nvidia's next CEO with the challenge of rebuilding trust and refocusing workers. His successor will need to keep day-to-day operations humming amid intense public scrutiny. Companies can't let extraordinary results be a license to follow different rules, a former Netflix talent exec said. During an NBA tech summit last year, former CEO Jensen Huang described having a management style at Nvidia built on open communication. "I spend all of my time being transparent," said Huang, who has long been lauded for steering the chipmaker's extraordinary rise. Now, reports of Huang's extramarital affairs — with a direct report, another employee, and a client suspected by US intelligence officials of spying for China — have exposed a gap between his professed commitment to candor and how he may have acted behind closed doors. Huang's exit leaves Nvidia's next CEO with a difficult task: rebuilding the trust of tens of thousands of workers at a company at the center of the AI boom . "When the CEO is having a romantic relationship with someone at the company, that can erode trust and engender cynicism," said Kim Scott, a former Apple and Google executive and cofounder of executive education company Radical Candor. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Refocusing on the work Huang ran Nvidia with a flat structure at the top, a setup he credited with helping the company move quickly. He worked out of a conference room, not a private office, and had dozens of direct reports. Nvidia didn't have a publicly disclosed succession plan. C-suite observers have said that the halo surrounding a successful tech founder, combined with an org chart light on top layers , can leave a company with a thin succession bench. After Huang's departure Wednesday, Nvidia appointed Colette Kress, chief financial officer, as interim CEO . The company launched a search for a permanent replacement, including both internal and external candidates. Kress, as well as whoever ultimately takes the reins permanently, will likely face a number of challenges. "The first thing employees want to know is: Is the company in good hands and will it continue to do well?" said Scott. "A lot of people are holding unvested options worth millions of dollars." Nvidia's new boss will have to navigate the intense public scrutiny surrounding Huang's exit, while ensuring day-to-day operations remain humming. "The combination of keeping people focused on the work while not pretending that the circus outside doesn't exist is really, really hard to do," said Katie Burke, chief operating officer of legal AI company Harvey. 'A grief process' There are no quick fixes in this situation. "Trust can be violated very quickly, but it's rebuilt slowly and consistently," said Alison Fragale, an organizational psychologist and professor of organizational behavior at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. The chipmaker's new leader will also need to help employees cope in the aftermath of the scandal and get back to work. That may be especially difficult for those who admire Huang and wanted him to stay, added Fragale. "It's like a bit of a grief process," she said. Meanwhile, other employees may be feeling betrayed or unsettled by the intense public scrutiny. "You can't pretend that everyone's family is not asking them what's going on," said Fragale. Nvidia's next leader will have at least one advantage in healing the company's culture, said Jessica Neal, a former chief talent officer at Netflix. Huang's departure shows that despite all of his achievements, he is still facing consequences for violating company standards. "One of the biggest mistakes companies can make is confusing extraordinary results with the permission to behave differently," Neal said. "Every time you make an exception for a high performer, you're sending a message to everyone else about what really matters. And over time, those exceptions become the culture." events.title: A Gen Zer shares 4 rules he followed to turn $35 into a 6-figure marketing agency from his dorm room
events.summary: Stavya Nilawar founded his creator-marketing agency, Nilawar, with about $35. Courtesy of Stavya Babson student Stavya Nilawar grew a $35 creator marketing agency into six-figure revenue. Nilawar's agency connects AI brands with YouTube creators for sponsored segments and dedicated videos. He shares four lessons that helped him grow it from his dorm room. When Stavya Nilawar isn't in class at Babson College, he's growing his creator marketing agency. His weekdays follow a disciplined routine: class from 8 to 11:15 a.m., lunch, then a five-hour work block. After dinner, he works for another hour or two. Nilawar's company connects brands with YouTube creators for sponsored segments and dedicated videos. He's worked with brands including AI companies CodeRabbit and Wispr Flow, as well as on campaigns involving Jack Link's x MrBeast. He earns a cut of the project fee, typically 20%. He said he spent about $35 to get started — for a website domain and two email inboxes. First, he built a network of creators by manually searching TikTok: "I would literally doomscroll on TikTok and just go on people's accounts and look at their emails." Once he had a roster of 10 to 15 creators, he began pitching brands. Today, his monthly expenses rarely exceed $1,500, while monthly revenue topped $100,000 for the first time in October. Business Insider reviewed monthly business-account statements to verify his revenue. "The main expenses are virtual assistants," Nilawar said. They cost him about $1,000 a month and help manage his agency's outreach, which can involve sending 200 to 300 emails a day, including follow-ups. Nilawar, who started the business during a gap semester before college, said these four rules helped him turn roughly $35 into a six-figure business. 1. Choose a niche based on opportunity — not just passion Nilawar doesn't buy into the standard advice to follow your passion when choosing a business niche. For him, the business model came first: He knew he wanted to run an agency that connects brands with creators. Then he had to decide which type of brands to serve. He chose to work with AI companies. "I was not passionate about AI at all, to be honest," he said. But he saw an opportunity: AI companies were growing quickly, and many had budgets for creator partnerships. In his view, that's the better order of operations for aspiring founders: Choose a business model you enjoy, then find a niche with clear demand and customers willing to pay. 2. Find people who are already where you want to be When Nilawar began exploring influencer marketing, an industry contact helped explain how brands work with creators and how agencies make money. He also learned that 20% was a typical agency cut on a deal. Since then, he's deliberately sought advice from people further along in the industry, including his current mentor, who runs a similar agency that generates about $10 million a year. Nilawar named his agency after his family name. Courtesy of Stavya Nilawar "I would reach out to agency owners who were in the position that I wanted to be in," he said. "I literally asked them what they're doing now in their day-to-day business and how they got to the next level." Nilawar's advice: Find someone who has built the type of business you want to build, and ask if they'd be willing to share what they've learned. 3. Build a repeatable outreach system In the early days, Nilawar did everything manually: sourcing creators, sending emails, following up with potential clients, and managing campaigns. "Emails are the main way that we get clients," he said. "If you don't have a system for that, you're not going to do very well in the beginning." For Nilawar, reaching the first $10,000 in revenue required volume. He tested different email copy and calls to action, then sent outreach to brands within his chosen niche. Today, he uses virtual assistants and software to scale that work, but outreach is only part of the system. In a crowded agency market, Nilawar said his edge is responsiveness. What sets him apart from his competitors is "our relationships and our speed," he said. His team aims to respond to clients within two to five minutes. 4. Treat mistakes as lessons, not reasons to quit Early on, Nilawar landed a big campaign involving three creators. Two went smoothly, but the third repeatedly missed deadlines, and when the creator eventually delivered the content, Nilawar said the brand was unhappy with its quality. The brand wanted to cancel that portion of the deal, leaving Nilawar caught between the brand and the creator's manager. He thought he might have to pay the brand $25,000. "I didn't have $25K," said Nilawar, who was 18 at the time. "I thought I was screwed." The parties ultimately worked out a solution, and the experience taught him that agency work involves more than landing the deal: He also has to manage expectations, maintain communication, and resolve conflicts when a partnership goes sideways. Rather than viewing that scare as proof he wasn't ready to run a business, Nilawar sees it as a lesson he got early — when the stakes were still manageable. events.title: 11 Silicon Valley tech founders who were cast out from the companies they helped build
events.summary: Jensen Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and resigned as CEO on Thursday. Joel Saget/AFP/Getty Images Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following an extramarital affair scandal. He's not the only founder to be kicked out of his own company. Elon Musk, Steve Jobs, and Sam Altman have also been ousted from the firms they started. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, following an extramarital affair scandal and a board investigation into concerns that he may have been the subject of a "foreign intelligence effort." It ends his reign at the chip company he cofounded in 1993. Over 33 years, Huang oversaw Nvidia's meteoric rise from a scrappy chipmaker to a multitrillion-dollar AI powerhouse. Founders being kicked out of their own companies is more common than you might think. Huang is in good company. Steve Jobs, Elon Musk , and Sam Altman of OpenAI are among the CEOs who have been ousted from the firms they founded. Some cases stem from minor disagreements and plunging stock prices, but some CEOs felt betrayed, launched lawsuits, or were arrested. Here are 11 tech founders who were cast out from the companies they built: Steve Jobs, Apple Steve Jobs in 1984. PAUL SAKUMA/AP In 1985, nine years after cofounding Apple, Steve Jobs exited the company. Slumping sales and Jobs' demanding management style led to a clash with CEO John Sculley. The board stripped Jobs, who was nominally Apple's chairman, of his duties, and he resigned. Jobs then founded another computer company, NeXT, which Apple acquired in 1996 for $427 million. He became Apple CEO the following year. Sam Altman, OpenAI Sam Altman. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Sam Altman cofounded OpenAI as a nonprofit in 2015 and was its cochair alongside Elon Musk. He became CEO four years later and was the face of the AI boom when ChatGPT launched in 2022. In late 2023, the board ousted Altman, saying it had lost confidence in his ability to lead the company and that he was not "consistently candid in his communications." After employees and investors revolted, Altman was reinstated just four days later. Jerry Yang, Yahoo Jerry Yang in 2007. Alex Wong/Getty Images Jerry Yang cofounded Yahoo while he was a Stanford student and later became CEO in 2007. Then, Microsoft offered to buy the company for over $44 billion, a substantial premium on its market value. However, Yang did not want to sell. After negotiations collapsed, Yahoo's share price dropped as much as 20%. The board faced criticism for its handling of the failed deal, with Yang being pressured to resign as CEO. He stayed at Yahoo in a different role until 2012. Jack Dorsey, Twitter Bloomberg/Getty Images Jack Dorsey has the rare accolade of being pushed out of the same company twice. In 2008, his Twitter cofounder, Evan Williams, fired him as CEO. Dorsey went on to start Square, the payments processor, before he was brought back as interim CEO in 2015. Not long afterward, Twitter dropped the "interim" from his job title. In 2020, the activist investor firm Elliott Management criticized Dorsey's divided attention between Twitter and Square, and pushed for his removal. Dorsey stepped down as CEO the following year. Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX Sam Bankman-Fried. Lam Yik/Bloomberg via Getty Images Sam Bankman-Fried became a poster boy for crypto, and his net worth peaked at $26 billion after founding the crypto exchange FTX. In 2022, CoinDesk reported that his trading firm, Alameda Research, had a balance sheet largely made up of FTX's own crypto token. Those close ties panicked investors, who rushed to withdraw their money from the crypto exchange — which didn't have enough to cover the withdrawals, partly due to lavish spending by FTX executives . FTX filed for bankruptcy, and Bankman-Fried was replaced by John J. Ray III, an attorney who specializes in recovering funds from failed corporations, including Enron. Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison in 2024. Elon Musk, X.com Peter Thiel and Elon Musk in 2000. AP Photo/Paul Sakuma Elon Musk founded X.com as a payments processor in 1999. A year later, it merged with Peter Thiel's Confinity, which created PayPal. The merged company initially kept the name X.com, with Musk as CEO. Leadership clashed with Musk over the name, his management style, and his desire to rewrite the platform's main infrastructure. While Musk was away on his honeymoon, Thiel and his cofounder Max Levchin organized a letter of no confidence. The board voted to replace Musk and install Thiel as CEO. Martin Eberhard, Tesla Martin Eberhard and Elon Musk. Chris Weeks/Getty Images Martin Eberhard cofounded Tesla in 2003, and Elon Musk joined the company the following year. Although Eberhard had served as CEO since the company's inception, he was ousted in 2007. He later told Business Insider that Musk phoned him and said the board had met without him and decided he should step down. Eberhard sued Tesla in 2009, accusing Musk of defamation and pushing him out of the company. The suit was settled. Travis Kalanick, Uber Travis Kalanick at the 2017 Vanity Fair Oscar Party. Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images Travis Kalanick cofounded Uber in 2009 and became CEO the following year. His leadership saw a string of scandals, and the company was criticized for a culture of bullying and misogyny. Some executives expensed visits to strip clubs, The New York Times reporter Mike Isaac reported in his book "Super Pumped: The Battle for Uber." In 2017, Uber lost hundreds of thousands of customers from a viral #DeleteUber campaign following accusations that the company intended to profit from President Donald Trump's travel ban. After a former engineer, Susan Fowler, alleged sexual harassment and HR failures, Uber launched an independent investigation into its workplace culture, which led to Kalanick's resignation. Eduardo Saverin, Facebook Eduardo Saverin. Wei Leng Tay/Bloomberg via Getty Images As depicted by Andrew Garfield in "The Social Network," Eduardo Saverin cofounded Facebook with Mark Zuckerberg while they were at Harvard. He served as chief financial officer until he was squeezed out of the startup in 2005. After Peter Thiel invested $500,000, the company was restructured, and the board issued millions of new shares. This led to Saverin's 30% stake being diluted to less than 10%. Zuckerberg wrote in an email at the time and obtained by Business Insider in 2012: "Is there a way to do this without making it painfully apparent to him that he's being diluted to 10%?" Saverin sued. The lawsuit was settled out of court in 2009, restoring his title as cofounder and leaving him with a stake worth over $2 billion when Facebook went public. Andrew Mason, Groupon Andrew Mason. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Andrew Mason started Groupon in 2008 as a company that sells discounts on local businesses. events.title: Binance targets full reopening of withdrawals by next week
events.summary: Binance said on Nov 14 that it aims to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week. SINGAPORE – Binance said that it aims to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week, as operations normalise for the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange after a security breach linked to North Korea saw US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) stolen from the platform in October . The company said on Nov 14 in a post on X: “This week, we reopened withdrawals for 87 networks. We will aim to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week.” Binance resumed withdrawals in phases earlier in November , after covering 95% of the US$6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform in what experts described as the largest cryptocurrency theft. The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the Binance hack, but Pyongyang has denied that. Blockchain investigation firms have attributed it to a North Korean group known as “TraderTraitor”. In its initial report on how hackers pulled off the heist, Binance detailed a multi-stage hacking endeavour that began in June and set off a series of security breaches culminating in the theft on Oct 29. The theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay customers in full. The company’s finance chief Kaiser Ng left the company just over a week after the heist , to pursue a new venture after more than five years at Binance. He was replaced by long-time finance executive Justin Yek, who was most recently vice-president of finance at Airwallex. Cryptocurrencies tumbled over the weekend, with Bitcoin slumping to a four-month low. The largest digital asset sank 5.7% in the US on Nov 14 and continued to drop in Asia on Nov 15 to as low as US$62,112, down a further 3.6% and its weakest since July 14. Second-biggest token Ether, which slumped 8% in the US session, fell another 3.4% on Nov 15 to US$1,711, its lowest since July 8. Crypto has been pummelled in recent weeks by a confluence of factors, including the expectation of higher interest rates, large outflows from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, an AI-fuelled risk-off mood and continued fallout from the recent US$6 billion Binance hack. Bitcoin has slumped about 25% since Oct 21. Its low for 2026 is US$57,742, reached on July 1. Large liquidation events – in which more than US$500 million worth of Bitcoin positions are wiped over 24 hours – are becoming a recurring feature in the market, as sharp swings repeatedly flush leveraged traders out of their bets. On Nov 13 , Bitcoin’s slide triggered the liquidation of roughly US$1.3 billion in long crypto bets over 24 hours, with Bitcoin positions accounting for the majority of that sum, according to Coinglass data . In the 24 hours through 7am on Nov 15 in Singapore, exchanges tracked by Coinglass recorded about US$2 billion of crypto liquidations, including US$774 million in Bitcoin and US$488 million in Ether. Long positions accounted for the vast majority of the liquidations. From Oct 30 through Nov 13, US-listed spot Bitcoin ETFs saw almost US$3 billion in net outflows. Richard Galvin, executive chairman at crypto investment firm DACM, said the impending initial public offering of artificial intelligence company Anthropic PBC may be drawing capital away from crypto. “Price performance looks very similar to what happened through the SpaceX IPO pricing period earlier this year,” Galvin said. “It appears crypto remains a short-term funding source, particularly for retail investors. This is in addition to all the other macro headwinds.” REUTERS, BLOOMBERG

events.title: Troubled Scottish steel supplier raises questions over Royal Navy contracts
events.summary: Liberty Steel Dalzell plant in Motherwell with order for 34,000 tonnes of metal plate to build three warships has struggled to pay bills The Royal Navy is facing questions over whether three new warships will be built with British steel as its Scottish supplier faces deepening financial difficulties. Liberty Steel Dalzell, a plate mill in Motherwell, has struggled to pay its bills and workers in recent weeks, according to several people with knowledge of operations. The government said it was “closely monitoring” the situation at the plant, amid growing concerns over its survival. The National Energy System Operator (Neso), the government body in charge of keeping the lights on, filed a winding up petition against the company last month, according to public court records. It is understood that its debt, thought to be for electricity transmission charges, has now been repaid and the petition will be withdrawn. The Dalzell plant has an order to make 34,000 tonnes of metal plate to build the navy’s fleet solid support (FSS) ships. They are due to be built in Belfast by the Spanish state-owned shipbuilder Navantia in a £1.6bn contract. The financial struggles of Liberty Steel Dalzell and its owner, the Gupta Family Group (GFG) Alliance controlled by the metals tycoon Sanjeev Gupta, have cast doubts on whether the plates will ever be made. The Dalzell mill is the only one in Britain capable of producing the plates needed, but its output has been limited for two years because of shortages in working capital. The first of the 216-metre FSS ships, designed to carry munitions, food and other supplies for the navy’s Royal Fleet Auxiliary, is planned to be delivered in 2031. The contract was awarded to Navantia in the hopes of revitalising Belfast’s historic Harland & Wolff shipyard that built the Titanic. Several people in the industry and unions believe Dalzell could be part of an integrated British supply chain if it had working capital. British Steel’s Scunthorpe blast furnaces, now under government control, could supply metal to Dalzell to make the plates that are then used in Belfast to build the ships. However, the longer Dalzell goes without producing the steel, the more likely Navantia is to source the metal elsewhere. Navantia has already said it would build the first ship largely in Spain because the Harland & Wolff shipyard was not yet ready, in comments to the Financial Times in September. Unions have called for the government to protect the Dalzell plant. Alasdair McDiarmid, the general secretary of the Community union, said: “We need to see a viable plan for Dalzell’s long-term future – the workforce deserve nothing less. If Liberty cannot produce this now, the case for government intervention will be unavoidable. We simply cannot afford to lose this crucial asset for Scotland , and for the entire UK steel sector.” A government spokesperson said: “This has been a difficult situation for the staff and local community supporting Liberty Dalzell. We want to see the company operational once more, and are closely monitoring the situation. “Navantia UK has a ‘local first’ policy when it comes to suppliers for the fleet solid support programme. Ministers have encouraged Navantia UK to use UK suppliers, including for steel, where possible.” The Dalzell plant has produced some plate in recent weeks, using steel that is said to have been sourced from Kazakhstan, but that is not suitable for the defence contract. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Workers’ pay packets have been late twice in recent months, including at the end of October. Staff are also concerned because the pension provider Aviva said it was “currently unable to accept further pension contributions into the workplace pension plans for members of this scheme”. A GFG spokesperson said the company was “engaging with Aviva and the Pensions Regulator to fix this as quickly as possible”. It is also understood that the company providing security to the Dalzell site walked away over the weekend after its bills were unpaid. Gupta’s businesses have been under financial pressure for several years because of the collapse of his main lender, Greensill Capital, in 2021. Companies within GFG remain under investigation by the UK’s Serious Fraud Office for suspected fraud, fraudulent trading and money laundering. A GFG spokesperson said: “Like the rest of the UK steel industry, Dalzell faces tough operating conditions with energy costs far higher than the prices its international competitors pay. Despite that the plant has restarted and GFG are pursuing new commercial deals to bring more volume through the mill. “The Navantia contract remains in place and Dalzell’s UK slab supplier has indicated capacity from early next year.” A Neso spokesperson said the body could not comment on specific debt recovery cases.

events.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
events.summary: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto , the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness. One month before release, it is quiet at Rockstar’s headquarters. A lot of people have finished their labour on the game and are taking time off in the run-up to launch – a well-deserved rest after more than 10 years of development. Those who remain here are caught in the strange no man’s land between finishing a piece of art and releasing it into the world. When it does come out, GTA VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of entertainment ever made, projected to shift tens of millions of copies and earn billions in its first year; its predecessor, 2013’s GTA V, sold 230m copies. In the midst of a horrible time for the games business, full of studio closures layoffs and soaring development costs, a whole industry is relying on GTA VI to give it a shot in the arm. On one near-deserted floor, a screen shows a countdown to the release date. For many players, meanwhile, the 13-year wait for a new Grand Theft Auto has become unbearable. When footage of GTA VI made its glitzy premiere on Netflix, it almost took the streaming giant’s servers down. Its first trailer has been viewed 300m times on YouTube alone. Across the world, people have booked days off work on 19 November to experience this event together – one of those increasingly rare shared global cultural moments in an age when we all live in our own algorithmic content bubbles. There is a slightly strained atmosphere at Rockstar North, and not just because of the pressure of GTA VI’s impending release. Over in Glasgow, Rockstar is also defending a high-profile employment tribunal case over the dismissal of 34 of its employees last year, who claim they were fired because they were involved in union organisation efforts . The case was due to wind up in October, but will now drag on right up to Grand Theft Auto VI’s release. A few days before my visit, head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe was testifying in court as former employees and their reps at the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) protested outside. Today, Kolbe is sitting in front of me with Rob Nelson, co-studio head of Rockstar North and one of the three creative leads on GTA VI, showing me what the studio has spent more than a decade and, by independent estimates that Rockstar will not confirm, more than $1bn making. On screen, Jason and Lucia – two young criminals on the run – are on their way from a bar to a nightclub, walking through downtown Vice City as the last vestiges of sunlight disappear and the streets become bathed in fluorescence. He is tall, square-shouldered, in a T-shirt and shorts; she has her hair up in a ponytail, wearing one of those merciless long-sleeved crop tops that almost nobody can pull off. After dancing with each other at the club, part of a crowded mass of virtual people gyrating in neon UV-reactive mesh tops, they will each don a cap, sunglasses and a bandana over the face, and hold up a jewellery store before escaping into the night in a beaten-up car, the boot stuffed with holdalls filled with cash and sizeable firearms, evading the cops by driving right through a cornfield in an apt echo of Bonnie and Clyde. Lucia is the first woman to have headline billing in a GTA game, part of a long lineage of criminal protagonists who range from the straightforwardly psychopathic (GTA V’s Trevor) to the unexpectedly sympathetic (GTA IV’s Niko Bellic, and San Andreas’s CJ). GTA VI is both her story and Jason’s.

events.title: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
events.summary: Illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital. Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help. The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital.  When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container. “They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said. Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt their family. “Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going to give me locked up.” Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how, weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground. “I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement. “He stated many.” According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.” In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe. Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences. The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged with murder. But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell. His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.  In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to prison. A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024 — and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs while pregnant.  Courtney Haney at a family member’s home last month in Dothan, Alabama. Her daughter was born healthy, but Haney spent four months in jail for prenatal drug use. A. Wallace for ProPublica Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January 2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed the treatment offered by the court. “During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”  As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek justice in this case,” he said. Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied, “That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital. “If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email. Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her organization has identified 2,298 cases of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy. Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for pregnancy loss appear to be on the rise compared with the years before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion. “Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting worse.” Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and eye. In that time, something shifted.  “I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.  She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. She also wasn’t sure if she and her daughters could safely leave him. events.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left company in August 2025
events.summary: A woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang leaving a restaurant after attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in Taipei in May 2025. Megaspeed said on Nov 15 that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , whose ties to former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang raised US national security concerns, had officially left Megaspeed on Aug 30, 2025, and has no current role there. The Singapore-based cloud-computing company is an Nvidia business partner in the Asia-Pacific region and has been in the spotlight after reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom the US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang’s personal and private matters,” the company added in a statement. In October 2025, the New York Times reported that Megaspeed was under US investigation over whether it helped Chinese customers obtain Nvidia computer chips subject to Washington’s export controls. China has denied the allegation and Megaspeed has not been found to have violated ​the rules. “Megaspeed is aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence, ” it said in the Nov 15 statement. The company said it conducted “legitimate and lawful business” and had retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation. It added that its operations and supply chain controls were designed to comply with applicable laws and regulations, including US export-control requirements. Alice Huang became the controlling shareholder of Megaspeed in March 2023, according to Washington-based research group C4ADS, which reviewed corporate records. The US government and Nvidia did not respond immediately to Reuters requests for comment on Megaspeed’s statement. REUTERS

events.title: Tata heir questions big bets as US$185 billion group feud deepens
events.summary: Noel Tata, chairman of the trusts that control Tata Group, questioned whether some of the conglomerate’s biggest investments are being executed with enough discipline. Noel Tata questioned whether Tata Group has enough discipline in major projects, as the group pours billions into semiconductors, aviation, electronics and EV batteries. The feud has deepened over capital allocation, governance and a possible Tata Sons listing, with Tata Trusts resisting outside shareholders and saying a public listing could change “the Tata way”. A confidential analysis said semiconductors, electronics and aviation need more than two trillion rupees in extra capital, while Tata Trusts remain “100% behind” national projects but want tighter execution. MUMBAI – Noel Tata, chairman of the trusts that control Tata Group, questioned whether some of the conglomerate’s biggest investments are being executed with enough discipline, deepening a dispute over capital allocation, control and a potential listing of its holding company. The clash has widened as the group commits billions of dollars to semiconductors, aviation, electronics and electric-vehicle batteries, while the trusts that own 66% of Tata Sons resist a listing that would bring outside shareholders into the closely held parent. The dispute now reaches beyond succession and ownership to how a group generating about US$185 billion (S$238.3 billion) in annual revenue is funded, governed and run. “The question is, do we have the discipline when we execute projects, and not the direction?” Tata said on Nov 14 at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi. “How will projects with a long gestation period succeed if we don’t have discipline?” Much of the expansion has been pursued under Natarajan Chandrasekaran, the professional executive who has led Tata Sons since 2017. A confidential analysis prepared by Tata Trusts and reviewed by Bloomberg News estimated that semiconductors, electronics and aviation would require more than two trillion rupees (S$27.33 billion) in additional capital. The governance dispute widened after Tata Sons’ board backed Chandrasekaran for another five-year term on Sept 17, despite Noel Tata’s opposition. A spokesperson for Tata Sons did not immediately respond to a request for comment on his remarks about execution, capital allocation and a possible listing, sent over the weekend. Tata companies generated about US$185 billion in revenue in the year through March and own businesses ranging from Jaguar Land Rover to Tetley tea. Tata Trusts owns 66% of Tata Sons, and profits from group companies ultimately help fund philanthropy. That ownership structure has also allowed Tata Sons to support businesses through periods of weak returns or heavy investment. Noel Tata has argued that a public listing, and the arrival of thousands of outside shareholders, could make that model harder to sustain. “My worry is that listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way,” he said. With 30,000 to 40,000 shareholders, “profit may take precedence over philanthropy”. Pressure to go public intensified after the Reserve Bank of India classified Tata Sons as an upper-layer non-banking financial company, a designation that carries listing requirements. The Trusts have opposed that outcome and explored a restructuring aimed at keeping the parent private. Noel Tata said the Trusts remain “100% behind” investments in projects of national importance, even as he called for greater discipline in how the group executes them and allocates capital. events.title: Pasta, pies and paperwork errors: the reality of Brexit food checks
events.summary: Delayed deliveries and inspection hold-ups among issues facing hauliers navigating post-Brexit border processes Three small boxes of spinach and ricotta cannelloni destined for a supermarket in Gibraltar languish on an EU inspector’s bench at the Eurotunnel terminal in Calais . They have been removed from a truck laden with perishables for British food lovers on the Rock – Morrisons steak and ale pie, family-size blocks of Morrisons cheddar cheese, ‘M’ Best coleslaw from Avondale foods in Craigavon in Northern Ireland and long-life milk. “We have been here nine hours now. It is very difficult,” said the lorry driver, Daniel Vasco, as he prepared to restart his 24-hour drive from London to Gibraltar. An official says the truck had originally planned to cross from England on a ferry from Dover but arrived via a freight train instead with the prerequisite dossiers of customs and food health certificates filed for arrival a few miles away. “We had to create 78 different files,” she explains, adding the pasta had to be removed because of a simple error. “The health official had put today’s date rather than the use-by date of 16 November on the paperwork,” said Olivier Colin, the director of customer service for Eurotunnel in France. This is the reality of Brexit and business is brisk. A few metres away in a refrigerated unit lie two pig carcasses wrapped in cellophane alongside several pallets of fresh food removed from different trucks that morning. The French official explains that when they opened the truck the found they had fallen from their hanging positions and with a risk of contamination had, under the rules, to be removed and destroyed. Paperwork that includes export health certificates, customs paperwork, veterinary certificates related to meat and transit documents did not exist when the UK was in the EU’s single market. Next Friday Andy Burnham and EU leaders are expected to sign a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal which will make exports of fresh food, drink and animal products such as leather easier. But without a full return to the single market, not all checks will disappear. Customs declarations will still be required along with other red tape. A report published last Friday by the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) showed that small to medium-sized businesses were worst hit by the Brexit checks. It is understood the earliest the new SPS deal will be implemented is January 2028. This is because of the need to pass legislation in the UK to realign continuously with EU regulations on food and animal products. For Getlink, the owner of Eurotunnel, it should restore some lost trade but it will also mean dismantling some of the €60m (£50m) Brexit infrastructure now made redundant. Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, said: “We would have preferred not to invest the money … but we decided not to complain, not to whine and say: ‘Ok, this has been decided by British citizens and, like it or not, it is our responsibility not to turn the new controls into a huge bureaucracy.’ “We carry 26% of the trade between Europe and the UK. That is why we invested,” he added noting however that trade had declined just over 20% in both directions since Brexit with exports of poultry and eggs in particular collapsing. Peter Roberts, the commercial strategy director for freight at Eurotunnel, said: “We have put everything we possibly can in place to make it as quick as possible but we can still end up with three packets of pasta on the table because someone made a paperwork mistake. When that paperwork is lifted it will be good for us, good for the driver, good for trade and the economy.” The efficiencies achieved over six years since Brexit are evident on one freight train over the Channel tunnel where the Guardian joined drivers. Just three of the 33 trucks and vans were redirected for checks on arrival – one for SPS checks and two for customs paperwork. Among those cleared to go is Gavin Woodward, bringing M&S labels to a food client in Belgium. He is returning with waffles but he recounts how in the past he has been stopped occasionally if he had “high-risk” cargo, which in his case, is chilled sliced ham. Carlos, a Spanish driver, is driving back to Spain after delivering fruit and veg from the Murcia area in Spain to Tesco in the UK. “I am stopped two to three times a month,” he says. “A deal will make a difference. Once I was stopped for two or three days. I was carrying meat.” Earlier this week, the Defra report showed that many small and medium-sized exporters had stopped exporting to the EU completely since Brexit. It cited a report by Aston University estimating that an SPS agreement “could boost UK agri-food exports to the EU by up to 22.5%”. A separate House of Lord report on Friday cited government estimates that the SPS deal “would increase GDP by up to £5.1bn by 2040 (up to 0.14%)“. “It could be a gamechanger,” said Leriche.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Cambridge museum celebrates the world's first business computer with films, family activities, and a little Python Vintage fun: Prodding AI agents using retro hardware just because you can 13 days ago Give him a hand: Dev publishes 25-year-old Palm OS tools to GitHub October 15, 2026 Spies, prime ministers, and balls: The BBC Domesday project @ 40 October 4, 2026 YouTube lunatic designed and 3D printed a working mechanical calculator September 30, 2026 A 1980s PDP-11 is still running Unix – and now you can watch September 23, 2026 Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all. The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children. The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories." Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids. Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it. LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013 . It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge . The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011 . The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory. The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948 . EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. events.title: ‘We will chase them down’: Debt collectors pursue claims exceeding $2m linked to Lao Huo Tang
events.summary: Debt recovery companies FDR Services and A.S.K Debt Recovery SG said they were separately pursuing claims amounting to more than $550,000 and close to $2 million respectively. Debt collectors say they are chasing more than $2 million in unpaid supplier claims linked to Lao Huo Tang Group, with visits to outlets and repeated failed contact attempts. FDR Services says it is handling $550,795.58 in claims from three suppliers, while A.S.K Debt Recovery SG says its cases approach $2 million across several businesses and creditors. The dispute adds pressure on the group, which has faced CPF arrears cases and a winding-up order for Singapura Heritage Food Hall, while management and Thomas Hong have not responded to latest queries. SINGAPORE – An unassuming mixed rice stall in Bedok Reservoir Road became the focus of debt collectors on a quiet afternoon on Nov 12, as they pursued unpaid claims from businesses linked to the Lao Huo Tang restaurant chain . The visit to Le Xin Mixed Veg Rice was among a series of attempts by debt recovery agencies to recover unpaid invoices involving companies linked to Thomas Hong, the founder and chief executive of Lao Huo Tang Group. Hong has held directorships in several food and beverage businesses. According to corporate records obtained by The Straits Times, he is listed as a director of companies such as Lao Huo Tang Investments, Lao Huo Tang Canton, Singapura Heritage Food Hall, Kenny Rogers Roasters and Le Xin Mixed Rice. He is also a shareholder of Lao Huo Tang Investments and has previously served as a director of other F&B companies. At the stall on Nov 12, debt collectors from FDR Services encountered an elderly man whom they believe to be Hong’s father. The commercial debt retrieval agency said the man declined to assist with their attempts to recover payment and indicated that he would contact the police. The visit to Le Xin Mixed Veg Rice stall in Bedok Reservoir Road was among many attempts by debt collectors to recover money owed to suppliers of businesses under or associated with Lao Huo Tang Group The collectors subsequently left a notice at the premises. Speaking to ST, FDR said it is pursuing claims totalling $550,795.58 on behalf of three suppliers, while another agency, A.S.K Debt Recovery, said it was handling claims approaching $2 million involving businesses associated with the restaurant group. It is unclear whether the amounts being pursued by the two agencies overlap. The claims involve various companies and outlets operating under several food brands. The amounts have been provided by the agencies and have not been independently established as debts owed by Hong personally, though he has become the central figure in the debt collection agencies’ pursuit of unpaid claims. More than $550,000 allegedly owed to 3 suppliers FDR said it was handling claims by suppliers that provided vegetables, meat, frozen food and other food products to restaurants and food stalls operating under various brands believed to be linked to Hong. According to documents provided by the agency, one vegetable supplier was pursuing $335,494.97 in allegedly unpaid invoices for deliveries to several outlets, including those at NEX, Jurong Point, Causeway Point, The Star Vista, Sun Plaza, Waterway Point and Seletar Mall. Of this amount, $63,740.21 was allegedly owed for deliveries at NEX, more than $59,000 at The Star Vista and $51,488.37 at Jurong Point. The invoices date back to 2025, with some outlets allegedly failing to settle payments for several consecutive months. FDR initially handled nine cases involving the vegetable supplier when they were referred to the agency in April. Its portfolio subsequently expanded to include claims from other suppliers, taking the reported total to $539,810.91. This was later revised to $550,795.58 after additional cases involving a meat supplier were included. The claims involve several companies, including Lao Huo Tang Investments, Singapura Heritage Food Hall and businesses operating other food brands. Another agency pursuing claims approaching $2m Separately, A.S.K said it was handling claims approaching $2 million involving several suppliers and creditors of businesses operating under or associated with Lao Huo Tang Group. In a statement to ST, the agency said one client had identified $356,138.36 in outstanding invoices across 10 accounts involving various outlets. These included $52,684.16 allegedly owed at The Star Vista, $50,360.43 at Waterway Point, $46,674.85 at Jurong Point and $36,277.32 at Bukit Panjang Plaza. The same client was also pursuing payments involving other businesses, including Singapura Heritage and Kenny Rogers, taking its total claims to approximately $570,000. Two other clients were pursuing more than $50,000 collectively, while another separate matter involved close to $1.2 million.

events.title: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader. He’s even eyeing the White House
events.summary: An Elon Musk acolyte, Tesla driver, and serial entrepreneur, Teague Egan was imagining ways of breaking into renewable energy in 2018 while he took a vacation to Bolivia. He learned about the country’s salt flats, their lithium reserves potential and, eventually, about the industry’s antiquated lithium mining techniques. “As an entrepreneur, I knew there had to be a better way. That was my ‘aha’ moment,” said Egan, now 38. He really began to think about how the lithium-ion batteries in Tesla’s electric vehicles are made and their massive global growth potential. He quickly founded EnergyX—short for Energy Exploration Technologies—and this year became the only company mining lithium commercially in the U.S. with modern direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology at its new Project Lonestar site in East Texas . This summer, EnergyX also opened a project in Chile extracting 170 metric tons of lithium a year. But these are still just demonstration plants. The real growth is about to begin, he touted. “EnergyX is just going to keep our head down and move towards commercialization,” Egan told Fortune . The plan is to commence construction next year. EnergyX aims to bring its Black Giant lithium project in Chile online by the end of 2028 with a first phase producing 7,500 tons per year and expanding to 52,500 tons annually by 2030. Project Lonestar in Texas would quickly follow with a 15,000-ton facility in 2029 and growing to 50,000 tons by 2031. These are admittedly aggressive timelines, but Egan is confident the progress will pick up quickly after achieving a watershed moment in October of inking its largest customer. But first, let’s take a quick step back. Two years ago, The Wall Street Journal ran this headline about Egan: “He Wants to Be the Lithium King. Run for President. And Live to 150.” The wording is brash but not inaccurate—yes, he says he still wants to occupy the White House and live well past 100—and he comes across as an over-the-top tech bro. Many didn’t take him seriously. Egan went to work proving the doubters wrong. Since then, EnergyX opened its new Austin, Texas headquarters, nearly quadrupled its acreage footprint in the lithium-heavy Smackover Formation in East Texas and southwestern Arkansas, completed its Texas and Chile demo projects, and received a $225 million influx from Italian energy giant Eni. Most importantly, in October, major energy trading house Trafigura signed a $2 billion, 10-year contract with EnergyX for 100,000 metric tons of lithium from its Black Giant and Project Lonestar enterprises. “To have that type of customer is not only really encouraging for us, but also really validating to the rest of the market,” Egan said. “This is actually the single-largest DLE offtake in history. That’s a cool little feather in the cap. The major thing that investors or project lenders need to see is that type of contract.” His expectation is that more buyers will quickly follow suit, bringing EnergyX close to commencing construction. The Trafigura deal also boosts EnergyX’s pending $690 million loan with the U.S. Export-Import Bank. While EnergyX’s success is far from assured, Egan has proven his company must be taken seriously. Drilling ahead Egan’s mentor and idol is his father, Michael Egan, who became the majority owner of Alamo Rent a Car, grew the company nationally, and sold it in 1996, continuing to chair the business until 2003. Now retired, Michael Egan sits on the EnergyX board. “I’m a serial entrepreneur. My dad was a serial entrepreneur. I learned from him,” Teague Egan said. “I don’t have an engineering or a chemistry degree. I’m an entrepreneur. I’m a problem solver. I feel like I have a Ph. D. in engineering from working at EnergyX for eight years.” After growing up near Fort Lauderdale, Florida, Egan moved to Los Angeles to attend the University of Southern California. While a college student, he started a record label and sport agency. He quickly found success in music after signing the Boston rapper Sammy Adams, who hit No. 1 on the iTunes hip-hop chart in 2010. Egan said his biggest regret might be declining to sign a deal with his label and Interscope Records because Egan didn’t find much continued success in music. Then again, if he had, EnergyX probably wouldn’t exist, he said. His music profits though led him to invest many of his gains. He was an early investor in Tesla in 2013 when the company still had a market cap of less than $10 billion. Today, Tesla sits above $1.5 trillion. Egan said he used some of those proceeds to help start EnergyX. Ever since, Egan has become an admitted follower of all things Elon Musk and his approach to business. And they’re both Austin, Texas-based now. “He’s transformed into arguably the greatest entrepreneur and innovator in the history of humanity,” Egan said. “People can say about what they want about his political views and stuff but, in terms of his contributions to humanity, he’s like unmatched. He’s essentially my idol other than my father. He has that same sense of curiosity and problem solving.” EnergyX Leaning into lithium Driven by EVs and now also by battery energy storage, global lithium demand has jumped more than 400% this decade, to over 1.5 million metric tons per year. By 2035, that demand could approach 4 million tons. With the lithium business focused on traditional hard-rock mining or evaporation ponds, Egan sought another way. Evaporation ponds can take two years to extract the lithium, literally waiting for the sun to evaporate the water and help filter out the lithium. Egan isn’t that patient. He jumped into direct lithium extraction technology. He didn’t invent it, but he wants to perfect and commercialize it. Using advanced filtration technology, DLE operates much like oil and gas by drilling wells, pumping out the brine water, processing and refining the lithium, and returning more than 90% of the brine underground. DLE can take two days instead of two years, although the upfront costs are extensive. But the legacy lithium industry wasn’t ready to embrace DLE, and especially not the required financial investments. “Our original business model was just to license our technology to the existing pond producers. We said, ‘Hey, we have a better mousetrap. This will be much better for you,’” Egan said. “They strung us along and, finally, we realized that, and we said we’re going to have to go acquire our own resources and vertically integrate to prove this and scale it and realize the technology.” That’s when EnergyX began acquiring its own acreage in Chile and the Smackover. Chile and Argentina count among the top lithium producers globally—with Australia and China—but the U.S. only accounts a little more than 1% of global lithium supplies. events.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
events.summary: Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can W hen you walk up from Haydons Road train station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium. AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter – but that makes running a loss‑making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board, which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.” Kitcher was speaking before kick‑off in Saturday’s League One game at home against a Blackpool side dealing with a suspected norovirus outbreak in their squad. A superb arrowed strike from Alistair Smith and some vital late saves from Nathan Bishop ended Wimbledon’s winless run of 10 matches in all competitions. The 1-0 victory moved Johnnie Jackson’s side four points clear of the relegation zone and put a positive spin on a week that started with the fallout from the withdrawal of £87m of proposed investment, leaving the club’s finances even tighter. Wimbledon made a £2.6m loss in the 2024-25 season – a figure expected to increase by £500,000 when they publish their accounts next month – which, as Kitcher pointed out, is not as loss-making as a number of other clubs in League One. Those clubs voted in the summer to reduce spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, but now many want to go further to curb the spiralling losses at this level. “It’s an ugly way of running a sport,” said Terry Hunt, a supporter who has been attending matches with his son Billy since AFC Wimbledon were founded in 2002 after the move to Milton Keynes. Wimbledon returned home to Plough Lane in 2020, but had to create a bond to complete the move and the club still owe £7.5m in debts. In November 2025, the DTB warned that competing in the EFL at their new stadium was “not currently sustainable” under their structure at the time. The makeup of the club has since changed. Supporters voted last April in favour of reducing their voting rights from 75% to 50.01% – the same 50+1 model that gives fans the final say on decisions at German clubs – and Wimbledon sought a cash injection. An £87m investment proposal from Sloane Street Capital, a venture including the sole funder, Omar Mir, and the former Chelsea and England defender Ryan Bertrand, was already being voted on by fans when Mir suddenly walked away last Sunday, citing a change in his investment priorities. Mir passed Wimbledon’s due diligence tests, but the tech businessman was not a unifying figure. A Josimar report has detailed his “various connections to some of the most influential and controversial figures in football, technology and global security”. The 44-year-old did not attend either of the information evenings at Plough Lane after the proposal was first made in October, instead sending a two-minute video message, which meant fans could not directly ask him about his intention to purchase 90% of the economic rights of a fan‑owned football club. “We really wanted to have some kind of knight in shining armour,” said Niall Couper, a former member of the DTB and author of three books on Wimbledon. “In this case, I personally wasn’t sure how shiny that armour was.” Couper, who raised questions about Mir’s background before his withdrawal, chose not to attend the Blackpool game owing to anger from some supporters at the deal collapsing. Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football But the SSC deal is not completely dead. Bertrand and his remaining SSC partners Stuart Fiertz, Oliver Ward and Hugh Rosen – who would have owned 1.25% each of Wimbledon’s economic rights in the original proposal – have renamed themselves Sloane Street Football and are talking to other potential investors. In the meantime, the board will seek approval from fans about taking out a loan of up to £3m to “manage the club’s cash position”, but they believe they are able to manage it through to the end of this season and into the next. Which division Wimbledon end up in next season remains to be seen – Jackson’s side survived relegation by four points last April and the manager will probably have his hands tied in January. “I think we’ll probably go down, but bouncing between League Two and League One is absolutely fine by me,” Billy Hunt said.

events.title: ‘I’m scared about my future’: young people on the stress and desperation of jobseeking
events.summary: In the second in our series, four young Britons reveal how the search has taken a toll on their mental and physical health ‘The social contract is broken’: young people on feeling shut out of careers Guardian to follow lives of eight young people in their search for jobs ‘There must be something I could do’ – Celeste, 24 “I had to quit and move back in with my parents because I had developed ME/chronic fatigue syndrome. I am now housebound and cannot look after myself. Although I cannot prove it, I strongly believe that prolonged period of high stress played a big part in the decline of my health.” When Celeste, 24, graduated from the University of Edinburgh last year she spent two months applying for more than 100 jobs in the Scottish capital “just getting rejected or not hearing back at all from applications, 90% of which were waitressing positions”. “It was a really desperate time,” she says. “I was paying rent all of that time, and it was one of the most stressful times of my life.” Celeste had been doing part-time work in cafes since the age of 14 and eventually got full-time work in one, which she described as “very high pressure with terrible hours”. She was feeling unwell before taking on the role, and became increasingly sick until she left to move back in with her parents in Dorset. She had a health assessment for ME/CFS in August this year, but says it could be three to six months before she receives a formal diagnosis. Once she has that, she can start to get more support, including being put on a course to “teach me how to manage my energy” and put in touch with employers “who understand ME and already employ people like me”. She says the wait for a diagnosis is “frustrating”. Meanwhile, her application for a personal independence payment (Pip) has been rejected. She has appealed, but a decision on that could take up to a year and a half, she says, adding that she is relying on her parents to support her. Describing a typical day, she says: “I don’t really go out very much. My mum sometimes takes me to a forest nearby. She pushes me around in a wheelchair, and I can draw for about 20 minutes, and then get too tired and have to stop. It’s mainly just resting.” She hopes once she receives the formal diagnosis she can get on a path to finding employment, but until then, she is trying to think of ways she can work, given her condition. “I’m still trying to figure out how,” she says. “There must be something I could do.” ‘The job market is a lottery’ – Lenny, 26 “I feel like I’m a Neet, but the difference is I’m a Neet who has experienced work. There are different levels to it. You can have Neets who have worked before, but aren’t working now. Neets who haven’t worked at all, or Neets who have gone to school or gone to university but just haven’t found a job since they’ve left.” Lenny, 26, is describing his experience of being Neet – not in education, employment or training. While Alan Milburn’s youth joblessness review is focused on Neets aged 16-24, other economic bodies such as the OECD apply it up to age 29 . He has been unemployed for the past three years, but before then he had worked for two years as a customer assistant at a DIY store, before leaving to take a break for mental health reasons. “I’ve experienced work, I’ve experienced being on the payroll and clocking in, so for me, going into work wouldn’t be unfamiliar.” “Years ago, you could go into a shop and hand in your CV,” says Lenny, who lives with his parents and siblings in Birmingham. “Not that they would necessarily give you a job, but still it was a bit more personal. Now everything’s online and you end up waiting for them to get back digitally.” Lenny, who describes himself as Black British Caribbean, decided against further education after finishing college in 2019, where he gained BTec level 2 in business studies and in music. He did not pass English or Maths GCSE. “I did retake them twice, but I think after the second time, I just wanted to go into employment.” From 2023 to 2025, he was on universal credit. After that, he started doing the odd gardening jobs while receiving some financial support from family. Over the past three years, he has applied for “maybe 30 or 40 jobs” in different fields, including warehouse work, delivery driving and retail. Ideally he would like a manual job or work based outside. So sometimes it can be hit or miss.” He adds: “The job market is a lottery. How many jobs can you apply for without feeling miserable about your prospects? Maybe the lucky number is 100, 200, or 300?
