events.title: ‘Prove you are not a robot’: how the Captcha scam captures your computer
events.summary: Unlike familiar Captcha tests, this con asks you to press a series of keys. And that’s a way in for fraudsters to install malicious software Y ou are looking for some gifts for Christmas and want to support small businesses when you shop. When you visit the site of one you’ve heard good things about you are asked to verify that you are human. Instead of clicking on a series of images, or typing letters that appear, just as you have seen before, you are asked to press a series of keys and then press enter. This is a tactic known as the “ClickFix” scam one of the most popular used by criminals to trick people into infecting their own computer with malicious software, according to Chris Fistonich, a researcher with cybersecurity company Malwarebytes. “ClickFix is really one of the most sophisticated malware campaigns there is,” he says. “People are not prepared for this. They are used to solving Captchas every day. They’re used to being able to trust their security software. So it really has opened a new security loophole that’s being exploited extensively.” He adds: “This is the most popular way to get malware on to your computer. Certainly not the only way, but today it is definitely the most popular.” Captcha tests are familiar to many people as ways for a website to distinguish real from automated users. They often involve being shown a photograph and asked to do simple tasks, such as clicking on bikes or trains, or typing out grainy numbers. The ClickFix fraud looks similar. The message may say “Verify you are human by completing the action below” and request you tick a box. By checking the box, you have given the system permission to copy some malicious code to the clipboard on your computer. It will then ask you to carry out a task: “To better prove you are not a robot, please: Press & hold the Windows Key + R. In the verification windows, press Ctrl + V. Press Enter on your keyboard to finish.” This combination of actions pastes the text into your system and means your computer will be infected. In other versions of the same scam, you might be told that “something went wrong when displaying this webpage” with similar instructions to fix the issue. Like many scams, the ClickFix fraud relies on people acting quickly and without thinking through their actions properly, so pause and consider what you are doing whenever you are online. Some security software systems can block malicious websites with malware traps on them, so check what you have in place. If you have been compromised, contact your bank immediately. Then change your passwords, with the most important first.

events.title: Could Budapest be the next digital nomad hotspot?
events.summary: Hungary ranked fifth for digital nomads, behind Spain, the United Arab Emirates, Montenegro and the Bahamas, on a 2025 index compiled by VisaGuide. The country's White Card scheme provides one- or two-year residency permits for digital nomads from outside the EU. AI will further enable the digital nomad trend, according to one workspace operator, because people can create services or businesses without the resources of a large organization. When mechanical engineering graduate and entrepreneur Lexi Vindisch wanted to run her business from a remote location, she didn't pick a town in North America where she lived. Instead, Budapest was top of her list. With its mix of grand sights, cafés, cultural events and inexpensive public transportation, the Hungarian capital has become a popular place for digital nomads — people embracing the "work from anywhere" trend that took off during the Covid-19 pandemic. Based at co-working space Create26 in Budapest, Vindisch runs a domestic cleaning company based in Victoria, Canada, as well as overseeing Lead Machine, a marketing software firm for home service businesses. Why Hungary is a digital nomad hotspot Hungary ranked fifth for digital nomads on a 2025 list of countries, behind Spain, the United Arab Emirates, Montenegro and the Bahamas. The index, compiled by visa information website VisaGuide, considered factors such as taxes, income and cost of living. Vindisch, who has worked in many European and North American cities, but has Hungarian roots, said Budapest feels different. "I've been in locales that are super beautiful, well organized, great facilities, but they lacked a personality ... I've never been able to replicate the feeling that Budapest holds anywhere else," she said. EU citizens can work remotely from Hungary long-term if they meet certain requirements, while Hungary's White Card scheme, which provides one- or two-year residency permits for digital nomads from outside the EU, requires a net monthly income of at least 3,000 euros ($3,370). There are around 35 co-working spots in central Budapest, according to the Coworking Hungary Association, several of which are in the bustling District VI, near the fashionable bars and restaurants of the Jewish Quarter. Alongside these hubs, the city offers around 35 serviced offices, including locations from larger providers such as Regus and DBH Flex. "Budapest has its own vibe," said Áron Levendel, a founder of co-working space Kaptar, which is within view of the city's striking St Stephen's Basilica. "Whoever wants to connect, make friends or meet people, has an easy job. Whoever wants to have fun, learn or get experiences in English, will have the challenge of choosing from hundreds of options every evening," he said. Levendel and his co-founders are organizational developers who wanted a workplace that was both sociable and professional. In 2010, they came up with the idea for Kaptar (the word means "hive" in Hungarian). "Gmail was already there, but most of the work was not in the cloud or online yet; people had folders and papers. Digital nomads were not a thing," Levendel told CNBC by email. "Co-working" also wasn't a term in common use at the time, so he called the space a "közösségi iroda," or community office. Since the Covid-19 pandemic, Kaptar has grown more than 30% every year, according to Levendel, including a "wave" of digital nomads who joined after the pandemic, often arriving initially for a month but staying for up to a year. Overseas members either keep an existing job and work remotely, or they are freelancers who can travel, Levendel said. Mónika Gyurity opened co-working space Liftoff in 2019. After a career as a television executive, she wanted to expand her digital skills and bring different generations together to learn from each other. Located in a former elevator factory close to Budapest's central Nyugati station, Liftoff attracts a mix of professionals — including short-term visitors in need of a workspace, as well as remote employees working for international companies. One of Liftoff's team members is also a remote worker who regularly participates in Nomad Cruise voyages, or "workation" trips that combine a conference program with land excursions. Gyurity expects the digital nomad trend to continue, noting that AI now allows individuals to create and launch services or businesses without the resources of a large organization. "More people will be able to imagine their knowledge, skills and opportunities outside the traditional corporate world," she said. At the same time, she recommends that those in the corporate world spend time in a co-working environment. "Most people are there because they are trying to solve something," she said. "Every day I meet younger people who are at a very different stage of their lives and careers, use different tools, and approach problems differently. We can learn from each other.

events.title: Protesters drive home message to data centre company
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rally organiser Magdalene Lippett says the community does not want to see just a "pause" to the Tungkillo data centre plan. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) More than 250 people rallied at SA Parliament on Sunday, calling for plans for a data centre in the Adelaide Hills to be scrapped. Quantum DC announced earlier this week it would pause its plans to build a data centre at Tungkillo, following a strong community backlash. The SA government says it is working on developing legislation that will "comprehensively deal with the rollout of data centres". Hundreds of protesters have doubled down on their message to data centre company Quantum DC that its plans for a 1,200-megawatt AI data centre are not welcome in the Adelaide Hills. It comes after the company announced it would pause its plans for the development at Tungkillo earlier this week, after deep frustration, anger and protests from the surrounding community. At least 250 people rallied on the South Australian steps of parliament on Sunday, with various political parties including the SA Liberals, Greens, One Nation and independent federal MP Rebekha Sharkie in support of the protest group. Campaign organiser Magdalene Lippett said the community was hopeful it had won the fight against the development. Local farmer Kym Gladigau said the proposed area was prime land for food production. "The Adelaide Hills is a food production area, that's what it's all about," Mr Gladigau said. Kym Gladigau says there is limited prime agricultural land and the area should not be put at risk of bushfires. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) "We're losing farmland at Mt Barker, we've lost it at Virginia. "The risk with this data centre, is that we lose that. "If this thing goes wrong … we cannot afford another big bushfire in the Adelaide Hills, and who is going to tackle it?" Liberal leader Ashton Hurn, who spoke at the rally, agreed the proposed area should be reserved for farming. Ashton Hurn says Tunkillo is prime agricultural land that should be protected. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) "We keep hearing that data centres are a part of our future, there are of course economic opportunities, but we also need to make sure the community is brought along for the ride as well." Greens leader Robert Simms said he wanted to see the Tungkillo plans rejected if they reached the government. "That's why Greens are moving a motion calling on the government to reject this proposal," he said. "We're also calling for a statewide moratorium on data centres. We don't want to see South Australia become the test dummy for the nation." An estimated 250 people were at the rally. ( ABC News: Trent Murphy ) Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis said he was "very disappointed" with the Tungkillo developers, referencing the company's poor method of community engagement. "I mean, they have behaved in a way that has really lit this fire," he said. Mr Koutsantonis said the developers had not approached government at all about the plans. "I'm the energy minister and the treasurer. They've never spoken to me, and you would've thought the first door you'd knock on is the government's," he said. "Data centres are an essential part of our future. There's no world where Australia cannot have data centres. "If we don't have our own data centres, we'll be price takers rather than price setters." Mr Koutsantonis said the government was working on developing legislation that would "comprehensively deal with the roll-out of data centres". "Data centres have got to have almost no impact on the grid for them to operate in South Australia, and until that time is achieved, we won't license them." In response to Sunday's protest, Quantum DC CEO Alby Tomassi said the company respected the right of community members to express their views. "We want people to know we have heard their concerns," Mr Tomassi said. "That is why we have put our development application on hold and will now prepare a longer-term and more comprehensive engagement program to work through their concerns in a meaningful way." On Wednesday, the Dubai-based conglomerate said it was investigating a cyber incident involving “unauthorised access” to Shukran, involving customer names, contact details and dates of birth. Shukran's initial assessment on its website remained unchanged on Saturday. Analysts caution that this type of data could be used to create convincing impersonation scams, phishing messages and other forms of social engineering in which a victim is coerced to reveal sensitive information. “The key concern is that a data breach does not need to involve financial information to create opportunities for financial fraud,” Mohamed Emam, a security researcher at Singapore-based cybersecurity firm Group-IB, told The National . “Even when financial information is not compromised, exposed customer names and phone numbers can still be valuable to cybercriminals.” How fast can stolen data be shared? After information has been extracted from a compromised system, it has the potential to travel very quickly through the dark web – in mere minutes with some reports even claiming instantly – including in cybercrime forums, illicit marketplaces and private messaging channels. “Stolen information can circulate rapidly within cybercriminal communities. Depending on the nature of the breach and the attacker's intentions, compromised data may be offered for sale or shared on underground forums within hours of being obtained,” Mr Emam said. “However, not every breach results in immediate publication or sale. In some cases, attackers may retain the information for their own operations or distribute it privately.” Stolen data “can also be combined with information obtained from previous breaches to build more detailed profiles of individuals”, Maher Yamout, a lead security researcher at Kaspersky, told The National . That point is related to what US data privacy firm Cloaked calls the archive and enrichment phase, which typically happens two years after the data was stolen. It is a part of a broader journey for stolen data, according to the New York-based company. The first three phases are the triage window, the first 24 to 72 hours in which data is sorted and tested before hitting a marketplace; the general sale from weeks two through eight, where data is made available for bulk buys; and commodity pricing from the third to the 12th month, where a collection of data pulled from multiple breaches is sold at lower rates. A domino effect is also on the table, because threat actors can weaponise the stolen data on a broader scale, particularly involving the other accounts of victims. An example is a scammer calling and coercing you to reset your bank app password. “In the Shukran incident … [the stolen data] may not sound as serious as passwords or payment card details, but this information is typically sold to other criminal organisations on the dark web for use in future attacks on consumers,” Danny Jenkins, chief executive and co-founder of US cybersecurity company ThreatLocker, told The National . “Containing a breach is essential, but it does not mean the risk to affected customers has gone away. Even if the most sensitive data has been protected, any personal identifiable information can be of value to criminals.” Worst-case scenario That's part of more severe outcomes. Mr Yamout said the worst-case scenario is that seemingly basic personal information becomes the starting point for targeted attacks, with names, phone numbers and dates of birth giving criminals the tools to establish credibility and tailor their approach to individual victims. “This could lead to phishing attacks, identity fraud, account takeover attempts or financial scams if the method of the attack is convincing enough to trick victims into disclosing additional information or security credentials,” he said. If scammers successfully obtain login credentials, verification codes or other authentication information, the consequences could extend to account takeover, unauthorised transactions or identity-related fraud, Mr Emam cautioned. “The severity of the risk depends on what information was actually exposed and whether attackers can combine it with data obtained from other sources,” he said. “The immediate concern is not necessarily what criminals can do with a phone number alone, but what they may convince someone to reveal by using that information to gain their trust.”

events.title: Jensen Huang’s ousting sends tech stocks tumbling; Singtel CEO sells shares: Markets this week
events.summary: In this column, ST’s business correspondents unpack the latest developments in Singapore and global markets during the week – and explain what they mean for investors. Jensen Huang’s departure added to the volatility in tech stocks following the US midterm elections. SINGAPORE - Nvidia lost about US$700 billion (S$902 billion) in market value over the past week as its chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned on Nov 12. It was also revealed that he allegedly had a third extramarital affair involving a company executive. The chipmaker’s share price fell by more than 12% through the week, its sixth straight weekly drop and the longest losing streak since 2012. Once the world’s most valuable company, Nvidia has since October lost about US$1.8 trillion in market value. Nvidia announced its chief financial officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO while it commences its search for a new leader. Its board was reported by the media to have approached British chip designer Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor, even as prediction market traders speculated that Huang could make a comeback. Many in the industry, from Nvidia employees to Elon Musk, have voiced support for Huang, who has run Nvidia for the past 30 years and become one of the most influential executives leading the AI boom. Huang’s departure added to the volatility in tech stocks following the US midterm elections. But tech stocks fell again when markets opened the following day, with chipmakers and major cloud providers among the decliners. AMD fell more than 8%, while Broadcom dropped more than 4%. Microsoft’s shares recovered marginally after falling through the week, but still closed 0.3% lower than a week ago as it grappled with a worldwide outage of its Outlook and Teams services on Nov 13 that lasted for more than 24 hours. The Nasdaq closed 0.9% lower, while the S&P 500 also fell 0.4%. Singapore tech stocks closed the week higher, rebounding after the previous week’s rout following the US midterm elections. Semiconductor equipment maker AEM Holdings rose by 14.5% through the week to close at $7.10, while UMS Integration was up 8.9% at $1.84. Frencken Group, another SGX-listed company on the global semiconductor supply chain dealing in high-precision component manufacturing, also closed the week 6.4% higher at $1.84. Singtel CEO sells 2m shares after telco raises guidance Singtel Group CEO Yuen Kuan Moon on Nov 13 sold two million shares in the company at $4.07 per share, or $8.14 million in total. The transaction came hours after Singtel raised its forecast for operating profit growth at the businesses it runs directly. It now expects mid- to high-single-digit growth for the 2027 financial year, up from the low- to mid-single-digit growth it forecast in May. The revision came on the back of an 8.7% rise in first-half earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) for its operating companies to $902 million, led by strong performance by Australian subsidiary Optus, tech service provider NCS and its digital infrastructure arm Digital InfraCo. The group’s operating revenue also rose 5.5% to $7.3 billion, up from $6.9 billion in the year-ago period. But the telco still reported a 54.7% drop in net profit to $1.5 billion for the first half ended Sept 30, in the absence of one-off gains seen in the year-ago period totalling $2.2 billion from the partial stake sale in Indian telco Airtel and Thailand’s Intouch-Gulf Energy merger. Its Singapore business also saw EBIT drop 4.5% as a result of the absence of one-off income in the previous year, though mobile service revenue grew 3.8% in the second quarter compared with the first quarter – its second consecutive quarter of sequential growth. Still, group chief financial officer Arthur Lang said at the media briefing for the telco’s first-half results that the company was entering the second half of the year “with a renewed confidence versus six months ago”. He noted that Singtel had previously set a lower guidance due to the growing level of uncertainty, as the Strait of Hormuz crisis had just broken out and rising inflation was a concern. CEO Yuen added that the Nvidia leadership crisis would likely not have an impact on deliveries of chips for its sovereign artificial intelligence cloud arm RE:AI, under Digital InfraCo. The company provides local infrastructure for enterprises and government agencies to train and deploy AI models while keeping their data within Singapore, and is currently the only Singtel business that purchases chips directly from Nvidia. Around 2 MW of chips is due to be deployed from the fourth quarter of FY2027, and the shipment is expected to arrive on schedule. Singtel shares fell by 3.6% when the market opened on Nov 13, before paring losses to close the week half a per cent higher at $4.11.

events.title: Bitcoin tumbles to three-month low as liquidations accelerate
events.summary: Bitcoin slumped to a four-month low of US$62,112 (S$80,000) over the weekend. Bitcoin fell to a three-month low of just above US$63,000 after leveraged long positions were liquidated, while Ether also dropped sharply. Traders blamed higher rate hopes, US spot Bitcoin ETF outflows, a risk-off mood, and fallout from the US$6 billion Binance hack. Coinglass data showed about US$1.9 billion in crypto liquidations in 24 hours, and GSR’s Rich Rosenblum said Bitcoin may be near a technical floor. WELLINGTON – Cryptocurrencies tumbled over the weekend, with Bitcoin slumping to a four-month low as leveraged long positions were liquidated. The largest digital asset sank 5.7% in the US on Nov 14 and continued to drop in Asia on Nov 15 to as low as US$62,112 (S$80,000), down a further 3.6% and its weakest since July 14. Second-biggest token Ether, which slumped 8% in the US session, fell another 3.4% on Nov 15 to US$1,711, its lowest since July 8. “I think this is a technical move, as Bitcoin broke down through its 200-day moving average of about US$73,000, which has caused a slew of liquidations and new shorts to develop,” said Rich Rosenblum, co-founder of crypto market maker GSR. Crypto has been pummelled in recent weeks by a confluence of factors including the expectation of higher interest rates, large outflows from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, an AI-fuelled risk-off mood and continued fallout from the recent US$6 billion Binance hack. Bitcoin has slumped about 25% since Oct 21. Its low for 2026 is US$57,742, reached on July 1. Large liquidation events – in which more than US$500 million worth of Bitcoin positions are wiped over 24 hours – are becoming a recurring feature in the market, as sharp swings repeatedly flush leveraged traders out of their bets. On Nov 13 , Bitcoin’s slide triggered the liquidation of roughly US$1.3 billion in long crypto bets over 24 hours, with Bitcoin positions accounting for the majority of that sum, according to Coinglass data. In the 24 hours through 7am on Nov 15 in Singapore, exchanges tracked by Coinglass recorded about US$2 billion of crypto liquidations, including US$774 million in Bitcoin and US$488 million in Ether. Long positions accounted for the vast majority of the liquidations. From Oct 30 through Nov 13, US-listed spot Bitcoin ETFs saw almost US$3 billion in net outflows. Richard Galvin, executive chairman at crypto investment firm DACM, said the impending initial public offering of artificial intelligence company Anthropic PBC may be drawing capital away from crypto. “Price performance looks very similar to what happened through the SpaceX IPO pricing period earlier this year,” Galvin said. “It appears crypto remains a short-term funding source, particularly for retail investors. This is in addition to all the other macro headwinds.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: AI retreat fuels India stock comeback in great rotation trade
events.summary: Global funds are turning more positive on India’s US$5.4 trillion equity market as oil prices retreat and earnings growth accelerates. India stocks have rebounded as money moves out of crowded AI trades. The MSCI India gauge is up 11% from an October low and has gained over US$400 billion in value. Foreign investors are buying back into India as earnings improve and oil prices fall. November saw net inflows of US$8.5 billion, the biggest monthly inflow in six years. Many funds still hold India underweight, so more gains may follow. India trades at about 20 times forward earnings, below its five-year average, but 2026 performance still lags the wider region. Indian stocks suffered bruising losses in the first nine months of 2026 as the artificial intelligence trade hoovered up global investor capital . The unwinding of that strategy has turned the Asian nation’s equities into world beaters. The MSCI India gauge has rebounded 11% from a six-month low set in October, adding more than US$400 billion (S$515 billion) in value and almost erasing 2026’s losses, as the country’s relative lack of AI exposure has become a prime advantage. Global funds are also turning more positive on India’s US$5.4 trillion equity market as oil prices retreat and earnings growth accelerates. “We’ve become more positive on India and have added back to our exposure in recent weeks,” said Tan Altundag, an investment manager for emerging equities at Pictet Asset Management in Hong Kong. “We see an improving balance between macro headwinds, portfolio flows and valuations,” while “diversification away from the increasingly volatile AI trade also appears likely to benefit India,” he said. The bounceback in Indian shares over November illustrates a broader rotation by global funds away from crowded tech bets toward markets backed by strong earnings. The shift signals a potential turning point for emerging markets as a whole, testing whether the world’s fastest-growing major economy can reclaim its status as a premier alternative to US tech giants after months of trailing its global peers. A return of overseas investors has underpinned the rebound in Indian stocks, and the process may still have room to run as global funds remain largely underweight. Overseas buyers have snapped up a net US$8.5 billion of Indian shares in November, heading for the biggest monthly inflow in six years, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That has reduced the total 2026 outflow to about US$22 billion. Active long-only funds globally remain US$74 billion underweight on Indian shares relative to the benchmark, Bank of America data show, close to their lightest positioning since the bank began compiling the figures in 2015. Earnings for Nifty 50 Index companies may rise around 18% year-on-year in the September quarter, accelerating from 13% growth in the prior three months since August, Bank of America data also show. US-based Calamos Investments is among those boosting its holdings. The money manager’s emerging-market strategy has lifted its India allocation to more than 10% over the past three to four months from as little as 1% to 2% in 2025 , co-chief investment officer Nick Niziolek said. “We’re adding to India because we’re seeing an inflection in earnings,” he said. “We’re seeing an improvement in fundamentals, and we see really attractive valuations.” Kabouter Management is another overseas investor that is growing more positive. “As long-term investors, we remain constructive on the outlook for India,” said Nikhil Rastogi, portfolio manager at the Chicago-based money manager. Indian shares have faced many challenges since 2024 , “but these headwinds don’t change the long-term picture, and some of the global shifts behind them are working in India’s favour,” he said. “Valuations that looked stretched two years ago have become more attractive, particularly in pockets of the market.” The MSCI India gauge trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of about 20 times one-year-ahead profits, a discount to its five-year average, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The recent decline in oil prices is also helping shares in India, which imports nearly 90% of its energy needs. Global benchmark Brent crude has dropped over 18% from a high set on Oct 30 as investors wager that the Democratic Party’s sweep of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has increased the likelihood of an end to the Middle East conflict. “I’m comfortable on India while Brent sits around US$100 a barrel or below,” said Lauren Hyslop, an investment manager at UK-based Mattioli Woods. Despite the recent rally in Indian stocks, the market remains a relative laggard for 2026. MSCI’s India gauge has still dropped 2.2% in 2026 , whereas the index provider’s regional benchmark has jumped about 12%. The Indian measure is on track for back-to-back years of underperformance against its regional peer for the first time since 2020, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

events.title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
events.summary: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew. Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions. Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.) Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals. Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week . (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct . The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him; Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security. Even if it had, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, told TechCrunch that a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said. Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill , Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.” It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible. In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone. What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.” The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.

events.title: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds but are they value for money?
events.summary: Published 15 November 2026, 00:01 GMT It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach. "I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering. Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar. Customers likened the contents of Kim Kardashian's Skims calendar to something you would find down the back of a sofa This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa. Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use. "I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid." Julia, 39, says she thinks fragrance calendars are usually good value for money Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated. High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight. And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows , external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out. But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier. "I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist. She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product. "For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales." Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist, says the calendars "serve the purpose of allowing me to try out different products" Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice. "I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items. "And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy." Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, is less keen on the calendars and says they leave consumers "bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items" Jessica Jasper, a marketing consultant, is more positive - she thinks it's worth it. But she also thinks some companies are just jumping on a trend and that "some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing". So can beauty calendars offer value for both the brands and the customer - an example of a win-win? Or are they mainly designed to make us spend more at Christmas than we need to? "Some brands are getting a little carried away with the pricing," says marketing consultant Jessica Jasper Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and beauty expert, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them. "Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous. "But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it." This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it. In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do. "The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says. events.title: New Orleans port sues to get control of tanker that crashed into cruise ship on Mississippi River
events.summary: New Orleans port officials have sued the owner of a tanker that slammed into a cruise ship on the Mississippi River Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city’s port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company. All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived Friday as well as the crew on the tanker. Officials said 32 people were brought to the hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled. But none of the injuries were critical and eight remained hospitalized Saturday. The National Transportation Safety Board said the tanker’s voyage data recorder has been recovered. A 16-member team will spend a week in New Orleans investigating the incident. NTSB member John DeLeeuw said the agency expects to release a preliminary report within 24 to 30 days, with the final investigation report expected in 18 to 24 months. The lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now. The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham told reporters Saturday. The first step is to make sure the 16,000 gallons (60,500 liters) of fuel on the boat are removed safely, she said. Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon. The tanker appeared to lose steering, but the exact cause of the crash is not known, Burnham said. The National Transportation Safety Board was sending investigators to New Orleans. The first warning people on board the American Heritage had was the tanker blasting its horn several times as it floated toward the cruise ship, passenger Joe Knab told WDSU-TV. The hit was hard, and the ship immediately started leaning. The crew gathered everyone on the third deck to put on life vests and start getting them off the boat, but it suddenly rolled and sent Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River, where the water was 66 degrees Fahrenheit (19 degrees Celsius). Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help. Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Lauren Boebert will lose her seat in Congress to Democrat Laubacher, AP projects Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible “It’s fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time. I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn’t taste very good,” Knab told the television station, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud. Knab said he thinks he was in the water about 15 minutes. He laughed and said his 20 years in the Navy likely helped him. “They taught us not to drown,” Knab said. Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered. The rest of his belongings were in the river. Somehow his cellphone still worked. He hoped to get on a plane soon back to Wichita, Kansas, but he was not sure how Friday’s nationwide ground stop was going to throw another problem at him. Putting the life vests on the passengers as they waited to get off the boat likely saved a number of lives when the boat suddenly turned into the water, New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. “Whether it’s 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we retrieve them — I think was the best factor of success,” Montroll said. The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations. The Atlantic Asphalt is a 520-foot-long (160-meter-long) vessel. It had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands. The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization and was one of the defendants in the lawsuit filed Friday. Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic. China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment. The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

events.title: SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first
events.summary: SpaceX successfully caught the upper stage, or spacecraft, portion of its massive Starship rocket from orbit. Elon Musk's aerospace company made the historic catch using its “chopsticks,” mechanical arms attached to a launch tower, at its Starbase, Texas, facility. During the first phase of the flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the rocket's booster, instead diverting it to splash down in the Gulf of Mexico, where it exploded before hitting the water. After a booster explosion on Friday, SpaceX successfully caught the upper stage, or spacecraft, portion of its massive Starship rocket from orbit on Saturday — a triumphant milestone for the company. SpaceX made the historic catch using its "chopsticks," mechanical arms attached to a launch tower, at its facility in Starbase, Texas. Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship test yet, marked the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the rocket's booster and upper stage. Musk posted a video on X inspecting the upper stage craft after completing the capture. During the first phase of the test flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the booster, instead diverting it to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded before hitting the water. The rocket's upper stage then continued into orbit and flew around the Earth 14 times before successfully landing on SpaceX's launch tower, nicknamed Mechazilla. The Hawaii Department of Transportation issued a temporary pause on some West Coast flights Friday, due to debris risk from the flight. Separately, the FAA issued a rare, nationwide ground stop due to telecommunications system failures. (Both of those orders have since been lifted.) Making Starship a reliable and fully reusable rocket is critical to SpaceX's ambitions. In the near term, the company needs Starship to send more satellites into orbit to expand its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center. SpaceX is also expected to use Starship to bring astronauts and cargo from lunar orbit to the Moon's surface and back for NASA . Musk also has a grand vision to use Starship to "colonize Mars" and "make humanity multi-planetary." During Test Flight 15 on Friday, SpaceX released another 26 of its newest Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, growing its commercial satellite internet network. The company's constellation already included over 11,000 satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket can carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites, the company has said.

events.title: Author Tim Winton says Exmouth wrong place for a port
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Author Tim Winton leads campaign to stop Exmouth port development Tim Winton has been a long-term advocate against plans for a port in the Exmouth Gulf. ( Supplied: BlueMediaExmouth ) A deepwater industrial port in a northern WA tourist town is facing a backlash from locals and conservationists. The Exmouth Chamber of Commerce backs the plan and says it will provide plenty of benefits to the community. If approved, construction of the port is scheduled to begin in early 2029. A proposed deepwater industrial port in northern Western Australia has been described as unnecessary, unjustified and unacceptable by locals and conservationists worried about the impact on marine animals. The Gascoyne Gateway Marine Complex is proposed to be built just outside of Exmouth, 1,230km north of Perth, where it will feature a single jetty wharf, bulk fuel storage, a solar farm, and a seawater desalination plant. The port is proposed to be built 10km south of the township. ( Supplied: Gascoyne Gateway Ltd. ) The port will be designed to service cruise liners, defence and commercial supply vessels. The proposal has caught the attention of conservationist and famous author Tim Winton who has opposed the project. Exmouth local Brinkley Davies also said she was concerned about the port's location so close to town and World Heritage Ningaloo. "It is worrying because it is my front yard, but also the marine ecosystem that is at risk is a major factor," Ms Davies said. Having worked in marine conservation herself, Ms Davies has been involved in the campaign against the port since its initial proposal in 2020. Brinkley Davies believes more people are now aware of the issues with the port. ( ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel ) "It was not widely spoken about then and in the last five or six years, the town has really boomed and there is a lot more people living here and more people standing up for the place," she said. "There are a few key species that really have an importance in this area, one of them is dugongs. "There is a very important seagrass meadows where they are feeding and they also come in here to nurse their calves and rest, and that area is at direct risk of being covered in silt if they are going to dredge." Signs with messages opposing the port have been placed around town. ( ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel ) Fellow Exmouth local Violeta Brosig said she was concerned the port could impact the humpback whales that rely on the Gulf. "My main concern is it is going to be right in the middle of the parts of the humpback highway in Exmouth Gulf," she said. "It needs to be preserved and protected instead of destroyed." However, the Exmouth Chamber of Commerce president David Gillespie said it was an opportunity of a lifetime for locals and there would be flow-on benefits for the community. "There will be upgrades and roads, jobs, " he said. "There's for and against on both sides with businesses that agree to disagree, but I just get back to what the positives are from an economic perspective and what that will do for the town, for increased housing and population." Exmouth Gulf is now the chosen site for the Gascoyne Gateway Marine Complex. ( ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel ) Gascoyne Gateway CEO Daniel Jackson said there had been extensive community consultation and believed the majority of locals and businesses were in favour of the port. "We certainly acknowledge that there's seasonal windows, we're talking a few months of the year in which higher degree of risk mitigation is required to manage interaction between vessels and fauna, as it does now. "There's commercial vessels operating there today that are moving in and out and around fauna in the Gulf." The project is still undergoing approvals, with the WA Environmental Protection Authority currently undertaking public consultation. World renowned author, conservationist and patron of Protect Ningaloo, Tim Winton, said the Exmouth Gulf was the wrong place for a port. "It is one of the world's most important humpback whale nurseries and the idea of building a wharf a kilometre long into the whale refuge and to bring up to 600 vessels a year into the whale nursery just seems fundamentally wrong," Mr Winton said. "We're of the view that this is unnecessary, unjustified and unacceptable in its impacts to the Ningaloo estate." While this proposal could be approved by and started by 2029, the Exmouth Gulf is also being considered for National Heritage Listing, with that decision not expected until 2030. The WA government is also looking to establish a new marine park covering the entire Exmouth Gulf.

events.title: 'Root cause’ of nationwide ground stop is unknown, FAA says
events.summary: The inability to pinpoint the reason for the infrastructure malfunctions led the FAA to take actions that resulted in the grounding order, Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters. Officials reported issues with routers and networking equipment on Saturday, citing products and services from Cisco and L3Harris Technologies. "Until I can build [the new architecture], I'm stuck with L3Harris, who owns this network," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. The root cause of the longest halt in flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 remains unclear after a Saturday press conference by U.S. transportation officials. Routers and networking equipment appeared to be involved in the technological disruption that grounded flights across the country, but a definitive cause has not been established as of Saturday afternoon. The inability to pinpoint the reason for the infrastructure malfunctions led the Federal Aviation Administration to take actions that resulted in the grounding order, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, told reporters. "Because of our lack of identifying the root cause, we were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a sensor losing connectivity with aircraft," he said. "What we saw was instability. We couldn't explain the instability," Bedford added. Officials reported issues with routers and networking equipment on Saturday, citing products and services from Cisco and L3Harris Technologies . In a statement on X, L3Harris said that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." On Friday, Duffy and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin called for an air travel overhaul, with Duffy requesting $50 billion from Congress. FAA administrator Bedford said that router updates were a matter of regular business for his agency and distinct from modernization allocations. "We are constantly replacing 2,000, you know, Cisco 600 routers with Juniper routers, right? So this is ordinary course of business stuff. This is not part of the … FAA $12.5 billion modernization efforts. So let's not conflate those two things," Bedford said.

events.title: $180 million Van Gogh tests the art market and collector confidence
events.summary: Total sales at Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips are expected to be around $2.4 billion, which would equal last year's total, according to ArtTactic. Sotheby's alone is expected to pull in over $1.1 billion, with a single collection from The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection estimated at $450 million. The collection includes the two big headliners of the week: Vincent van Gogh's landscape "Châtaigniers en fleurs," (Chestnut Trees in Flower) estimated at $180 million and Paul Cézanne's "Arlequin," estimated at $120 million. A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions straight to your inbox. The art auctions in New York next week could top $2 billion, as a treasure trove of masterpieces comes to the market for the first time in decades. Total sales at Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips are expected to be around $2.4 billion, which would equal last year's total, according to ArtTactic. Sotheby's alone is expected to pull in over $1.1 billion, with a single collection from The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection estimated at $450 million. The collection includes the two big headliners of the week: Vincent van Gogh's landscape "Châtaigniers en fleurs," (Chestnut Trees in Flower) estimated at $180 million and Paul Cézanne's "Arlequin," estimated at $120 million. Neither has been seen in public for a half a century. Sotheby's CEO Charles Stewart said demand is strong in the art market, especially for the highest quality blue-chip works, as rising stocks markets and private wealth boost the confidence of collectors. "There's been enormous wealth creation and a lot of confidence in markets," Stewart said. "It's a global phenomenon. We're seeing recovery and greater interest across Asia and something really exciting happening from the Middle East across to Singapore and Europe and the U.S." Christie's star of the week is Wassily Kandinsky's "Betonte Ecken," estimated at $60 million to $80 million. Christie's CEO Bonnie Brennan describes the market is "confident but discerning, rewarding truly exceptional works." She said recent gyrations in the stock market and fears of an AI bubble aren't likely to deter serious collectors. "At the very highest end of our market, collectors tend to take a much longer-term view," Brennan said. "They understand that the opportunity to acquire a masterpiece may come only once in a generation, and that can be far more important than what the stock market has done in any particular week. In uncertain moments, the very best can actually become even more compelling." The art market has continued to rebound this year after declines in 2023 and 2024, with auction sales in the first half up 70% over last year, to $6.8 billion, according to Bank of America. Drew Watson, head of art services at Bank of America, said blue-chip art is outperforming, with Impressionist & Modern sales up 133% in the first half. "Our outlook for the art market this November is cautiously optimistic," Watson said. "Improving liquidity, combined with an unusually strong concentration of fresh-to-market private collections, creates a favorable backdrop for the marquee sales." events.title: Is his money mine and my money his? Here’s how my husband and I split finances
events.summary: Today, we are seeing a growing share of couples where wives out-earn their husbands, alongside more fathers quitting their full-time jobs to care for their children. SINGAPORE – As newlyweds a couple of years ago, my husband and I were determined to keep money talks to a minimum. A piece of advice a mentor gave me then was to prolong our “honeymoon period” as long as possible – “before life happens”. I interpreted that as avoiding conversations about money. It doesn’t help that my husband and I generally have conflict-avoidant personalities and so we don’t like to talk about money. For at least the first two years of our marriage, we set aside a few hours in the last week of December, sitting across from each other at a cafe to discuss goals for the year ahead and write down financial commitments we each would take care of. And that was about it. We have a neat plan, or so I thought. But as we know, life often doesn’t fall neatly into the little “boxes” we plan for. This means there are always additional expenses we haven’t factored in, such as unexpecte d health check-ups or the thousands of dollars we might suddenly need for car and appliance repair or replacement . Clearly, it does not make sense to review money commitments only once a year. So who pays for what? What’s fair? What are some healthy ways to split finances while keeping the marriage intact? US financial author and speaker David Bach aptly recounted the tension that arose from his first financial fight with his wife as a newly married couple in his book, Smart Couples Finish Rich. Just back from their honeymoon, Bach thought paying the bills and managing money as a couple would be “bound to be a breeze” since they were both working as financial professionals. Instead, their differing ideals took them by surprise. While Bach believed he could easily organise and separate the bills to see who would pay for what, his wife assumed they were going to put all their money into a joint account and pay everything together. “We are married now, we love each other, and from now on everything we have is one and everything we do as one,” she said, as Bach recounted in his book. Months later, they were still dealing with late fees because they couldn’t agree on who was responsible for what. They eventually created a system to manage their finances together – which was the whole point of the book – but more than that, I learnt it’s not a taboo to discuss money daily. Most couples have never been taught how to plan their finances together, said Bach, so most of them rarely discuss money unless they are fighting about it. Do ‘traditional’ notions still exist? I may have chuckled at his wife’s assumption that everything they have is one, but isn’t there some truth to the adage that his money is my money and my money is his? If we are going to build a home together, it feels neater to put everything into one pot and settle the bills from there. In Singapore’s context, however, the reality can be more complex, especially for dual-income couples with unequal earning power. A more educated workforce and an increasing proportion of women with tertiary qualifications have challenged traditional notions of husbands paying for everything or giving their wives an allowance. Furthermore, inflation and the rising cost of living in Singapore have made it imperative for women to contribute financially. Today, we are seeing a growing share of couples where wives out-earn their husbands , alongside more Singaporean fathers quitting their full-time jobs to care for their children . Some male friends say they prefer contributing a larger share to the household finances rather than giving an allowance to their wives who work . Gidon Jerome Kessel, group head of deposit and wealth management at UOB, told me that giving a spouse an allowance would depend on the couple’s circumstances and how they choose to manage their finances. Couples must also consider the lower- or non-earning spouse’s longer-term financial security, he said. For example, a working spouse can make CPF top-ups for his or her partner to build savings and support future retirement payouts. “If one spouse has no income because he or she is caring for the family or is earning less from part-time work, the important consideration is whether the couple’s financial arrangement adequately provides for that spouse’s day-to-day needs, personal spending and longer-term financial health,” Kessel added. Today, my husband and I have separate salary accounts along with a joint account that we both contribute to for big-ticket items like home renovation . He earns more than me, so he covers a larger share of our fixed household expenses, such as the car loan, insurance and utility bills. I chip in for other miscellaneous expenses like house maintenance, and help track our tax-related obligations. I also look for ways to invest and grow our combined savings.

events.title: From tour guide to HSBC strategy chief: How a Dutch student found his future in Asia
events.summary: Hong Kong-based Dutchman Herald Van der Linde, head of Asia equity strategy at HSBC, worked as a tour guide in China and Indonesia in the 1990s to earn money to fund his university studies. Herald Van der Linde left the Netherlands to work in Asia after a life-changing trip to China and now leads Asia equity strategy at HSBC in Hong Kong. He says his best money lesson is to “diversify and stay invested”; his ETF portfolio has grown nearly tenfold since 2005, despite major market falls. He values education, books and South-east Asian history, and would donate part of a windfall to education before investing the rest in an ETF. SINGAPORE – In the early 1990s, Herald Van der Linde wanted to earn some money to fund his university studies in the Netherlands. He also wanted to broaden his horizons and travel. The Dutchman decided to take on several jobs, including working as a tour guide in China and Indonesia. He recalled: “My first trip to China was particularly eventful: I was robbed of US$100 in Shenzhen and later found myself on a plane that made an emergency landing in a padi field near Guilin.” But he continued his journey, and the experience changed his life, he said . “From that point onwards, I knew that I wanted to stay in Asia and live and work there.” After getting his master’s degree in economics, Van der Linde bought a one-way ticket to Indonesia and became a financial analyst there. The 56-year-old is now head of Asia equity strategy at HSBC and is based in Hong Kong. He also channelled his love for the region into books. In addition to his financial leadership role at HSBC, he is a historian who has published books including a biography of Jakarta, an exploration of Majapahit, which he calls Indonesia’s greatest empire, and a book on Srivijaya, Indonesia’s first maritime empire. He said: “I was fascinated by the region, particularly South-east Asia, and immersed myself in its languages and cultures. I learnt Chinese and Indonesian, studied the region’s history, and eventually began writing books about it.” He is married to an Indonesian whom he met on a flight in Jakarta. The couple have one son, who lives in Amsterdam and is building a career in the music industry. Around 90% of the money I have saved, and do not expect to need in the next five years, is invested in global equity exchange-traded funds (ETFs). I focus on ETFs because they offer one of the most cost-effective ways to build a diversified portfolio through a single investment. I consider ETFs a significant financial innovation. They enable millions of people to invest at relatively low cost, helping to make diversified investing more accessible. In the past, building a well-diversified portfolio was often limited to those with substantial capital. What’s your approach when it comes to investing? I am a strong believer in investing in global equities and in the value of education. I regularly take part in continuing education programmes to broaden my knowledge and support my personal development. In the past, I completed online university courses in art history. However, as I have been busy writing a history book over the past few years, I have devoted less time to online study recently. Did you collect anything when you were younger? Books – I still love them. Nothing in my collection is particularly rare or valuable, apart from a few early editions; they are simply books I enjoy reading. My rare books focus mainly on Indonesian and South-east Asian history, including works written by Dutch archaeologists and historians. What was your first exposure to investing? Very early on, while we were students in the Netherlands in the 1990s, a friend of mine – now a professor of finance in Canada – and I tried to invest together. However, the bank turned us away because we did not have enough money. That was one of my earliest investment setbacks. I have occasionally tried to time the market, convinced that I knew what would happen next. On two occasions, the market moved in the opposite direction. Those experiences taught me an important lesson: invest and then stay invested. The power of compounding returns is substantial, so why take money out of the market and forgo that potential over the long term? What has been your biggest financial mistake? I once believed I could trade the markets successfully and make profitable short-term decisions. I learnt the hard way that it is generally better to remain invested and take a long-term approach. What has been your best financial decision? My best investment decision was simply to remain invested. Since I first invested in ETFs in 2005, their value has increased nearly tenfold, illustrating the long-term potential of equities. There have been significant downturns along the way, including the 2008 financial crisis and sharp market declines in 2020 and 2023. Through each of those periods, I stayed invested and maintained a long-term perspective. Moneywise, what were your growing-up years like?

events.title: Tens of thousands march in Portuguese cities against surging home prices
events.summary: Tens of thousands of people have marched in Portugal in the biggest protest yet against surging housing prices LISBON, Portugal -- Tens of thousands of people marched through more than 30 cities and towns across Portugal on Saturday in the largest protest yet against soaring housing costs that many say have put buying or renting a home beyond their reach. The housing crisis has fueled weeks of demonstrations. Some activists have camped in central squares in Lisbon and Porto, the country’s two largest cities. Riot police with dogs have dispersed some protests, drawing accusations of heavy-handed tactics. The demonstrations took inspiration from protests that began in neighboring Spain last month over similar housing concerns. They come amid widespread social unrest across Europe this autumn. Marching under the slogan “We won’t let them steal our right to housing,” participants ranged from teenagers to retirees. Drums, music and chants accompanied the Lisbon march as protesters carried large banners and flags. Susana Pacheco, a 35-year-old data analyst who works part-time as an astrologer to help pay her mortgage, said she worried about whether her younger sister could afford to move out of their parents’ home. “I’m really worried about young people,” Pacheco said. “I don’t know how they’re going to be able to pay” for their own home. “Things have become intolerable,” said Ana Encarnação, 42, citing rising living costs and the widening gap between rich and poor. Activists want ceilings placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction, and more affordable housing. House prices in Portugal have risen much faster than incomes, statistics show. Between 2015 and 2025, Portugal posted the biggest jump in the European Union in the home price-to-income ratio, with an increase of 61%, followed by the Netherlands with 34%, the EU statistical office Eurostat said last week. There is no indication that the rise in housing costs is slowing. Between the first quarter of last year and the first quarter of 2026, housing prices rose by almost 20%, the National Statistics Institute, a government agency, said last month. Foreign buyers and investment funds have fueled price rises by buying Portuguese real estate. The country’s mild climate and long coastline have helped it grow popular with digital nomads and other remote workers, as well as retirees. Tourism has also surged, with many city center apartments switched to short-term rentals. The government has responded with measures such as lowering taxes on new construction, restricting short-term rentals and promising to build 145,000 new homes. But it acknowledges that the effects won’t be immediate. Portuguese President António José Seguro, whose role is mostly ceremonial but who wields political influence, convened a Council of State, an advisory body, to discuss the protests earlier this month and met Friday with some of the protesters. events.title: US government says wire replacement caused nationwide grounding of flights
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Travellers in Atlanta wait for news about rescheduled flights. ( Reuters: Elijah Nouvelage ) Flights have resumed in the US after being grounded for about five hours, but airlines are struggling to clear a backlog. Officials are blaming the aviation shutdown on the replacement of old copper wires with new fibre ones. Nearly 29 million passengers are expected to fly on US airlines during the Thanksgiving travel period from November 20–30. The US government has blamed a nationwide aviation shutdown which has disrupted more than 20,000 flights on a program to replace copper wires with new fibre ones. Airlines are struggling to clear a backlog of delayed and cancelled services after a major air traffic control communications failure forced authorities to suspend departures across the country for about five hours on Friday, local time. Flights have since resumed , but airlines are warning it could take days for services to return to normal. The US government says it may have been the fault of a single router installed by a government contractor. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters on Saturday, local time, that contractor L3Harris had been replacing a section of the air traffic control system's old copper wire with new fibre wire, and that work somehow caused the system overload. Mr Duffy said the work caused "intermittent" communications and radar gaps. He said officials were investigating whether contractor "incompetence" or a faulty router was the cause. "Our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn't meet the moment," Mr Duffy said. L3Harris said it took the issue seriously, and was "supporting the FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the ground stop of our nation's air travel". Race to replace old copper wire system The issue began overloading communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centres across the country, which prompted the authority to halt departures because it could not identify a root cause. Mr Duffy said the new routers started flooding other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, which sparked communications issues with planes and radar at FAA facilities. The FAA is still trying to understand the root cause of what went wrong. It said communications did not go down but led to instability in data at the centres, and it did not lead to centres going dark. Mr Duffy said the routers being replaced were about 25 years old and were supposed to be replaced in 2006. The FAA spends $US1 billion ($US1.47 billion) annually to maintain its old copper wire system and is racing to replace it with modern fibre-based communications. "We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job," Mr Duffy said. "Virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fibre, from analog to digital." L3Harris noted it has completed more than 70 per cent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fibre-optic system. The disruption comes less than a week before the Thanksgiving travel rush, with industry group Airlines for America forecasting nearly 29 million passengers will fly on US airlines between November 20 and 30. Almost 10,000 flights were cancelled, including 1,800 on United Airlines. ( Reuters: Eduardo Munoz ) While officials expect operations to return to normal before the holiday rush, Mr Duffy has warned the process will be gradual. What we know about the US flight groundstop Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for a communications outage. Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed, leaving passengers stranded at airports across the country and forcing airlines to rearrange aircraft and crew schedules. Nearly 10,000 flights were cancelled during the disruption, including more than 2,200 each at Delta Air Lines and American Airlines, and 1,800 at United Airlines, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24. Some aircraft at major airports were forced to wait more than five hours for a gate, the website reported. US airlines will not be required to compensate stranded passengers because the disruption was caused by failures in the Federal Aviation Administration's systems rather than the carriers themselves. Flights in Europe were also afected by the problems in the US. ( AP Photo: Mike Stewart ) The impact extended beyond the United States, with European aviation authorities asked to suspend US-bound departures during the emergency.
