events.title: Got an iPhone Duo? These 9 settings make it easier to use
events.summary: Apple’s new foldable , the iPhone Duo, has proven popular enough that the company can’t keep the device in stock . While the Duo introduces a new way to use an iPhone, getting the most out of this initial version may require adjusting a few settings to make it work better when it comes to everyday tasks, like unlocking the device with Touch ID, navigating the interface, and taking photos. After spending some time with the Duo, we’d recommend making the following adjustments to make the new iPhone a bit easier to use, most notably when it comes to the use of Touch ID. Settings to make it easier to live with Touch ID Unlike modern iPhones, the Duo doesn’t support Face ID. That means you have to adjust to pressing a finger on the side of the device once again to authenticate with apps, unlock the device, and use Apple Pay. But there are a few things you can do to make the switch back to the older technology a bit less painful. Register extra fingerprints: This may seem like an obvious suggestion, but if you’re used to just registering a fingerprint or two with Touch ID, prepare to rethink that strategy with the Duo. Because the device can be held in multiple orientations, flipped both horizontally and vertically, and because of the small size of the Duo’s screen, you may find that a lot of your fingers (and thumbs!) can now reach the Touch ID button. We’d recommend holding the device in your hand and turning it in different ways, then register the fingerprints where you end up holding the device the most — on both hands. Yes, setting up Touch ID can be a bit tedious compared with Face ID, as there are multiple prints to register. Still, it’s a one-time setup, and later on you’ll be glad that you took the time to make more of your fingerprints work. To register a fingerprint, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Add a Fingerprint. Unlock with Apple Watch: If you’re in the market for the iPhone Duo, there’s a good likelihood that you own other Apple devices, like the Apple Watch. If that’s the case, you’re in luck because you can use your Watch to unlock the Duo without having to bother with Touch ID. This will save you time and frustration in the long run, so get used to wearing your Apple Watch more often, especially when you’re out and about and don’t want to fiddle as much with finger placement. To use the Apple Watch unlock, your watch will need to be passcode-protected and worn near your phone. To turn this feature on, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Unlock with Apple Watch. Rest finger to Open : This is an optional setting, not necessarily a “must” like the above, but we’ve found it useful. The “rest finger” setting is actually an accessibility feature, but it can double as a usability feature, too. When enabled, you only have to rest your finger lightly on the Touch ID sensor to unlock the device, instead of having to press down. Those who prefer this setting find it can make unlocking the phone faster and more convenient, but others may disagree, as they like the more tactile sensation of a button press. Try it both ways and see which one fits you best. To enable this one, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Rest Finger to Open . There are a few settings that could also improve your experience with the iPhone Duo, as they may make it easier to perform certain everyday tasks, like taking screenshots or reaching different parts of the screen, among other things. Turn off Fixed Volume Controls : This is a favorite hack for new Duo owners, as it makes using the device in any orientation much easier. By default, the iPhone Duo’s volume buttons are “fixed,” which means that no matter how you rotate the device, the Volume Up button remains the button that increases the volume and the Volume Down button decreases it. But many people find it’s easier if the buttons’ functionality rotates with the device. That is, the buttons re-orient themselves based on how you are holding the phone, making the “up” option always on the top or right. As you fold, unfold, and flip the phone, having buttons that flip with you actually makes more sense. To turn off the fixed volume controls, go to Settings > Sounds & Haptics > Fixed Position Volume Controls . Back Tap for Screenshots : The Duo tries to make it easier to take a screenshot by pressing the side button and either the Volume Up or Volume Down button at the same time. However, you still might find the process a two-handed affair (unless you just ask Siri to do it for you). That’s why many Duo owners are turning to a buried Accessibility feature to make taking screenshots a bit less complicated. In the phone’s accessibility settings, you can configure whether a double tap or triple tap on the back of the device triggers a particular action — which you can set to ‘take a screenshot.’ (Some people prefer the triple tap so they don’t accidentally trigger the feature.

events.title: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
events.summary: Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker asked Nvidia’s board to conduct a slow, deliberate CEO search that leaves open the possibility of Jensen Huang’s return. The firms disclosed about $2.13 billion of Nvidia stock combined as of June 30. Huang resigned as president, CEO and director on Nov. 12 after reports about personal relationships and amid an independent board investigation; Nvidia’s resignation announcement did not state a reason. Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang." Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker. Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing , with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June. The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress , who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence. "But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement. Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang , who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed . The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees. Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost." Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee. Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify . The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times. President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit China on Thursday, but doesn't plan to raise Nvidia and the suspected spy affair during his meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping , according to U.S. officials. Musk is expected to join Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

events.title: Transportation secretary blames ‘routine’ equipment upgrade for grounding flights nationwide
events.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a nationwide ground stop halting flights across the United States was caused by seemingly routine maintenance work. Duffy said that during “routine maintenance,” copper wire at a remote location was upgraded to fiber optic cable by L3Harris, a longtime contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration. After the upgrade, a router overloaded a critical communication system, leading to the ground stop. “It’s pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location,” Duffy said during a Saturday press conference that appeared to have technical issues of its own . “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence — meaning, was it user error or [installer] error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” The FAA’s acting CTO Rebecca Guy added , “When we started to see the occurrence where our network was having instability, we started to look at what was the cause. And as such, we saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate — a thousand connections over every four to five seconds.” Guy said the FAA disabled “both of those, right away and were able to stabilize our network,” and is now performing a root cause analysis. Duffy has repeatedly insisted, at multiple press conferences, that Congress needs to provide more funding for aviation equipment upgrades. Asked why the upgrades were made at 3pm on a Friday afternoon — rather than, say, at midnight on a Saturday — he responded that while “switchovers” at bigger airports will take place late at night, remote switchovers happen during the day. “There will be reevaluation of when we do this work,” he said. This was only the third nationwide ground stop of the 21st century. More than 8,200 flights were canceled on Friday evening, according to aviation data firm Cirium . And the effects continued after the ground stop was lifted, with at least another 3,000 flights canceled on Saturday. The ground stop came just a day after the FAA announced the rollout of an AI tool for air traffic controllers; the air traffic controllers union said it was not consulted in designing the system. However, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency sees “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related.” “We want to be clear that we have an equipment issue, and we’re working through what this defective piece of equipment was,” Bedford said. When Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked earlier if the ground stop was caused by AI, he replied , “We call it SI [ super intelligence ] around here, remember? events.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
events.summary: Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. Soon after, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown, too, citing competition in the market. “We got close, but ultimately couldn’t keep up,” co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon said on X . Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them. Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December. Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard.

events.title: Retail sales and Fed minutes in focus next week
events.summary: A report on retail sales will anchor the calendar of economic updates this week, which also includes details about the most recent Federal Reserve meeting and the latest take on consumer sentiment NEW YORK -- New data on retail sales will headline U.S. economic updates this week, but there will also be details from the most recent Federal Reserve meeting and a new read on consumer sentiment. The latest economic data showed that inflation remains hot . High prices on everything from groceries to clothing and gas have squeezed millions of Americans and cast a shadow over the broader economy. Democrats swept Congress in midterm elections and for many voters, the cost of living was the top issue. Here’s a look at some of the key reports coming in the week ahead. Retail activity may have slowed last month. Economists expect a 0.2% overall increase, easing back from 0.8% in September and 1.3% in August. At the same time that overall retail sales are slowing, spending at gas stations has surged amid persistently higher fuel costs because of the U.S. war with Iran. The war disrupted shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, slashing global oil supplies and raising prices. That has made gasoline more expensive and indirectly raised costs for anything that is shipped. Shoppers have been pulling back on spending just as retailers head into the vital holiday shopping season . The squeeze from stubbornly high inflation is expected to persist as long as the war stifles global oil supplies and tariffs from the U.S. trade war with much of the world keep putting pressure on prices. Details from the Federal Reserve's latest policy meeting will be released Wednesday. The minutes from that meeting could shed more light on the central bank's decision-making process as it tries to cool inflation. It held rates steady at its October meeting following the first rate hike in three years at its September meeting. Raising the benchmark interest rate can help slow economic growth and cool inflation by making borrowing more expensive. India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain Timeline of the FAA nationwide ground stop: How it developed Heat-trapping carbon pollution drops, but scientists cite Iran war Higher interest rates, though, could also stunt job growth, which has been strong but is showing some signs of weakening. Supporting the labor market is also part of the Fed's mandate along with taming inflation and taking action to support one can often be detrimental to the other. Inflation has remained stubbornly above 3%, which puts it well above the central bank's 2% target rate. The Fed is expected to raise rates again at its December meeting and anxiety over stubborn inflation likely means more rate hikes to follow in 2027. The latest weekly update on unemployment claims, which are a proxy for layoffs, will be released Thursday. Economists watch them closely because they can provide signs of where the job market is headed. Claims have remained at historically low levels amid a broader jobs market that has remained a strong point in an economy pressured by rising inflation. The resilient jobs market has made it easier for the Fed to focus on raising interest rates to cool inflation. The last broad employment update for October showed that U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. The reports have shown that the job market remains solid, but unspectacular. Employers have added an average of 86,000 jobs a month throughout the year, which is modest by historic standards. The University of Michigan on Friday will release an update to its November consumer sentiment survey. It is expected to remain unchanged from its initial reading, which continued to show that consumers remain pessimistic as they deal with pressure from inflation on household budgets. Other reports on consumer confidence revealed similar concerns about inflation. The Conference Board's consumer confidence index for October showed some improvement in confidence levels, but they still remain on an overall downward trend. Responses to that survey continued to echo worries about the high costs of gas, goods and services. events.title: FAA back at "full operations" after Friday outage, Transportation Sec. says
events.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that all FAA systems are back to "full operations" after an hours-long outage Friday evening that grounded all air traffic across the U.S. The big picture: Duffy reiterated his plea to Congress to fund upgrades to the nation's air traffic control equipment, explaining that proper upgrades could have prevented the ground stop. Driving the news: Duffy explained that the outage was caused when a contractor performed routine maintenance on a telecommunications line to upgrade a copper wire to fiber-optic cable and install a new router. "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down. So we had to switch it over from old copper," Duffy said. Duffy said it's unclear whether the outage occurred because of contractor error or faulty equipment, but they are working to figure that out. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford warned that up to 5,000 flight cancellations will remain throughout today, but airlines have assured the agency that they should return to normal operations by the end of the day Sunday. "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," Bedford said. According to numbers from FlightAware , over 4,700 international and domestic flights have been canceled, and over 13,500 delayed, as of 11:50 am ET. Zoom out: Bedford and Duffy both said the ground stop was ordered out of an abundance of caution for the safety of passengers and airplane crews. Bedford added that they have no reason to believe a cyberattack or an AI issue prompted the outage. "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious," Bedford said. Zoom in: Duffy used the press conference to again plead with Congress to fund upgrades for the aging air traffic control system. Duffy has previously said the FAA needs $30 billion to update airports and air traffic control. Congress had previously awarded $12.5 billion in July 2025 for upgrades into 2030. After Friday's outage, Duffy upped the funding request to $50 billion. "For me, it gets to be frustrating where everyone says they want to do it, and the president is pushing it, but we don't get the resources," Duffy said. "And I think this is the moment. If we don't start to switch out our systems, how long are we going to wait, America and Congress? And I think this is a sign for them to lean in. This is bipartisan." Bedford offered a blunt assessment when reporters asked about the system's function, saying it's the "worst-kept secret in government" that it needs an upgrade. "We have to keep the existing system operating at the very best of our ability," with the funding they have, he said. "But," Bedford continued, "let's not kid ourselves. It will continue to break until we replace it."

events.title: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry. China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang. Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain. In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration. In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case. South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report. Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project. In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors. events.title: How Nvidia turmoil and a Democratic Congress could reshape the AI trade, according to ETF experts
events.summary: The largest technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade could stand to benefit the most from Nvidia's woes and a Democratic-controlled Congress pushing back on data centers, according to investing experts interviewed on CNBC's " ETF Edge " earlier this week. "We may have been put in an environment, as much as investors have sort of been looking for areas outside of Big Tech, where net-net Big Tech ends up as the winner once again," said Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza, whose firm manages the Magnificent Seven ETF ( MAGS ). Part of his bull case: Other players in the AI trade are positioned to fill Nvidia's chip demand if investors lose trust in the company after a tumultuous week that saw its iconic founder and CEO Jensen Huang resign. "If we get into an environment where people can't trust … Nvidia, they're going to look for other sources for these chips because they need them," Mazza said during the "ETF Edge" interview, which occurred Monday as the Nvidia scandal grew but before Huang had resigned. Discussing recent fund flow activity for the MAGS ETF, as well as for the Roundhill Neocloud ETF ( NCLD ) — which focuses on smaller market cap, specialized cloud computing companies — Mazza said, "In a weird way, [hyperscalers] may continue to benefit from this because they have the compute available. It's going to be more valuable if the demand is there." The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF ended the week in the green, albeit with a gain of less than 1%, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF was up over 1%, though earnings from top holdings Coreweave and Nebius presented a mixed picture. CoreWeave had its best day since April 2025 on Wednesday after its latest quarterly results, while Nebius shares sank after its Thursday report. The neocloud ETF remains deeply in the red since its August 2026 launch, down 39%, amid concerns about balance sheet strength, which could linger given Nvidia's role in financing the AI buildout. CoreWeave shares sank again on Friday, and Nvidia posted its longest losing streak since 2012 after its latest weekly losses. Nvidia's interim CEO and current chief financial officer Colette Kress will have her first opportunity to reassure the market when Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday. "Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," Kress said in a statement issued on Thursday morning when the company announced Huang's exit. Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives said on "ETF Edge" on Monday that the market will remain optimistic about other AI chip players, like AMD and Alphabet, if Nvidia faces prolonged headwinds. Ives helped create the Dan IVES Wedbush AI Revolution ETF ( IVES ) while at Wedbush Securities, where he served as the managing director and global head of technology research before departing Wedbush to form his own firm earlier this year. AMD finished trading this week up close to 13%, with Broadcom posting similar gains. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index posted its best week since August as Nvidia's slump reshuffled the AI trade. Yorkville Ives lowered its price target on Nvidia to $225 from $300 on Thursday after Huang's resignation, but maintained a buy rating on the stock, which finished the week at $162.85 per share. "Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution. They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone," Ives wrote in a note to investors on Thursday. "The strategic roadmap is already essentially built around the next few family of chips and physical AI with 42k employees driving it. ... Valuation at roughly 10x 28 EPS is way too cheap once Nvidia gets through this storm and emerges on the other side." The compute that does exist could become even more indispensable against the backdrop of a potential slowdown to the data-center buildout by Congress after the Democratic Party gains of Nov. 3 swept control of Congress, Mazza said. Ives estimates that the "blue tidal wave" in Congress could mean 10% of planned data centers won't materialize on the low end, and 15%-20% on the high end, but he added that demand still outstrips supply four to one. "The compute is just that much more valuable in the capacity today than it was a week ago. So I could argue just more and more bullish, strong, get stronger," Ives said. "The game is going to change for Big Tech. It will slow it down. But there's no overbuild, no bubble concerns. And I view that as actually a positive thing," he added.

events.title: Rising rents draw Wall Street money to industrial outdoor storage lot investments across the U.S.
events.summary: Brookfield and Blackstone, two of the world's largest alternative asset managers, are among the institutional investors moving in on what the industry calls "industrial outdoor storage." Ownership of lots used to store industrial equipment is fragmented in markets across the U.S., which the Wall Street giants plan to capitalize on. But real estate experts say local investors can still find opportunities to invest, especially in lots of three to five acres in size, and it is a market where rents have doubled since 2020. Nondescript lots holding idle bulldozers, trucks and other industrial equipment are a common sight in local real estate markets across the U.S., and increasingly, a focus for Wall Street private investment giants. If you haven't noticed them, it's probably because they so easily fade into the landscape, just another non-branded bit of land in the miasma of suburbia. But Brookfield and Blackstone, two of the world's largest alternative asset managers, are among the institutional investors moving in on what the industry calls industrial outdoor storage, or IOS. Investors are eyeing these lots as the AI build-out increases the demand for heavy equipment. "We have strong conviction in industrial outdoor storage, which plays a critical role in our supply chain," said Devin Barnwell, a managing partner and co-leader of Brookfield's logistics business. He says that up until now, the segment has been fragmented, but Brookfield sees that changing. "We see significant opportunity to bring institutional capital and operating expertise to this fragmented sector, improving the quality and efficiency of these assets while strengthening the resilience of our industrial supply chains," Barnwell said. Brookfield spent $1.2 billion earlier this year to take Peakstone Realty Trust private, a deal completed in May that gave it a portfolio of more than 70 industrial properties, most of them outdoor storage yards. Blackstone is also ramping up in the sector, mainly as a lender. Its real estate debt arm has made six loans to outdoor storage owners totaling more than $1.1 billion, including a $244 million loan in June to Alterra IOS to buy 37 properties. Despite the billions being bet on the market by Wall Street, there is still opportunity in the market for individual investors and local entrepreneurs looking to park their money where others park their equipment. "1,000 percent yes," said Adam Petrillo, an executive managing director at Newmark, a commercial real estate advisory firm, who co-leads its industrial outdoor storage practice. Petrillo said smaller, non-institutional investors, still control a significant amount of well-placed storage in secondary markets. "The good news for smaller investors and mom and pops is that a good individual IOS site isn't necessarily 50 acres," Petrillo said. Lots as small as three to five acres in primary or secondary markets can still yield a robust return, he said. "At that bite size, an individual can step in. We are not talking about tens of millions ... a three-acre, well-located IOS with multiple use cases can be found, marketed, leased, and stabilized," he added. Hottest outdoor storage property markets The numbers help explain the appetite. Rents for industrial outdoor storage roughly doubled across eight major markets between 2020 and the third quarter of this year, according to data from Newmark Research and Alterra IOS, an owner of such properties. Average rent per usable acre rose 103.5%, to nearly $11,000 a month, compared with a 66% increase for traditional industrial space, such as indoor warehouses. Rent growth, according to Alterra, is most closely tied to infrastructure and energy activity in the area, even more so than data center development specifically. The value of these properties can also increase if located near a seaport, rail line, or highway. But the gains weren't uniform. Baltimore (204%), Houston (159%) and Norfolk (148%) led, while South Florida and Savannah IOS actually trailed traditional industrial. Lisa DeNight, managing director, head of North American industrial research at Newmark, said that Savannah's IOS vacancy remains quite tight despite the rent figures. Recent port activity is a potential factor, according to Alterra. Savannah's container volumes more than doubled between 2010 and 2022 but have since declined, while Houston saw roughly 15% growth from 2022 to 2025. Petrillo said that there is still plenty of room left for values to increase, so an investor jumping in now hasn't missed the game. "We are still in the very early innings," Petrillo said. Sam Cheema co-founder of CanTex Capital, a Dallas-based firm that acquires overlooked industrial real estate in Texas, is seeing increased demand for these lots. "It comes down to supply and demand," he said. "If you need a warehouse you can usually find one.

events.title: How Rockstar's 'GTA VI' release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time off
events.summary: "Grand Theft Auto VI" launches Nov. 19, with third-party estimates pointing to exceptional preorder demand and Wall Street expecting tens of millions of copies sold by March. Creators, streaming platforms, food delivery services and Miami tourism could all feel the impact or see spending shift with the game's launch. The game could pull holiday attention from streaming and movies in the week before Thanksgiving. It's been 13 years since the last installment of Grand Theft Auto , and fans are getting ready for what analysts say could be the biggest video game launch of all time. The latest game in the franchise, "Grand Theft Auto VI," is set to launch on Nov. 19, after Take-Two Interactive's Rockstar Games delayed its launch twice. Roth analyst Eric Handler estimated the game maker spent more than $1 billion developing the game. Sales figures could end up breaking records. Sensor Tower estimated over 12 million preorders through Nov. 13, and Morgan Stanley forecast the game could sell 40 million copies by March 2027. Beyond launch week, the Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, franchise has a track record of lasting engagement over many years. Even 13 years after launch, "Grand Theft Auto V" is one of the top five most viewed games on Twitch this year. In anticipation of the game's launch, investors have been taking note: Take-two's stock has more than doubled since the beginning of 2023. The release is seen as not only a monumental moment for developer Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two, but also a massive opportunity for the entire gaming industry. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick addressed demand in a recent "Squawk Box" interview , saying, "We tend to be pretty judicious when we talk about this sort of thing, but our expectations were high and they are being vastly exceeded so far." Streamers and creators across the digital ecosystem are looking at the launch as a massive opportunity to drive engagement with their content and fuel subscriber and ad revenue growth. A creator who goes by the name Deansocool, who has 375,000 followers on Twitch and posts content to YouTube and other social platforms as well, said "GTA VI" will enable creators to grow their audience and provide a massive opportunity for newer streamers to make a name for themselves. "This game is going to make a lot of millionaires in 2027. A lot of creators gotta understand this is it. This is that golden ticket. This is like a hundred times bigger than Fortnite," he said in an interview with CNBC. "It goes beyond this launch moment into this sustaining opportunity for them to grow, build, engage and retain their audience and ultimately support themselves by making money," said Twitch Chief Product Officer Mike Minton. The release of the latest Grand Theft Auto title could draw so much attention that its impact will be felt beyond just the world of gaming. BambooHR, a workplace time-off platform, reported that paid time off requests for the "GTA VI" release date are nearly 13% higher than equivalent days in 2024 and 2025. It also noted that nearly one in five workers are planning to take time off for the launch. PwC issued a report examining all the different sectors of the economy that could benefit from the game's launch — or be hurt by it. The firm projected that food delivery companies could see a surge from hunkered-down gamers, and Miami tourism could benefit. PwC noted that foreign visitors to Seoul's Bukchon Hanok Village, which inspired a location in the hit Netflix movie KPop Demon Hunters, increased 118% in the four weeks following the movie's debut. Music streaming also looks set to get a boost. Tom Petty's "Love Is a Long Road," which appeared in the first "GTA VI" trailer in December 2023, reportedly saw Spotify streams jump by more than 37,000%. On the downside, the game could distract from movies and streaming entertainment. "How are people spending Thanksgiving? There's a lot of sports on TV, but you've also got a pretty solid group of your demographics that are going to be focused on playing 'GTA VI,'" said Bart Spiegel, who leads PwC's Global Entertainment & Media sector. events.title: Heating oil prices are up 59% from last winter. The spike is 'crushing folks,' Maine nonprofit says
events.summary: Heating oil prices averaged $5.91 per gallon as of Nov. 2, a 59% jump from a year earlier, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. In Maine, where roughly 50% of the homes rely primarily on heating oil, the jump "is crushing folks" who already were struggling due to the high cost of living, said Jason Parent, CEO of AVEC Community Action, a nonprofit agency in Presque Isle, Maine. While the average benefit through a heating assistance program is higher this year, it won't go as far for households that need heating oil, Parent said. The Trump administration has released some reserve barrels in an effort to bring down prices, and some congressional lawmakers are calling for additional funding for heating assistance. Winter heating bills can strain household budgets. This year, a spike in heating oil prices could make the season especially difficult for households that depend on the fuel and have little financial wiggle room. The national average price of heating oil was roughly $5.91 a gallon as of Nov. 9, up about $2.19, or 59%, from a year earlier, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. In Maine, the average price per gallon is roughly $5.83, up about $2.49 from a year earlier, or about 75%. The state is among those whose residents may feel the price rise acutely — about 50% of homes there use heating oil. The jump "is crushing folks," said Jason Parent, CEO of AVEC Community Action, a nonprofit agency based in Presque Isle, Maine, that provides heating assistance and other social services in three of the state's 16 counties. Many residents face immediate crises, he said, such as empty fuel tanks or reliance on unsafe heating sources. "My fear is that there are households out there who have secondary fuel sources like wood stoves, pellet stoves and other things that are no longer operating and functioning in a safe way," Parent said. IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap Why Nvidia stock drop isn't a big deal for many ETF, mutual fund investors Social Security could pay benefits until 2059 if payroll kept pace with GDP: AARP CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The price surge comes on the heels of years of high overall inflation that has already squeezed household budgets, he said. "The cost of living has made it impossible for households who had been figuring out how to get by without [financial help]," Parent said. The price spike comes amid a tight global market for refined fuels, a category that includes heating oil and diesel . Supply shocks tied to the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war , low inventories and limited refining capacity have constrained supplies and added upward pressure on fuel prices, according to recent research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City. The EIA predicts that a warmer winter in the Northeast will reduce consumption, helping to offset higher prices. In October, the agency forecast that the average household using heating oil will spend $2,115 from November through March, about 21% more than last year. Meanwhile, homes primarily heated with natural gas are expected to spend an average of $640 this winter, down 9%, while those using propane are forecast to spend an average of $1,246, down 3%, according to the EIA's October forecast. Households using electricity for heating are expected to spend an average of $1,196, up 4% from a year ago. These are national figures. Roughly 4.1 million U.S. households use heating oil as their primary means of heating their homes, according to the EIA. Most of them — close to 3.4 million — are located in the Northeast. Unlike electricity or natural gas, heating oil is delivered in large quantities. Payment terms vary, but some dealers require a minimum delivery or charge extra for smaller orders. In Maine, for example, ordering at least 100 gallons for a standard 275-gallon tank can avoid a surcharge, according to the state attorney general's office . At current prices, that 100 gallons would cost about $600 — a tall order for some households. AVEC's Home Energy Assistance Program, or HEAP, provides financial assistance to qualifying households, based primarily on income and the number of people living in the home. Funding originates with the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP, which is run by the U.S. Health and Human Services Department and overseen by state agencies, often working with local organizations such as AVEC. Maine and tribal grantees in the state received about $38 million from LIHEAP in October, according to a press release from outgoing Republican Sen. Susan Collins. AVEC administers about $4 million of that through HEAP, Parent said. AVEC also gets donations from community fundraising to help residents cover heating costs.

events.title: Juice your growth and save on taxes in this workplace investment account
events.summary: It's open enrollment season at work, meaning employees are set to choose their healthcare benefits for 2027. Healthcare costs have been climbing for workers and employers alike, with total family premiums averaging $28,303, including the employer's share, according to KFF. Health savings accounts offer a tax-advantaged way to save for medical expenses and stash away money for the long term. Workers are in the heart of open enrollment season for next year's benefits, and rising healthcare costs are shining a spotlight on an offering that includes a tax-advantaged investment account. Healthcare expenses are climbing for workers and employers alike, with average total family premiums, including the employer's share, averaging $28,303, up 5% from a year ago, according to data from health policy organization KFF , formerly the Kaiser Family Foundation. To manage the costs, a growing number of employers are moving to high-deductible health plans, which work alongside health savings accounts or HSAs. Almost 40% of companies with at least 10 employees that offer health benefits also have an HSA-qualified plan, KFF found. Health savings accounts have three major tax advantages. First, contributions that your employer automatically deducts from your pay aren't taxed. Second, money stashed into the HSA grows free of taxes. Finally, you can make tax-free withdrawals for qualified health expenses – just be sure to save your receipts. "I love HSAs because of their triple-tax advantage," said Eileen Olson, CFP and founder of Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, near Savannah, Georgia. "For people who can afford to leave it alone, it can be one of the best retirement accounts they're going to have." In 2027, those with individual healthcare coverage through a high-deductible plan can stash up to $4,500 in an HSA, including any contributions from employers. That number goes up to $9,000 for family plans. Individuals can kick in a catch-up contribution of $1,000 if they're aged 55 and older and not enrolled in Medicare. The HSA differs from the healthcare flexible spending account, known as the FSA. FSA funds must be used by the end of the plan year unless your employer allows a carryover of up to $700 or an additional 2.5 months to use the money. HSAs, however, have no expiration date on their funds – and that's what makes them such a powerful tool for long-term planning. You can also take the HSA with you if you change employers. "Get the money deployed, take advantage of the pretax contribution, and allocate the money into a growth portfolio," said Mark Stancato, certified financial planner at VIP Wealth Advisors in Decatur, Georgia. "With the HSA, you can keep compounding year over year." The structure of an HSA and the available investment menu will vary from one plan to the next, and some will require that employees keep some of their holdings in cash. Preset HSA fund menus tend to have 15 to 25 funds to choose from, and providers say that accountholders who invest tend to use two to four funds, according to Greg Carlson, senior research analyst for equity strategies at Morningstar. How you allocate your HSA will depend on several factors, including your family's health prospects in the next year, your cash flow needs – how much you can comfortably sock into the HSA – and your risk tolerance, said André Small, CFP and founder of A Small Investment in Houston. Health savings accounts contributions and plan info for 2027 Small's standard is to keep an amount equal to 120% of the plan's out-of-pocket maximum held in cash in the HSA. "That covers a bad year without forcing a sale at the wrong time," he said. "Above that amount? I typically advise investing the amount the client is comfortable investing, allocated to their risk tolerance, their time horizon and the goal of spending these dollars on care later." For 2027, the IRS defines a high-deductible plan as one with an annual deductible no less than $1,750 for self-only coverage ($3,500 for family plans) and with an out-of-pocket expense limit that doesn't exceed $8,700 for self-only (or $17,400 for family coverage). Out-of-pocket expenses include deductibles, copays and other costs – but not premiums. Other advisors suggest having up to the deductible in cash, though some HSA plan providers require a stated minimum amount in cash. Beyond this cash reserve, financial advisors recommend allocating into stocks. Patrick Swift, CFP and president of Amplius Wealth Advisors in Blue Bell, Pennsylvania, aims for an allocation of up to 60% in U.S. large cap stocks, 20% in small and mid-cap stocks and 20% in international stocks. "We believe the equity portfolio should be well diversified," he said. "If the [HSA] balance is 2% to 10% of your net worth, why not be aggressive? That can change based on the situation, but if you are comfortable with the philosophical aspect, why not be growth oriented?

events.title: Fitch expects UAE GDP to rise this year and maintains high-grade credit rating
events.summary: Fitch Ratings is expecting the UAE's economy to expand in 2026 and has maintained the country's high-grade credit rating, citing resilient fiscal buffers. Real gross domestic product in the Arab world's second-largest economy will grow by 0.5 per cent this year, despite an estimated 1.5 per cent contraction in non-oil GDP, the New York-based agency said on Friday. Analysts at Fitch said Dubai's real GDP would remain below its 2025 level next year, as it continues to recover from the effect of the Iran war. The emirate's economy hit Dh473 billion ($128.8 billion) in the first half of 2026, down 2.3 per cent from a year earlier, as growth in financial services, health care and construction helped offset weakness in other sectors, government data showed last month . Hydrocarbon GDP is expected to rise by about 7 per cent in 2026, then spike by 26 per cent next year, with oil production no longer constrained by Opec+ quotas, Fitch said. The Emirates formally withdrew from the oil group in May . “Fitch expects all the emirates will put recovery programmes in place, but non-oil trend growth will be below prewar levels over our forecast period,” the Fitch analysts wrote. Fitch also kept the UAE's sovereign credit rating at AA-, with a stable outlook, reflecting low consolidated government debt, strong net external asset position and high GDP per capita. An AA- rating is the fourth-highest on Fitch's rating scale. Investment grade makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funding when the need to borrow arises. Fitch said the Emirates benefits from Abu Dhabi's sovereign net foreign assets which, at 180 per cent of UAE GDP in 2026, are among the highest Fitch-rated sovereigns, it said. Fitch had rated Abu Dhabi AA in May . “The stable outlook reflects demonstrated resilience of oil export revenues during the Iran war, which largely offsets the immediate negative impact of the war, as well as abundant fiscal and external buffers, and our expectation that individual emirates will bear the cost of the war rather than the federal government,” Fitch said. The UAE economy has fared relatively well despite geopolitical headwinds. GDP grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to GDP during the first six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre revealed last month. Last week, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, said the UAE’s foreign trade rose close to a record Dh3 trillion in the first nine months of the year, despite the challenges. Fitch added that Abu Dhabi's export revenue in 2026 is expected to be higher compared to its prewar forecasts despite the disruption, reflecting elevated crude prices and higher export volumes via pipeline to Fujairah and the Strait of Hormuz. “Crude oil constitutes the bulk of exports, and we consider Abu Dhabi's oil export infrastructure less vulnerable to long-term damage than more concentrated and bespoke downstream oil or liquefied natural gas plants,” Fitch said.

events.title: AI's four colliding crises
events.summary: AI's titans were handed an extraordinary mandate: Police yourselves. But the industry faces a four-pronged crisis of trust as Democrats surge to power and many Americans rebel over AI and data centers. Guardrails for the industry will be a priority for the new Congress, with some populist Republicans eager to pile on. Why it matters: The collision of safety scares, political blows, financial turmoil and leadership scandals threatens to derail AI's once seemingly unstoppable ascent. The big picture: Just six weeks ago, President Trump announced that top AI CEOs had agreed to a voluntary safety accord . But cracks were already showing and, since then, four crises have converged. 🏛️ 1. The political crisis: AI was on the ballot for the first time during the midterm elections through a series of data center measures across America. People voted against data centers in 40 out of 41 cases, and swing-state incumbents linked to the facilities, including Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), were voted out. Now Democrats are planning a flood of AI bills once they take control of Congress in January, Reuters reports . They'll also bring some of the most powerful AI executives to D.C. to testify. 🦺 2. The safety crisis: OpenAI's Hugging Face breach , revealed in July , was a terrifying look at what could happen if machines operate beyond humans' control — and it was the first in a wave of revelations through the summer and fall. AI CEOs and engineers came forward with stark warnings about the dangers of the tech they've been building, including its potential to destroy humanity. Axios' Madison Mills reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of security incidents and that unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts. 💰 3. The financial crisis: The AI trade is looking more vulnerable as investors question when or whether the industry's sky-high spending will deliver sky-high returns. Tech stocks tumbled , with Nvidia falling 13% this week amid the ouster of founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The stock has lost nearly 25% of its value since the first New York Times report in late October about Huang's links to a suspected Chinese spy. Anthropic's IPO may not be what some hoped, with its projected valuation coming in roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago. 🧐 4. The leadership crisis: Huang's stunning resignation, following revelations about affairs, is raising new questions about the vulnerability of the people running America's most powerful companies. Nvidia's stock slide exemplifies the risk of putting so much power in the hands of so few AI executives. Pop culture has turned on the AI titans , with three year-end films — " The Social Reckoning " and " Musk ," out last month, and " Artificial ," opening Christmas Day — savaging Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Reality check: The AI industry's hurdles are partly growing pains — investors start demanding returns, lawmakers seek accountability, the public grows skeptical. The trust collapse echoes the moment social media companies went from Silicon Valley darlings to public enemies. But AI's reckoning — just like its rise — has come much faster.

events.title: MAGA turns on Lutnick amid China spy scandal
events.summary: Commerce Secretary Lutnick has become the face of the Trump administration's troubled response to Chinese espionage and potential national security threats. The most intense scrutiny is coming from Republicans on the Hill, fellow Cabinet members and the MAGA base. Why it matters: Regulators and policymakers on both sides of the aisle want someone's head for an affair that may have exposed sensitive technology to the nation's top foreign adversary. Two names are currently at the top of that list: former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — and now Lutnick. The big picture: Over the past year, Lutnick slow-walked broader administration efforts to address suspicions that Singapore-based company Megaspeed was illegally diverting chips to China, Axios first reported . Administration officials had pushed to place Megaspeed on the Commerce Department's Entity List, which would have restricted exports of U.S. tech to the company. Driving the news: On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed as much. "Treasury, War, USTR, and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC . Trump himself supported taking action on three occasions, but those efforts were delayed by Lutnick, Axios reported . There's a widespread belief in Trump's broad circle of advisers that the Nvidia scandal might be too much for Lutnick to survive — but Trump is standing beside him for now. Behind the scenes, the White House has not expressed concern regarding efforts to have Lutnick testify before Congress. MAGA commentators are also tearing Lutnick apart on shows like "War Room with Steve Bannon," while Republican senators openly take him to task. For the record: " Secretary Lutnick plays a fundamental role in advising the President across many different industries. The reports you have issued are inaccurate and false and literally misstate the topic, creating a false impression," the Commerce Department said in response to Axios' inquiries. Friction point: The brewing scandal hangs in part on a CIA warning that Jensen Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang, who ran Megaspeed and was also alleged to be a Chinese spy. That warning appears to have been ignored by Commerce Department officials, sources told Axios. Context: Last fall, CIA intelligence indicated Huang was the target of the espionage, which was reported in a "book" assembled by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence for a small circle of administration officials with top secret clearance, according to sources familiar with the matter. In March, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who's also White House national security adviser, compiled a memo about the issue to ensure that Cabinet officials with "equities" in Nvidia and AI were informed, one of those sources said. "The memo was made so that Lutnick and Bessent and others knew what was up," said one source. "Howard was given the memo. He ignored the memo," a second source said. In May, as Trump traveled to China aboard Air Force One, Rubio verbally briefed the president as a "reminder," one of the sources said. Reality check: Through it all, Trump has repeatedly been in Lutnick's corner. The president has defended Lutnick time and again, whether over tariffs, immigration or the latest China tussle. There are no indications Trump has changed his stance since publicly defending Lutnick on Thursday. The bottom line: While Trump continues to defend Lutnick, administration officials and congressional Republicans have clearly picked a target.

events.title: Wholesale food prices are on the rise
events.summary: Food prices are rising sharply even before they reach supermarket shelves. Why it matters: Americans are already paying more for groceries. New inflation data this week suggests that the pressure is not letting up. Wholesale fresh and dry vegetable prices surged 27% last month, adding to a 31% price jump the previous month. These are the prices paid by food distributors, grocery chains and other businesses to farmers and other producers for eventual sale to consumers. Wholesale food prices overall are up 1.7% from a year earlier, ending a three-month streak of annual price declines. Zoom in: Unusually warm weather, crop disease and insect infestations have reduced lettuce and other leafy green harvests in California. The Iran war, meanwhile, has driven up the cost of fertilizer and fuel, making it more expensive to grow and transport food. A regional grocery chain recently told Federal Reserve officials that it now costs more to transport a head of lettuce from California than to buy the lettuce itself, citing high diesel fuel prices. Truck freight costs are up almost 25% over the past year, the largest annual increase since 2022 and on par with the surge seen during the pandemic-era inflation shock. The big picture: It's unclear how much of the surge in producer prices will be passed along to consumers. But steeper price increases were already showing up at supermarket checkout counters last month. Grocery prices rose 0.4%, the biggest monthly increase in 6 months, driven by higher prices for meat, dairy products and snack foods. Fresh vegetable prices climbed 2%, including a nearly 8% jump in lettuce prices.

events.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status
events.summary: An international health organization has determined that the United States has lost its measles elimination status, according to multiple news reports. Why it matters: It's an official recognition of how much the country's public health has deteriorated due to a rolling series of outbreaks since early last year. Increased public skepticism about the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, a barrage of distrust from federal officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and funding cuts for response efforts have all factored in the surge of cases, according to public health experts. The big picture: The Pan American Health Organization concluded there has been sustained transmission of the highly contagious virus for longer than 12 months, bringing the U.S. case count to its highest level in 35 years. The measles elimination status hinges on whether the same strain of measles stays in circulation for 12 months or longer without a break. The overwhelming majority of cases are in unvaccinated people. While overall measles vaccination rates remain relatively high, public health officials say they have to remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity. Driving the news: An expert panel convened by the Pan American Health Organization made the widely expected decision following a three-day meeting in Washington, D.C. What they're saying: "It is no surprise that the resurgence of measles has coincided with an administration that has inflicted significant damage to our health care system while spreading false claims about vaccines," said Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and a former acting director of the Centers for Disease Control. "It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026," the Infectious Diseases Society said in comments prior to the decision. The group cited the potential long-term toll on infants infected this year, some of whom could develop serious neurologic disease years after the initial infection. By the numbers: There have been 5,412 confirmed cases so far this year, compared to 2,289 for all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's latest tally. The last time measles cases were higher was in 1991, when the U.S. had 9,643 cases. Pennsylvania is in the grip of an outbreak that has accounted for more than 1,500 cases so far and six measles-associated deaths. Those reports are widely considered to be an undercount, due to the lack of widespread testing and unreported instances of mild illness. While most measles cases aren't severe, they can have long-lasting effects because of the way the virus can suppress the body's immune responses, leaving people more susceptible to other infections. About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles is hospitalized, per the CDC. How it works: Experts rely on disease tracking by local health departments and genetic sequencing, and can also factor vaccination rates and surveillance efforts. Canada and the United Kingdom have both lost their measles elimination status over the past year. The determinations are largely symbolic, but mean the virus has become endemic and is spreading freely in pockets of unvaccinated people, according to Yale epidemiologist Katelyn Jetelina. Since early 2025, there have been large-scale outbreaks in West Texas, along the Utah-Arizona border and in South Carolina.

events.title: No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?
events.summary: On September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the new air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration quickly announced that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.” New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms. None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls. According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe? Depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this new technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” says a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.” Aviation’s embrace of AI traces back to the early 2000s, when advances in batteries and microelectronics suddenly made drones much more capable and inexpensive. The surge convinced officials that robots and humans would eventually need to share the airways, and that new infrastructure would be necessary to allow that. At the time, virtually all aircraft were human-piloted, and there was no way for drones to avoid human-flown planes or each other. In 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed. Joby’s aircraft flying past Lower Manhattan, New York, in April. With a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, big players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious plans for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia . The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia . Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come. Around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the company unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year. For more than a decade, various eVTOL builders have been promising that production models were just around the corner .

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Collabora and Nextcloud pitch alternatives as education customers weigh the cost of losing free services LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in 10 hours ago Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum 1 day ago FAA blames ground stop on faulty copper wiring 1 day ago Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 1 day ago This year’s bug count just passed 100K 1 day ago The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure. "Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy." Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service.
