events.title: I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account.
events.summary: ProPublica reporter Jake Pearson tests DraftKings’ guardrails at a Manhattan bar this spring. After a ProPublica investigation published this fall, the company closed Pearson’s account. Gerardo del Valle/ProPublica Late last month, I was getting dinner on the table when an email hit my inbox with some bad news. “Upon review your account has been closed at DraftKings’ discretion,” the message read. “We understand that this is not the decision that you were hoping for but this decision is final.”  I hadn’t bet on sports in months and had withdrawn all but a few cents of my balance. Why, I wondered, would my account even be under review? Was it something I’d said? In September, I’d published an investigation into how online sports betting companies like DraftKings court customers — and whether the internal guardrails they’ve put in place to stop their users from spiraling out of control are firm enough. For that piece, I’d intentionally bet like a problem gambler , recklessly escalating my betting behavior over 10 weeks. My wagering had been informed by a panel of professional sports bettors, recovering addicts and addiction specialists. As I flagrantly waved the red flags, DraftKings made me a VIP and assigned me my very own personal host. My recklessness was being rewarded. It just took three weeks and about $6,000 of losses. What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out. If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files. Share Your Experience The company, like the rest of the industry, says it doesn’t want to profit off of addiction, and has invested heavily in a system of tools and in-app prompts designed to help bettors put conditions on their gambling and slow them down. But my experiment raised serious questions about the effectiveness of this system, what’s known as “responsible gaming.”   So on one hand, I could understand how a story like mine, which scrutinized a core business function, might rankle company executives. But on the other hand, DraftKings had been downplaying the significance of my story for weeks.  In an interview for the piece, the company’s chief responsible gaming officer, Lori Kalani, had told me that the system “worked the way it was supposed to” in my case by feeding me some 30 responsible gaming messages over the course of my 10-week betting spree. And on Oct. 22, about a month after publication, DraftKings CEO Jason Robins doubled down, telling a CNBC journalist that he had “personally looked” at my entire betting history and was “pretty proud of how we handled it.” (He also made false claims about my reporting, but I’ve already addressed that on X .) So as I read the notice of my account closure, I wondered: What changed, exactly? DraftKings didn’t respond when I asked. All I got was a check in the mail for 94 cents, the remainder of my balance. But what was clear was that my investigation was reaching more and more people — including state regulators and federal lawmakers. Since publication, it had gone viral. A 27-minute, behind-the-scenes documentary of our work that we posted on YouTube on Oct. 10 had been viewed more than 6 million times in just three weeks. Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting Experiment Lisa Seville and Nadia Sussman/ProPublica The video offered viewers who may not be familiar with ProPublica (or perhaps not inclined to read 4,000-word stories) a way to learn about the reporting in the venue where so much sports betting content lives. Most of our viewers were young men — the prime sports betting demographic. And boy did they engage, leaving 3,500 comments on YouTube and flooding my inbox with messages about the same features and VIP perks detailed in my story. Regulators from across the country were citing my investigation when announcing that they were going to take a look for themselves at how DraftKings and its ilk incentivize users to keep betting. Federal and state officials were also demanding answers about how the company lures in its customers and keeps them in the action . In Ohio, regulators were even proposing a rule to restrict the apps’ marketing practices that spoke directly to one of the findings in my piece.   On the morning of Oct. 27, I sent DraftKings a series of questions for a story about that impact .  That evening is when the unsigned notice from DraftKings Support about my account closure appeared in my inbox. Two hours later, the company sent me a formal response to my questions, writing, in part, that “regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business” and denying that the company improperly targets losing gamblers. I may no longer be able to access my account, but I’m still reporting on DraftKings and the online gambling industry. In fact, right now, we’re collecting wagering data from bettors to better understand how the major operators handle problem gambling. You can help by submitting your data here . If you’ve got a tip, you can also reach me directly at 917-512-0276 and jake.pearson@propublica.org . The post I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account. appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Tesla invites select customers to order their own driverless Cybercab
events.summary: Elon Musk's Tesla Motors is inviting select customers in the US to order its fully autonomous Cybercab, the company's new focus after scrapping the Cybertruck earlier this month . The Cybercab, also dubbed the Robotaxi , is being sold for personal use for $29,990 before taxes and is expected to be delivered in December, the Texas-based company said in a post on X. That makes it Tesla's cheapest vehicle, $7,000 lower than the entry-level variant of the Model 3. Select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use pic.twitter.com/LDIkKuseAZ — Robotaxi (@robotaxi) November 13, 2026 However, the Cybercab requires a $3,600 annual autonomy subscription, which is the fee to use its driverless capabilities – a non-optional feature as the vehicle does not have a steering wheel or pedals. Maintenance and insurance costs are excluded from Tesla's pricing. Also, Cybercab deliveries are limited to Texas, one of only two states – the other being Florida – where Tesla's Robotaxi services are authorised to operate in a handful of cities. The driverless cab will be arriving in Arizona and Nevada soon, according to the company's website. Tesla described the launch as “early access” and “limited release”. It is unclear how many customers have been invited, whether the period will be extended and whether deliveries will be made available in Florida. “Select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use,” Tesla said. The Cybercab was released to much hype in October 2024, nearly a decade after Mr Musk first told Tesla shareholders that the company's cars would achieve full autonomy within three years. In 2016, he said that by the end of 2017, a Tesla car would be able to drive across the US without human intervention. In 2019, he said Tesla would have one million robotaxis on roads in 2020. None of those came to fruition. There were several reasons for the delay and failed promises, most notably the challenge of developing the technology, as well as regulatory scrutiny – especially after accidents involving driverless cars, and what has been perceived as grandiose ambitions in such a short period. The company, however, was able to stick to its roll-out plan for the Cybercab after its pledge in 2024. The Cybercab is also one of Tesla's focal points moving forward after it announced on November 6 that it would cease production of the polarising Cybertruck pickup. Mr Musk defended the Cybertruck this week, saying that its order rate “far exceeds” the production rate and that “the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production”. Tesla also unveiled its next-generation Roadster in another hyped launch last month, with its top-end Rocket variant model having the ability to “fly” using thrusters made by Mr Musk's other venture, SpaceX.

Chief executive Elon Musk said in a post on X that the offering would be available across the US as Tesla receives regulatory approval. “The monthly fee is too high,” Musk said, adding that it should match the cost of Tesla ’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) driver-assistance system and connectivity for other models, which is about US$115 a month. The electric vehicle maker aims to start selling its Cybercab robotaxis to the public by the end of 2026, Lars Moravy, Tesla’s vice-president of vehicle engineering, said in October. The Cybercab will work unsupervised in all the same geo locations as Tesla’s robotaxi services , Tesla’s head of artificial intelligence, Ashok Elluswamy, said in a separate X post. Tesla launched its unsupervised robotaxi service in Austin, Texas, in June 2025, expanded the offering to Dallas and Houston in April 2026 and rolled it out in Miami in July 2026. REUTERS

events.summary: Binance resumed withdrawals in phases earlier in November, after covering 95% of the US$6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform. Binance said it will reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week after a US$6.3 billion hack in October. The FBI and Binance blamed North Korea, while Pyongyang denied it; investigators linked the attack to the North Korean group “TraderTraitor”. The theft exposed digital asset risks and raised questions for Binance, which has promised to repay customers in full and has changed its finance leadership. Binance said on Nov 14 that it aims to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week, as operations normalise for the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange after a security breach linked to North Korea saw US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) stolen from the platform in October . “This week, we reopened withdrawals for 87 networks. We will aim to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of next week,” the company said in an X post. Binance resumed withdrawals in phases earlier in November , after covering 95% of the US$6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform in what experts describe as the largest cryptocurrency theft ever. The FBI and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the Binance hack, but Pyongyang has denied that. Blockchain investigation firms have attributed it to a North Korean group known as “TraderTraitor”. In its initial report on how hackers pulled off the heist, Binance detailed a multi-stage hacking endeavour that began in June and set off a series of security breaches culminating in the theft on Oct 29. The theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay customers in full. The company’s finance chief Kaiser Ng left the company just over a week after the heist , to pursue a new venture after more than five years at Binance. He was replaced by longtime finance executive Justin Yek, who was most recently vice-president of finance at Airwallex. REUTERS

events.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
events.summary: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories. With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process. Success of user reports trails away As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially. Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent. Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures. The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly. Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests. Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report , it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny. Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment. The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference " to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves. Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms. She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.' "In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered. "So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

events.title: Football kit giveaway aims to boost participation
events.summary: Millie Bright said she wanted girls to feel "comfortable and confident" in their kit Former England captain Millie Bright has helped hand out new kit to grassroots football teams in Leeds as part of an initiative aimed at keeping girls in sport for longer. Thirty teams based in communities facing social or economic challenges were chosen by anti-discrimination charity Kick it Out for the donation. Bright, who began her career at Doncaster Belles, said it was "vital" to keep girls playing sport. "Every young girl deserves a kit, no matter what level they play at, and, whilst the top of the game is doing really well, real life still exists. People can't afford to give their children kits, but that doesn't mean they should go without." Craig Gilmore set up Champions CIC, in Beeston, six years ago, to provide free Saturday morning training for children in the local area, as well as breakfast and lunch. "With the cost of living, football's expensive [and] bills come first," he said. "We work with a lot of families that can't afford the direct debits and the ongoing costs of grassroots sport nowadays. "The new kit is amazing. It gives them that sense of belonging, that team pride, it's a massive boost for them." Bright spoke with young footballers during the event in Leeds The new kit was provided by Kick it Out, in partnership with the Morrisons Foundation. They hope it will inspire these girls to continue sport as young women and adults. "Girls' participation struggles with drop-out rates," said Gemma Clark, from Kick it Out. "One of the barriers is kit. We want to remove that barrier so that more local girls can keep playing." Bright told the BBC she was fully behind the campaign. "As a girl or a woman, it's about feeling wanted and equal," she said. "We deserve to have kits. I don't want to see any girl dropping out of the game because they don't feel valued or comfortable. "These are the days that really make a difference. Hopefully this shows the girls that the people at the top care. The power of having a kit is a small gesture, but has a massive impact." events.summary: Leo KoGuan, who has a US$13.2 billion fortune, began investing in Nvidia in March. He began buying in March and has also backed Tesla, SpaceX and Alphabet. Huang was abruptly removed after reports of three affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. KoGuan said investors should buy and hold super-intelligence companies for the long term. Billionaire investor and Nvidia shareholder Leo KoGuan expressed support for Jensen Huang on Nov 13 and said he will not increase his stake in the tech company with someone else at the helm. “No further investment without Jensen,” KoGuan said in a text message, saying he has invested around US$1.3 billion (S$1.7 billion) in Nvidia. In a series of posts on X, KoGuan called Huang “the supreme creator” and acknowledged that while the executive had made errors, “we must prioritise rewards” rather “than punishments”. The posts followed Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia after reports of three affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. That ended his decades-long reign over a company at the centre of the artificial intelligence buildout and, by extension, the global economy. Singapore-based KoGuan, who has a US$13.2 billion fortune, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, began investing in Nvidia in March. It was a notable move for an investor whose net worth for years had been tied up largely in one stock: Tesla. The size of KoGuan’s Nvidia stake could not be independently verified. Earlier this week, KoGuan said on X that he is also an investor in Space Exploration Technologies and Google, whose parent is Alphabet. He told Bloomberg that he plans on increasing his positions in those companies. Investors must buy and hold super-intelligence companies for the long term, he wrote on X. “I hope and plan to invest in Jensen Huang if he creates or buys” another super-intelligence company, he wrote on Nov 13. “I hope he will offer me the opportunity to invest in his future company.” Bloomberg

events.title: What do Christmas market traders say about rising prices?
events.summary: Nils Borstel said his business was making less money despite more than doubling the price of a sausage Mention Christmas markets these days and the conversation often turns to rising prices – from £8 bratwursts, £11 Yorkshire pudding wraps and even £5 for a few marshmallow sticks. But what do the people behind the stalls think? Are they benefiting from the hikes or are their own profits being squeezed? Traders at Manchester's Christmas markets told the BBC they were feeling the pressure of increasing bills for staff, ingredients and energy, with some saying they were making less money despite charging more. One trader said it costs at least £4,000 a day to run each her four stalls, while another has cut prices to keep customers coming back. Nils Borstel, 25, helps run Bratwurst King, a family business which has operated at the markets since 1999. He said a sausage that previously cost £3.50 now sold for £8, with much of the increase taking place over the past five or six years. "But we don't earn more money," he said. Manchester Christmas market traders explain prices Borstel, whose family operates four stalls across the city centre, said rising costs for meat, electricity, staffing and accommodation had forced the business to increase prices. About 15 workers travel from Germany to help run the stalls, alongside staff recruited in the UK. He said that despite busy crowds and dry weather during the opening weekend, people appeared more cautious about spending than in previous years. For example, some customers were now buying one portion of food to share, rather than purchasing one each, he said. Borstel said he had seen a change in spending habits since 2019, when customers were more willing to buy food and drinks without worrying about the cost. He acknowledged that prices were high and did not want to increase them, but said the they were necessary to cover expenses. Poppy (left) and Neve questioned whether the portions they bought justified the prices Among those questioning the costs were Neve and Poppy, both 18. Neve, a student, said she had spent about £15 on one dish, while Poppy, who is taking a gap year, paid £11 for a Yorkshire pudding wrap. "I think it was pricey for what it was," Neve said. Poppy also felt she had not received much food for the money, although said it was tasty. Both said they enjoyed going into the city and looking around the markets, while Neve sympathised with traders, saying she thought the cost of renting space could force businesses to raise prices. Charlotte Whittle, director of CT Catering, has been trading at the markets for 10 years and now operates four stalls. She said each stall cost at least £1,000 a day to run, bringing her total daily operating costs to at least £4,000. Whittle, who employs a range of staff, said customers often underestimated the work and expense involved. Before the markets opened, her business spent two weeks preparing its stalls, with another two weeks needed to dismantle them after Christmas. CT Catering director Charlotte Whittle says her business employs 57 people across four Manchester market sites She said the costs included staff wages, accommodation, deliveries, storage, packaging and card payment fees. Parking three vans in Manchester city centre could cost £100 a day alone, she said, with the vehicles needed to replenish stock throughout busy trading periods. "They think that you're just selling cookies," she said. Whittle, who began her business selling homemade cakes at street food markets, said the cost of stock and packaging had increased significantly over the years. Although she had increased some prices, she said she had chosen to absorb part of those costs rather than risk putting customers off. "We've had to take a massive cut on profits," she said. She also argued that the standard of street food had improved and customers were receiving food comparable in quality to that served in restaurants. But not every trader has responded to rising costs by putting up prices. Clark Murphy, whose family has traded at the markets for 22 years, runs Mr Crimble Crumble, which sells fruit crumbles from two stalls. He said the business had kept most prices unchanged for three years and had reduced the cost of its largest portion by £2. Clark Murphy (left), pictured with his nephew Davis, said his business had reduced the price of its largest crumble Murphy said cooking oil and biodegradable packaging had become more expensive, but the business wanted to retain customers who returned each Christmas. "We haven't increased our prices for three years now," he said. A notice at one food stall offered customers £1 off each drink or dish if they paid in cash He said the business remained profitable, although margins were under pressure and card payments added to operating costs. At another food stall, a notice offered customers £1 off each drink or dish when paying cash. "Card fees are crazy – help us keep it simple," it said.

events.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
events.summary: Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption. The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected. The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide. Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent. Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers. Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday. By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America. Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge. Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost? Published 2 days ago Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world Published 2 days ago In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected , as were some schools and police forces. UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network. In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails. In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook. Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday. In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook. The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals. Pete says his business has been brought to a standstill Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill". His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations". Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that. "The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she said. "We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible." Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally. It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world. By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region. Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously." A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review. Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services. "The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure. Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

events.title: Food bank sees donations drop by 10% each year
events.summary: The year ending in 2024 saw a 9% drop, then another 13% in 2025, and finally a 6% drop in 2026 A food bank that has seen a drop in donations of about 10% each year since 2023 is hoping government stockpiling advice will not affect the public's generosity. Someone eats a meal provided by Cambridge City Foodbank "every two minutes" and it claims to have provided more than 260,000 in the past year. In October, the government launched its "Be Ready" campaign and encouraged households to stock up with enough non-perishable food and water to survive for three days in case of an emergency. Chief executive Steve Clay says he does not know if this will affect the Christmas appeal - their busiest period - but confesses: "It is a concern." A government spokesperson said it had "no serious evidence of stockpiling or indeed a supply shortage" with the campaign and it had worked with voluntary organisations and charities to address any concerns. Steve Clay, chief executive of Cambridge City Foodbank, said they had discussed the possibility that stockpiling would affect donations The food bank team estimates it will provide more than 45,000 meals to people in the city between 13 November and 15 January. Clay says that with cold weather and pressure on spending, Christmas is "more difficult" than the rest of the year. "Budgets are tighter, more has to be spent on fuel and energy," he said. "So people are contacting us all the time for emergency support and we need to make sure that the support is always there and is continuing to be there." Donations are used to purchase emergency hampers, treats or provide advice and assistance. While the food bank's doors close on Christmas Day, meals they have provided mean more people can enjoy the festivities. Every pound donated, up to the first £15,000, would be doubled as part of a match-funding commitment. Dr Liam Loftus, development director of the food bank, said: "As we head into winter and the cold draws in, thousands of individuals and families will be forced to make the heart-breaking choice between heating or eating. "This winter, can you take two minutes of your time to support our Winter Appeal? "You'll be helping restore hope and dignity to people facing hardship and providing one of your neighbours with their next meal at what should be one of the happiest times of year." The government spokesperson said of the Be Ready campaign: "We've worked hand-in-hand with voluntary organisations and charities, including food banks, to address any concerns and ensure the guidance is as accessible as possible. "Where households can act, that frees up emergency services to prioritise those most in-need during any emergency." Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below. events.summary: This week the Soil Association withdrew certification from organic salmon after 20 years. What went wrong? The first haul of farmed salmon in Britain was a relatively modest 14 tonnes, produced off the west coast of Scotland near Fort William in 1971. For Unilever, the vast multinational that pioneered salmon farming, it was a triumph after years of experimenting with how to cage fish, battle against diseases and cope with the wild weather. Unilever had spotted in the 1960s that farming salmon, which until then was caught wild and remained a relative luxury, would create a mass market, lower costs and provide steady profits. By 1976, it had expanded into three Scottish sites producing 116 tonnes of fish each year. Continue reading...

events.title: UAE Property: 'Should I waive the penalty if my tenant can no longer afford the rent?'
events.summary: Question: I own a one-bedroom apartment that I rent out. My tenant renewed only three months ago but has now lost his job and says he needs to leave the UAE . The tenancy contract says early termination requires two months' rent as a penalty. He has asked me to waive it because he has a family and says he genuinely cannot afford it. I'm sympathetic, but I'm also paying a mortgage and I'm worried the apartment could sit empty while I find another tenant. What would you do? Am I being foolish if I let him leave without enforcing the penalty? DH, Dubai Answer: There's the legal answer and then there's the answer I would give you after many years of dealing with landlords and tenants, and they aren't always exactly the same. Let's start with the contract. If you have an agreed early termination clause requiring two months' rent, that is the basis from which the two of you negotiate. A tenant losing their job doesn't automatically erase their contractual obligations. But of course, I wouldn't immediately turn this into a dispute . Ask the tenant when they realistically need to leave and whether they'll co-operate with viewings (presumably you will want to find an immediate replacement). Then, speak to a good local brokerage firm to establish how quickly the apartment could be re-let and at what level of rent. Suppose your existing tenant helps you secure a replacement who moves in immediately after he leaves. If you suffer little or no financial loss, insisting on the full two-month penalty may achieve very little other than making an already difficult situation for him worse. On the other hand, if the property is likely to sit vacant for six weeks and you'll incur cleaning, maintenance/preparation costs, or perhaps agency fees, it's therefore perfectly reasonable to negotiate compensation. If I had to be practical and you pressed me for my view, I would release him early provided he allows viewings , returns the apartment properly, settles utilities and rent up to the agreed handover date and perhaps pays a reduced termination amount if there's a genuine vacancy period. One piece of advice though: whatever you both decide ensure you put everything in writing. I've always believed the best landlord-and-tenant outcomes aren't necessarily the ones where somebody squeezes every last dirham out of the contract. They're the ones where both sides walk away feeling the agreement was fair. You have a mortgage to pay, so this isn't charity. But if you can replace the tenant quickly and help somebody through a genuinely difficult period without leaving yourself out of pocket, I'd call that sensible property management rather than weakness. Q: I own an apartment in Dubai that I bought as a long-term investment. My service charges have increased over the years, but the condition of the building seems to be going in the opposite direction. The gym has had broken equipment for months, there are regular problems with the lifts, the swimming pool has been closed several times and the common areas look tired. I don't mind paying reasonable service charges if the money is being spent properly, but as an individual owner I feel I have absolutely no influence. Can I refuse to pay until these issues are fixed, and how can I actually find out what I'm paying for? LM, Dubai A: Straight off the bat, I wouldn't refuse to pay. This puts you in a weak position and ultimately you will be falling foul of the law. Service charges in Dubai's jointly owned properties are regulated and the budgets are subject to Rera's approval. The charges can include security, cleaning, maintenance, utilities for common areas, insurance, management costs, master-community charges and contributions to any reserve funds. Your first step should therefore be to establish what the approved charge actually is. You can check this through the DLD Service Charge Index, Mollak or Dubai REST. DLD specifically states that management entities should not demand service charges before they have been approved by Rera. After you have thoroughly checked this out you can go ahead and separate the two issues of how much you're being charged and what standard of service you're receiving. A high service charge isn't automatically unreasonable if you're in a building with extensive facilities, cooling of common areas, several lifts, pools, landscaping and 24-hour security. But owners are entitled to question why facilities they are funding are not being fully maintained. Document the problems. Dates, photographs, emails and previous complaints are far more useful than simply saying the building is badly managed. Raise them formally with the management company first. If the standard of common-area maintenance remains unacceptable, DLD says owners can submit a complaint through Dubai REST using the Real Estate Violations System. From an investment perspective, I'd take this seriously. Poor building management doesn't just irritate residents, over time it can affect rents, tenant retention and of course resale values. Two identical apartments in neighbouring buildings can perform very differently simply because one building is well run and the other isn't. The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. Please send any questions to mario@evadxb.com

events.title: 'The line-up is huge': Australians caught up in US flight chaos
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australians stranded as US flight chaos grounds thousands of planes Adelaide woman Trish Crabb is stranded at JFK Airport in New York after thousands of flights were cancelled and delayed. ( Supplied: Trish Crabb ) A major air traffic control outage in the US has disrupted thousands of flights, leaving Australians stranded and warnings about global flow-on impacts, including international delays. Airlines are working to clear the backlog as US authorities investigate what caused the outage. Australians have been caught up in widespread flight disruptions across the United States after a communications outage forced aviation authorities to ground flights nationwide. More than 11,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, with passengers left stranded at airports across the country after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an unprecedented ground stop. The grounding has since been lifted, but airlines are warning it could take time to clear the backlog, with disruptions also affecting flights departing Australia for the US. Look back on our live blog for the latest on the issues affecting flights in the US and Australia. Sydney Airport said flights to the US would now resume from Mascot after being temporarily grounded on Saturday morning, and urged passengers to contact their airlines. The disruption has affected travellers at major airports including New York's JFK, Los Angeles International Airport and San Diego. Adelaide traveller Trish Crabb snapped this photograph while in line at JFK airport in New York. She was among thousands of travellers caught up in US flight cancellations. ( Supplied: Trish Crabb ) Trish Crabb, from Adelaide, was among those caught up in the chaos after her flight from New York to Miami was grounded. She and her husband were due to fly out of JFK Airport when they discovered their Delta flight had been cancelled. The couple are holidaying in the US and had planned to drive from Miami to Fort Lauderdale to board a cruise. "My husband is going to try and find us a hotel room somewhere close by, and hopefully we will be able to get a flight out at some stage," she said. Despite the disruption, Ms Crabb said passengers appeared to be keeping their composure. "Everyone was very calm," she said, adding most people were taking the situation in their stride. Rivkah Brown, from Myrtleford in Victoria, was stranded at San Diego Airport after her Delta flight was cancelled. Rivkah Brown from Victoria was stranded at San Diego Airport following a cruise in the US. She's now boarding a bus to get to Las Vegas. ( Supplied: Rivkah Brown ) Ms Brown had just disembarked from a cruise and was stopping over in San Diego before travelling to Las Vegas, where she was due to meet her fiancé. She said she would now take a bus to Las Vegas instead, a journey of almost 10 hours. "It's disappointing but it is what it is," Ms Brown said. The FAA ordered the nationwide ground stop on Friday, local time, after communications problems affecting air traffic control centres across the United States. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the issue was affected all Air Route Traffic Control Centres, with technicians investigating the cause. What we know about the US flight groundstop Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage. The FAA said the decision was made because of "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety". US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said preliminary investigations pointed to a telecommunications outage, with no immediate indication of a deliberate attack. "There's no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It's just a telecommunications outage as of right now," he said. The outage affected the 22 regional air traffic control centres responsible for directing aircraft between airports across the country. At least 600 flights had been diverted, including aircraft sent back to their departure airports or redirected elsewhere. The order to ground all departing US flights was finally lifted after more than five hours. ( AP Photo: Tony Gutierrez ) About 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to depart US airports after 4pm Eastern time on Friday. Planes already in the air were able to continue to their destinations, with authorities prioritising their safe landing. The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a computer system failure at the FAA caused thousands of delays.

events.title: 'Plastic farmers' in Indonesia unaware of the dangers of burning waste
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Researchers investigate health impact of burning plastic waste in Indonesia Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Plastic waste was regularly burned in limestone kilns in Sumberejo, a village in East Java. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Ahmad Yani spent hours each day sifting through piles of rubbish, searching for recyclable materials to sell to help make ends meet. For decades, his family and other people in his village in East Java, in Indonesia, would buy truckloads of waste residue from factories recycling imported paper and cardboard. They would spread the waste on the ground, and separate plastics from paper and cardboard. The paper would be sold back to the recycling factories and most of the plastics to industries that needed fuel for furnaces. "It had become a source of livelihood for many low-income residents," Mr Yani said, adding he would make about 300,000 rupiah ($24) a month. Any plastics still left over would be used in his village to fire limestone kilns, to produce building materials to sell or use. Ahmad Yani says plastic waste from overseas has been coming to his village for decades. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Mr Yani said among the rubbish he noticed food sachets and cat and dog food packaging with Australian labels, as well as labels of countries in Europe. While burning plastic has helped support the family's livelihood, the smoke from their home and neighbouring households may be having a devastating impact on health. Mr Yani said some people he knew who had operated the limestone kilns had died from respiratory diseases and causes were never determined. He said the burning of plastics in his village was no longer happening. It stopped about a year ago. Several local media reported companies had stopped distributing waste to his community to sort, which had sparked anger among locals who lost their source of income. The ABC couldn't independently verify the reasons for the change. But health concerns for people who have been exposed to air pollution from burning plastics remain. Women sort through waste in East Java. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Researchers from the Climate and Health Centre at Brawijaya University were investigating the health effects of air pollution in East Java when they found locals were burning plastic waste. One of the researchers, Sekar Aqila Salsabilla, said pre-screening tests earlier this year on those in their study produced some worrying findings. She said at least 20 per cent of the more than 4,000 participants across six East Java villages were at high risk of cardiovascular disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Sekar Aqila Salsabilla has been researching the health effects of air pollution in villages in East Java. ( Supplied: Sekar Aqila Salsabilla ) "When we first entered these communities, one of the most distressing findings was that many people were unaware of the dangers associated with burning plastic waste," said Ms Salsabilla, who, as part of a broader study, worked with more than 30 researchers, the majority of whom had medical backgrounds. People earning money from sorting waste, known as "plastic farmers", knew their health was "slowly declining" but did not understand the source of the problems, she said. "Despite the income they generate, many do not realise that the long-term health burden they may face is likely to be far greater than the money they earn from handling and burning this waste," Ms Salsabilla said. Environmental activists say Australian plastic waste was in this rubbish heap in East Java, Indonesia, in 2024. ( Supplied: Ecoton ) Most plastic waste was no longer burned in people's homes but rather converted into refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and burned in a designated facility, she said. "But I think this only relocates the problem rather than actually solving it," Ms Salsabilla said, adding the facility still required humans to sort the waste. Emissions from open waste burning, such as burning plastics, include a variety of air pollutants, some of which have particularly harmful effects on both the climate and health, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). "Exposure to these pollutants, whether short or long-term, can lead to adverse health effects such as coughing, skin irritation, respiratory diseases, and other negative outcomes," the WHO says on its website. Environmentalists say plastic waste from Australia is often found in East Java. ( Supplied: Ecoton ) Ms Salsabilla said the waste imported to East Java was coming from places including Australia, the US and Europe.

events.title: India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain
events.summary: India has set an ambitious goal to install enough clean energy to power over 1 billion homes by 2035 BENGALURU, India -- With the United Nations climate talks underway, India has set an ambitious goal of installing enough clean power to supply more than 1 billion homes by 2035, and has approved nearly $20 billion in power grid upgrades to ease bottlenecks that prevent some solar and wind energy from reaching consumers. The world's most populous country and one of the biggest carbon polluters is also among the fastest to expand clean power. Accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels is a key goal of this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, in Turkey. India announced the 900-gigawatt goal in late September. It covers nonfossil power sources, including solar, wind, hydropower and nuclear energy. It is nearly twice India’s existing target of 500 gigawatts of clean power by 2030. India's current clean power capacity of just over 300 gigawatts ranks it third behind China and the United States. Experts say meeting the target could lower electricity costs, curb coal construction and accelerate the transition to clean energy. The push comes as India struggles to use all the renewable electricity it can generate because of inadequate transmission infrastructure . The new goal refers to installed generating capacity, rather than the amount of electricity actually produced. “If the grid doesn’t catch up, then there is no way India can meet this target,” Nikit Abhyankar from the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley, said. “A robust and innovative transmission grid is an absolute must.” The government also approved nearly $20 billion in funding for transmission infrastructure and battery storage under its Green Energy Corridor plan. Economist Ajay Shah of the Mumbai-based XKDR Forum described the transition as the emergence of an Indian “electrostate,” in which electricity increasingly replaces coal and petroleum products. “So now in India you have two assets — not only do you have cheap labor, you also have cheap energy,” Shah said. The shift mirrors a global trend toward cleaner power, even as fossil fuel energy remains a key energy source amid rising electricity demand. Brazil, which ranks close behind India in clean energy capacity, projects renewables will supply nearly 90% of its electricity in the next decade, even as it expands oil and gas production. In the United States, where President Donald Trump supports fossil fuels, electricity demand is expected to grow by 40%, with natural gas remaining a major source. India’s clean energy expansion could help industries replace costly imported fossil fuels with domestically produced electricity. Abhyankar said solar and wind power, even when combined with battery storage, are increasingly cost-competitive with power from coal, oil and natural gas. Lower generation costs could eventually translate into cheaper electricity for households, though utilities also factor in transmission costs and other expenses. However, India’s continued dependence on coal presents a major challenge to its clean energy transition. Coal generated about 71% of the country’s electricity in 2025, according to energy think tank Ember. India’s power planners remain concerned about meeting growing demand and maintaining reliable electricity when solar and wind output fluctuates. Ghanshyam Prasad, chair of the Central Electricity Authority, said earlier this month that India could need as much as 150 gigawatts of additional coal-fired generating capacity by 2035. Ember energy analyst Neshwin Rodrigues said coal will remain important for years, particularly until large-scale batteries can store solar energy to reliably meet demand when the sun isn't shining. Existing coal plants also pose operational challenges. Many cannot quickly reduce output when renewable electricity becomes available, making it difficult for the grid to accommodate growing solar and wind power. events.title: FAA ends hours-long nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday night after hours of chaos and thousands of delays and cancellations. Why it matters: The effects of the rare and extreme move will likely ripple through the weekend, with travelers stranded and airlines' planes and crews out of position. Driving the news: In a Friday evening press conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was issued after outdated air traffic control communications equipment suffered from "overloaded data, and they went down." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin added that officials are looking into incompatibilities between that older equipment and newer technology currently being installed. Mullin added that there's no evidence that the problems were tied to a cyberattack. Yes, but: Duffy and Mullin didn't specify the exact initial cause of the problems. "We're still working on the details of what went wrong today," Duffy said. Duffy spent much of the press conference pushing Congress for more funding for air traffic control upgrades. "I can't build things if I don't have money," he told reporters at the White House briefing room. He later added that similar problems could occur again without more funding. Catch up quick: The FAA initially issued the stop due to "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety." "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the agency said in an earlier statement after the ground stop was issued. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates." Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often simply called "centers," mostly handle high-altitude en route airspace between airports. Between the lines: The FAA has been rolling out a new AI tool designed to help manage airspace congestion, but it's unclear if that system has any connection to Friday's communication issues. The developer of that tool denied any connection. By the numbers: As of 9 p.m. ET, FlightAware reported more than 6,000 cancellations over the course of the day Friday. Many travelers are stuck at the airport or on their planes on the tarmac Friday evening. Editor's note: This story has been updated with details from a press briefing.

events.title: FAA lifts rare nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The FAA on Friday lifted a rare nationwide ground stop that impacted more than 14,500 flights after a major outage affecting the US’ air communications system. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed “an incredibly old air traffic control system,” and said the government didn’t suspect any nefarious causes, such as a terrorist or cyber attack. He said the issues were connected to old equipment that was overloaded, and that flights should start taking off again over the next day. “Hopefully tomorrow, we are going to start to see far better movement,” he said, while trying to reassure travelers that the US remains “the safest system in the world.” The stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, caused widespread disruption and prompted shares in airlines to drop. American Airlines shares dropped more than 2% in after-hours trading, while United shares fell 1.6%. Those airlines are now navigating thousands of rebookings and frustrated passengers. This is only the third time the agency has ever issued such an order. The most recent was in January 2023; before that, air traffic was halted nationwide on Sept. 11, 2001. Duffy used a large portion of a press conference on Friday evening to blame the Republican-controlled Congress for withholding funds for air-traffic control repairs. He urged lawmakers to approve $50 billion to upgrade infrastructure through an emergency funding bill. “I’ve asked, the president’s asked for $30 billion. I want $50 billion,” Duffy said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Albanese, Bowen caught talking phones and 'dicks' in hot-mic gaffe
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts PM Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen caught on hot mic at COP31 climate summit A private exchange between Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen was inadvertently recorded at the COP31 summit in Türkiye. The prime minister's office said the pair were joking between meetings, but the Coalition has criticised the hot mic moment as "weird and gross". Mr Albanese has travelled to the Philippines for the ASEAN summit, while Mr Bowen remains in Türkiye. A conversation between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen about phone radiation and "dicks" has been caught on camera on the sidelines of a UN conference. The Coalition has criticised the hot mic moment as "weird and gross", accusing the pair of behaving like "14-year-old schoolboys". Mr Albanese's office said the pair was sharing a "joke" between meetings when the exchange was recorded by Australian media at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye. The comments were captured shortly before a business roundtable spruiking renewable energy transition investment opportunities in Australia began overnight on Friday. Anthony Albanese left Türkiye shortly after a business roundtable. ( AAP ) Cameras were rolling ahead of the event, during which time Mr Albanese and Mr Bowen were privately chatting to each other. Mr Albanese put his phone in his jacket pocket and — as he did so — told Mr Bowen he had heard it was better to store the device away from the heart because "it can interfere with your rhythm". Mr Bowen responded in a joking tone, asking if it was because the phone was "a little bit radioactive". The prime minister laughed, saying the idea "makes absolute sense". Mr Bowen then responded he was more conscious about putting his phone in his pants pocket. Mr Albanese asked, "Because of your dick?" The pair laughed and Mr Bowen agreed, adding it was "arguably more important than the heart". On Sunday, Liberal deputy leader Jane Hume said the gaffe undermined Labor's message about pitching Australia to the world on climate. "It's bad enough that these guys sent almost 200 bureaucrats to Türkiye at a cost of more than $2 million and spent $36,000 [sic] of your taxpayer money on a coffee cart so that Greta Thunberg could have a free latte, but they justified it on the basis they were 'selling Australia to the world', 'attracting investment from overseas'," she said. "Well, great salesmen you clowns are. "The only thing you've attracted to Australia is ridicule on the world stage." Hot-mic gaffe came ahead of roundtable The exchange, which did not appear to be overheard by anyone in the room but was captured by a news camera microphone preparing to record the opening remarks at the event, was later broadcast by Channel 7 after it was noticed in production. A spokesperson for Mr Albanese's office said, "They were having a joke in between meetings." Labor frontbencher Murray Watt agreed that the comments were made in jest. "This is really just about people having a joke," he said. Mr Watt laughed off a question about where he kept his own phone, and defended Australia's presence and performance at COP31. "I know there's been a lot of criticism from some quarters about every aspect of this COP, but the reality is participating in and in fact leading the discussions at COP is in Australia's national interest," he said. During the official proceedings of the business roundtable, the prime minister made a pitch to international investors to back Australia's clean energy transition. "If you're an investor, there's nowhere you'd rather be than Australia," he said. Mr Albanese said having abundant renewable resources, critical minerals and a stable investment environment meant Australia was well placed to capitalise on the multi-trillion-dollar industry. The prime minister left Türkiye shortly after the roundtable to travel to the Philippines for the ASEAN summit in Manila. Mr Bowen has remained in Antalya, where he is playing a critical role as the co-president of negotiations for COP31. events.title: Mississippi River cruise crash has no fatalities, critical injuries
events.summary: Thirty-two people are in local hospitals and all passengers and crew are accounted for after a tanker collided with a Mississippi River cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans , officials said Friday. The big picture: With approximately 180 people on the ship, the rescue of all aboard is "truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a press conference. What they're saying: While the investigation remains ongoing, officials said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker appeared to have lost control, causing it to collide with the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking after the collision, the cruise ship began to sink and eventually toppled over and flipped — leaving people in the cold water. Video from the scene shows passengers, in life preservers, swimming in the river toward safety. The first 87 passengers got off while the ship was still afloat, Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. She added it "was normal conditions" on the river and that there wasn't a high current, despite how notoriously challenging that stretch of the Mississippi River usually is. "The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said. He added, "I've never been prouder of a group of people than those people that came off of that boat." Catch up quick: The American Heritage, a vessel operated by American Cruise Lines, had docked for passengers to disembark at the port Friday afternoon about two hours before it was hit, according to a press release from the Port of New Orleans. A city spokesman confirmed to Axios that the riverboat had rolled onto its side in the water, which social media videos appear to corroborate. Zoom out: The Atlantic Asphalt tanker is registered in the Marshall Islands, and had arrived at the Port of New Orleans on Nov. 11. Per data from myshiptracking.com, the tanker began its current journey in Paulsboro, New Jersey, in late October. Zoom in: The tanker was immobilized on the river Friday at about 2pm CT, with two tugs positioned on either side. Another dozen vessels were in the water nearby as a helicopter roamed overhead and sirens rang out over the water. Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

events.title: Questions remain after Nvidia CEO's departure
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Despite Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, questions remain over the whole affair Jensen Huang was one of the world's most influential figures in the tech and AI industry. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) Mounting speculation over an espionage plot against Jensen Huang and his multiple alleged affairs reached a tipping point on Friday, when the tech billionaire quit as Nvidia's CEO. The controversy centred around his relationship with Alice Huang, who US intelligence reportedly suspects to be a Chinese spy, before claims emerged he had another two extra-marital affairs. While Mr Huang's resignation puts an end to his long reign over Nvidia, questions about America's national security and the US president's knowledge of the whole saga remain. China's foreign ministry said allegations of spying in relation to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang (no relation) were "unsubstantiated" and "smears against China". ( Reuters: CTI ) When reports of an espionage plot against Mr Huang first emerged almost a week ago, top Republicans called on the tech executive to front Congress later this month. Senator Tim Scott reiterated those demands after Mr Huang's resignation, saying there were "serious concerns" to address. Separately the chairs of three House committees — the foreign affairs panel, the China select committee and the intelligence committee — wrote to Mr Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter requiring them to appear for closed-door transcribed interviews on December 1 and 2. After news broke of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset Nvidia's value plummeted. Why? Mr Huang and Mr Teter have not publicly commented on the requests, but they could face subpoenas to compel their appearances. "There are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three committee chairs wrote in the letter. Mr Huang is also yet to comment publicly after reports emerged he allegedly had another two extra-marital affairs — both with Nvidia employees. His last statement was on Sunday, local time, when he admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife of over 40 years but did not name who he had been intimate with. In that statement, he said he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security". Meanwhile, Nvidia and Mr Huang are facing a ‌proposed class action accusing them ‌of ⁠defrauding ‌shareholders . Questions for the US administration Next to Mr Huang, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been called on to testify in front of Congress on concerns he did not do enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China. In December 2025 Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to China in exchange for a cut of the sales, after Mr Huang argued that restrictions only accelerated Beijing's own AI development. That was despite concerns from both sides of Congress about China's access to the technology. Howard Lutnick is facing pressure over whether the US government was properly overseeing Nvidia's exports to China. ( Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz ) Mr Lutnick has also been criticised for the administration's refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a trade blacklist. In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration had held ⁠off adding more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the list. The US ⁠has not added to the list since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in more than a decade. Previous reports said that Mr Lutnick's US Commerce Department had not blacklisted new Chinese companies for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China. Under-Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler has been called on to testify at a December 3 hearing as well. The Commerce Department did not respond to Reuters' request for comment. In America's pursuit to lead the AI race, Mr Huang had become a close ally of Mr Trump and was one of the few people known to have a direct line to him. He has visited the White House at least five times during Mr Trump's second term, is part of a council advising the president on science and technology, and accompanied Mr Trump on a trip to Beijing in May. The Washington Post reported in mid-October that Nvidia committed $US25 million ($36.7 million) for Mr Trump's contentious White House ballroom project, while the president disclosed buying and selling Nvidia stock earlier this year. The New York Times reported Mr Trump was briefed on intelligence findings about a suspected espionage effort against Mr Huang about a year ago, and took no action.

Yothu Yindi manager Alan James says travel costs will put emerging artists out of business before their careers have taken off. With the cost of regional airfares soaring, musicians and band managers say touring has become untenable for both famous bands and emerging artists from regional Australia. An interim Productivity Commission report released this week revealed a significant price gap between regional and metropolitan flight routes. It found long regional and remote flights cost 67 per cent more on average than major city routes, while short regional flights cost 173 per cent more per kilometre. Alan James says high airfares are pricing Yothu Yindi "out of the market" for live music. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Yothu Yindi manager Alan James said the cost of travel had forced the internationally-renowned band from Arnhem Land to turn down shows within Australia. "It's $5,200 return from Gove to Brisbane, it would be cheaper for us to go do a concert in London than it would be to do a concert in a capital city of Australia," he said. Yothu Yindi bassist Stuart Kellaway — who now manages fellow Arnhem Land rock band King Stingray — said the next generation band's recent flights to shows in the United States cost less than domestic flights. Yothu Yindi played the 2025 Garma Festival but had to turn down shows interstate. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) "We've had to turn down three or four shows in the past month or so because it just wasn't going to work financially with the airfare components," he said. Mr Kellaway the sky-high airfares were affecting the ability even of artists in the prime of their careers to make a living. "With streaming and everything else, gigs are one of the last, decent income streams for bands," he said. Limited options limiting opportunities Mr James said while all bands were impacted by the exorbitant airfares, for new artists in particular, the costs could make sustainable careers in the music industry impossible. "If you're an emerging group, you've got no shot, you're out of the business," he said. "It really means for musicians, if you're not based in a capital city, then you're not in the market anymore." King Stingray manager Stuart Kellaway (third from left) says bands based outside capital cities are "not in the market anymore". ( ABC / Matt Garrick ) Both Mr James and Mr Kellaway said they had noticed a decline in the number of airlines servicing Arnhem Land throughout the course of Yothu Yindi's career. Their observations align with the findings of the Productivity Commission's report, which noted competition in regional aviation was severely limited. Several airlines have reduced NT services recently, leaving flights between Darwin and capitals such as Sydney, Adelaide and Canberra serviced only by Qantas and its subsidiary Jetstar. In a statement, a Qantas spokesperson said rising costs had dramatically influenced the price of tickets in and out of the NT. "Aviation costs, including labour, airport charges and government air traffic control fees, are rising faster than the rate of inflation, while fuel costs also remain significantly higher," they said. "Great value fares can still be found on flights to and from the Northern Territory and we encourage customers to book ahead whenever possible to secure the best fare." events.title: Nvidia’s next CEO: Some prediction market traders bet Jensen Huang will make a comeback
events.summary: Nvidia has yet to name a permanent successor to Jensen Huang, with some in the industry calling him irreplaceable. Some Kalshi traders bet Nvidia may rehire Jensen Huang as permanent CEO by 2028, even after his Nov 12 resignation. Ian Buck leads the market at 33%. Huang stepped down after reports of three affairs and admitted ties to Alice Huang, who is suspected by the US of spying for China. Supporters, including Shaun Maguire, Elon Musk and Donald Trump, praised him as vital to AI leadership. Nvidia faces big risks because it has no succession plan and 60 executives report to Huang. Shares rebounded after the shock exit, but Washington scrutiny and investor concern remain. SINGAPORE – Jensen Huang has stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive , but some traders on the prediction market Kalshi are betting that the chipmaker will name him its next permanent CEO before 2029. Nvidia has yet to name a permanent successor to one of the AI industry’s most influential leaders, with some in the industry calling him irreplaceable. On Kalshi, which is regulated in the US but banned in Singapore, the implied odds of Nvidia naming Huang as its next permanent chief executive by the end of 2028 rose as high as 15% on the evening of Nov 13, before falling to around 7%. Nvidia executive Ian Buck is currently in the lead, with a 33% chance on Kalshi of becoming Nvidia’s next CEO. Buck is vice-president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing at Nvidia. He leads its multibillion-dollar data centre business, which supplies AI chips and software to major tech companies worldwide. Kalshi put the odds of Colette Kress getting the permanent job at 13%. Kress is Nvidia’s chief financial officer and was made interim CEO following Huang’s resignation on Nov 12. She is tied with Rene Haas, chief executive of British chip design company Arm Holdings. Other executives Kalshi traders are betting on include Apple chief hardware officer Johny Srouji, Palo Alto Networks chairman and CEO Nikesh Arora, Nvidia executive vice-president Jay Puri, and AMD chairman and CEO Lisa Su. Puri oversees Nvidia’s global sales, business development and partnerships. Tech executives, investors and fans have voiced support for Huang, who stepped down following reports of three affairs. He has admitted to being involved with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based, Alibaba-backed data centre firm Megaspeed . She is suspected by the US of spying for China. “Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, wrote in an X post on Nov 8. He concluded that Nvidia’s Huang is “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership”. About an hour later, Elon Musk quoted the post, noting: “I agree.” Maguire added on Nov 12 that Huang’s ousting “will leave a huge void, with the loss of a technical, aggressive, founder-CEO. “The American AI community needs to work double-time in an attempt to fill this void.” Even US President Donald Trump called Huang before he stepped down, urging him to keep fighting for his job , according to The New York Times, quoting sources familiar with the call. After Huang announced his resignation, Trump wrote in a Nov 12 Truth Social post : “Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – Tim Cook of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!” On prediction market Polymarket, trading implied a 6% chance that Nvidia would name Apple executive chairman Tim Cook as its next permanent chief executive by the end of 2028. There is also a 11% probability on Polymarket that Nvidia does not find a CEO by Dec 31, 2028. Regardless of who takes over, Nvidia’s stakes are high because so much of the AI industry relies on chips, delivered by a company that Huang co-founded, transformed and led for the past 30 years. A total of 60 executives across the firm report directly to him, and there is no succession plan. Huang’s departure therefore leaves Nvidia investors weighing several risks, Saxo UK investor strategist Neil Wilson said in a Nov 13 note. Nvidia is “about to find out whether Huang’s grip on the company and flat organisational structure was effectively storing up trouble”, said Wilson. While a successor could keep Nvidia on the same course, Huang’s detailed knowledge of its products and his hands-on management style is unique and would be hard to replicate. Wilson also pointed to scrutiny in Washington, citing reported US Justice Department inquiries involving Megaspeed and Alice Huang, and a request by three House committee chairs for a closed-door briefing on Nov 18 over national security concerns. He expects Nvidia’s relationship with Washington to become more difficult, even with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s support. Investors, however, appear to think otherwise.
